articles.title: Binance Says 90% of Assets Replenished After $6.3B Hack
articles.text:
Binance says 90% of stolen assets replenished, targets Sunday withdrawals
Less-liquid tokens make up the remaining shortfall as Binance continues buying replacement assets through market and over-the-counter trades.
Binance said Saturday it had replenished 90% of the assets stolen in its $6.3 billion hack, up from 80% a day earlier, and remained on track to resume withdrawals Sunday.
The exchange is using a combination of its corporate treasury, a partial deployment of its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and a portion of its futures insurance fund, a spokesperson told Cointelegraph.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not users,” the spokesperson said, adding that the insurance fund would remain above required risk management levels.
The update follows Thursday’s theft, the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, which TRM Labs has since attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacker group.
Following the hack, Binance said Friday it had set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses, including $5 billion in the affected cryptocurrencies. Industry partners like Tether and Circle froze about $3 billion in affected assets after the hack, but those funds are separate from Binance’s replacement of stolen tokens.
Still, CertiK told Cointelegraph on Friday that it needed more information to verify Binance’s claimed $5 billion in replacement cryptocurrencies. Binance has since published a new reserves snapshot, but says the full cryptographic proof is still being generated. “The full zero-knowledge proof takes approximately 40 to 50 hours to generate due to the computational workload,” the exchange’s update reads.
Binance said in its update on X that customer balances in Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and eight other assets were fully backed. The remaining shortfall consists of less liquid tokens that it continues to buy through market and over-the-counter transactions, the update reads.
The spokesperson’s statement did not specify how much each funding source contributed or disclose the insurance fund’s minimum required balance. It also did not quantify how much stolen crypto had been recovered.
Read Cointelegraph’s full coverage of the Binance hack here.
Magazine: Binance hackers raced to move billions before it could be frozen

articles.title: Jupiter Lend’s withdrawal liquidity rebounds from near zero to 29 million USDC
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Jupiter Lend reported about 29 million USDC withdrawable in liquidity data last updated at 09:25:56 UTC on October 31.
- Available USDC represented about 6.6% of reported total assets of 443 million USDC.
- Jupiter's withdrawal rules depend on both dynamic ceilings and available unlent funds, leaving full exits sensitive to pool liquidity.
Jupiter Lend's reported USDC withdrawal liquidity stood at about 29 million USDC in a 09:25:56 UTC reading on Oct. 31, easing the immediate cash constraint at Jupiter's lending product after near-zero availability the previous afternoon.
Bitquery reported that only $88.89 of USDC was free to withdraw at 16:18 UTC on Oct. 30, against $416 million owed to Jupiter Lend's USDC savers. The October 31 reading indicates a substantial increase in reported funds available for exits.
An earlier API snapshot captured the initial overnight recovery:
The official Earn API reported about 31.23 million USDC withdrawable, with its liquidity data last updated at 02:37:21 UTC on Oct. 31. It also reported approximately 445.77 million USDC in total assets. Available withdrawal liquidity therefore represented about 7.01% of those assets.
By 09:25:56 UTC, the API showed about 29 million USDC withdrawable against 443 million USDC in total assets. Available funds were about 6.6% of total assets. These balances measure withdrawal capacity; Bitquery’s amount owed to savers describes depositor claims.
The improvement marks partial recovery in withdrawal capacity.
Why withdrawal limits do not guarantee cash
Jupiter's documentation describes two constraints on immediate withdrawals: dynamic ceilings that control how quickly funds can leave, and the liquidity actually available. The latter consists of assets that have not been lent to borrowers.
The ceilings adjust over time, limiting the pace at which supplied funds become eligible for withdrawal. Even when a ceiling permits a withdrawal, the pool must have enough available liquidity to meet it. A larger allowance therefore cannot, by itself, remove a shortage of unlent funds.
In the 09:25:56 UTC reading, the API showed about 221 million USDC in withdrawableUntilLimit, compared with 29 million USDC in withdrawable. The larger field should not be mistaken for immediately available cash. Jupiter’s mechanics documentation explains the general ceiling constraint, without explicitly defining those API field names.
For a depositor seeking a full exit, the available balance remains consequential. Jupiter says users may need to wait for borrower repayments or new deposits when most of an asset is borrowed.
The October 31 figures show more reported room for withdrawals than Friday's near-zero reading. Sustained access still depends on the funds available as withdrawals, repayments and deposits change the pool's balance.

articles.title: Bitcoin Holds Up After Binance Hack, Strive CEO Says
articles.text:
Bitcoin held up better than expected after Binance hack, Strive CEO says
Strive CEO Matt Cole says the Binance hack has not changed his long-term case for Bitcoin, but cautions it is too early to call a market bottom.
Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis.
Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction on Friday, Cole said the breach had not changed his long-term investment case for Bitcoin. He compared the attack on Binance’s wallets to a bank robbery rather than a failure of Bitcoin’s network.
Bitcoin traded near $77,400 at 4:00 pm on Saturday, about 4% below its price shortly before the attack began Thursday, according to CoinGecko data.
Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct. 23.
“I do have conviction that over any reasonable time frame, this does not change the investment thesis on Bitcoin,” Cole said.
Cole said Bitcoin’s decline was less severe than he expected given the scale of the breach and broader market weakness, although he acknowledged that it was too early to determine whether the cryptocurrency had reached a price bottom.
Cole described the market as being in an “early spring” recovery phase that could last another six to nine months, with prices gradually rising rather than surging to new highs.
Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network. “It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph.
Related: Strive closes $630M SATS IPO, leaves Bitcoin allocation unspecified
Bitcoin reaction compared with Bybit
According to Glassnode, Thursday’s Binance breach was the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, with around $6.3 billion affected, exceeding the combined losses from the next nine largest hacks. The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025.
Glassnode said three of the 10 largest crypto hacks have occurred since the beginning of 2025, all involving exchanges.
Binance hack exceeds the next nine largest crypto exploits combined. Source: Glassnode
By comparison, following the Bybit hack in 2025, Bitcoin fell roughly 5% from nearly $100,000 to around $95,000 amid the breach and broader market volatility, according to a Bitfinex market report.
Anchorage Digital data cited by CNBC put Bitcoin’s average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%.
Binance hack exposes exchange security vulnerabilities
Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan said the attackers appeared to have compromised Binance’s transaction signing process. Binance said Friday that it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys, though its investigation remained ongoing.
Blockaid’s analysis identified an Ethereum transaction containing 50 signed authorizations covering different transaction counts. A matching authorization allowed attacker-controlled code to operate through the wallet. Ben-Natan argued that checks before signing could have blocked the malicious authorization.
Magazine: Tampered Ledger reported in Singapore a month before news broke: Asia Express

articles.title: Binance Hack: Everything You Need to Know About the Biggest Crypto Heist in History - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Attackers stole roughly $6.4 billion from Binance on Thursday in the largest crypto hack ever, more than four times the previous record.
- Binance says it will cover all losses with company funds and its emergency reserve, having set aside more than $6.34 billion.
- Here's how it happened and what's being done about it.
Crypto just suffered the largest hack in its history.
On Thursday, attackers drained roughly $6.4 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a breach that dwarfs every theft before it and has triggered a cross-border law-enforcement investigation, a scramble by stablecoin issuers to freeze funds, and a tense wait for millions of users.
Here’s what’s known about the Binance hack so far.
What happened
The theft began at about 4:05 p.m. ET on Thursday, after U.S. markets had closed, when attackers moved funds out of Binance hot wallets across roughly 10 blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes.
Blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and TRM Labs put the total at around $6.4 billion, more than four times the previous record, February 2025’s $1.5 billion Bybit heist.
Crucially, the attack targeted Binance’s own infrastructure, not the blockchains themselves. Binance initially traced the breach to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which may have let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals.
The exchange has since said its investigation uncovered “additional points of breach,” with CEO Richard Teng describing “a more complex attack process” that “did not simply use one engineer’s permissions.” Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that the attacker used a self-destruct mechanism to wipe tooling and traces along the way.
The Ethereum wrinkle
On Ethereum, the attacker leaned on EIP-7702, a feature introduced in 2025 that lets ordinary wallets temporarily run smart-contract code.
Using 50 pre-signed authorizations, the attacker turned a Binance hot wallet into a “sweeper” contract and drained its assets, according to TRM Labs.
Teng said that delegation “did not pass through our normal approval controls.” The episode didn’t expose a flaw in Ethereum itself, but rather, TRM said, pointed to a compromise of Binance’s signing infrastructure.
Who’s behind it
TRM Labs and Chainalysis both attributed the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked group also blamed for the Bybit heist.
After that attack, the group converted roughly 84% of the stolen Ethereum into Bitcoin via the cross-chain network Thorchain. The attribution pushes North Korea’s 2026 crypto haul well past $1 billion, and the Binance figure alone would dwarf the rest.
What Binance is doing
Teng said Binance will cover every dollar of the losses with company funds and its Secure Asset Fund for Users, an emergency reserve, stressing that customer assets were never touched.
The exchange has set aside more than $6.34 billion, about $5 billion of it already held in the exact tokens stolen, including BTC, ETH, BNB, USDC, and USDT, and is buying the rest on the open market and over the counter.
Binance paused withdrawals to rebuild and retest its systems, is running a full security review, and aims to restore withdrawals by Sunday while publishing a complete proof of reserves by Monday. Deposits are operating normally.
The freeze, and what’s still loose
Stablecoin issuers moved fast following the initial reports of a suspected attack, unlike previous security incidents.
Stablecoins are the backbone of the crypto economy—dollar-pegged tokens designed to hold a steady value that enable quick and easy transactions on both centralized and decentralized exchanges. Unlike traditional digital currencies, like Bitcoin or Ethereum, stablecoins are centralized, issued and managed by private companies. That means these funds can be frozen at any time, and for any reason.
Tether, the company behind the biggest stablecoin on the market USDT, froze more than $1.5 billion in assets. Circle, which issues the second largest stablecoin USDC, froze around $823 million tied to the attack, both using their ability to blacklist specific addresses.
In all, roughly $3 billion has been frozen or located. But a large sum remains beyond reach: the attacker still controls more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, plus other tokens, worth over $3 billion that no issuer can freeze, and has kept shuffling funds through Tron and other networks. Security firm Elliptic estimated the hacker still controls around $3.3 billion.
The investigation
Binance is cooperating with law enforcement worldwide, including the FBI and the U.S. Secret Service.
The FBI confirmed it was aware of the incident and coordinating with partners; the Secret Service, which investigates financial and digital-currency crimes, declined to comment.
It echoes earlier joint efforts like April’s Operation Atlantic, which traced tens of millions in stolen crypto.
How markets reacted
For a theft of this scale, markets stayed remarkably composed.
Bitcoin fell to about $76,400 on Friday, down roughly 4%, and more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated.
That’s a far cry from March 2018, when a failed attack on Binance knocked nearly 11% off Bitcoin in minutes. Analysts credit a bigger, more mature market, now worth around $2.6 trillion, with spot Bitcoin ETFs holding roughly 1.3 million BTC in hands that don’t panic-sell.
Wall Street firms including Cantor Fitzgerald, TD Cowen, and Compass Point even urged clients to buy crypto-linked stocks on the weakness, framing the hack as a Binance security failure rather than a threat to the underlying technology.
The fallout
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig seized on the breach to argue offshore exchanges need U.S. oversight. Selig said in an interview with CNBC that the breach “proves our exact point” behind the crypto-market regulations the agency proposed earlier this month.
And the episode sparked a public spat between Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, better known as CZ, and Elon Musk. The SpaceX and Tesla founder appeared to troll Binance over the hack on X, and CZ fired back, citing Musk’s own SpaceX stake. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support," CZ posted.
CZ struck a defiant note overall: the theft is the largest in dollar terms, he said, but not in Bitcoin terms, and unlike Mt. Gox or FTX, Binance is absorbing the loss itself.
“It hurts, but we survive,” he wrote.

articles.title: Crypto Today: Binance $6.3B record hack sparks pre-election political clashes
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto: Soon after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, some political and administration figures began offering their opinions with a US election approaching on Nov. 3 and voting already having begun in many locations. Coinbase led a selloff in crypto-linked stocks following Binance’s record-breaking $6.3 billion hack, and Binance said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover losses from the attack.
Binance hack sparks pre-election political clashes
Soon after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, the biggest in crypto history, some political and administration figures began offering their opinions with a US election approaching on Nov. 3 and voting already having begun in many locations.
President Donald Trump was asked at a news conference on Friday about the hack of Binance. “We don’t know. We’re looking at that, the hack with Binance. They’re saying they’re going to get it back, they’re saying they’re guaranteeing it,” he replied.
The crypto exchange said in a post on X late Friday that it would cover any losses. “We want to be clear about our commitment: Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users.” It added that about $3 billion of the stolen funds had already been frozen in various locations. On Saturday, Binance said it had already covered 90% of the impacted amount of the hacked loss.
It was not clear whether there was any immediate political advantage to be gained from the hack, which was widely attributed to a North Korean group, but Republican and Democratic sides began staking out positions almost immediately.
Coinbase leads crypto stock selloff following $6.3 billion Binance hack
Shares of publicly traded cryptocurrency companies fell sharply Friday, with Coinbase dropping more than 13% a day after reporting a decline in third-quarter revenue, as the industry dealt with Binance’s $6.3 billion hack.
Other crypto-linked stocks also declined, with stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group (CRCL) falling more than 9% and Bitcoin treasury company Strategy (MSTR) dropping about 8%, according to Yahoo Finance data at the time of writing.
The selloff also hit Bitcoin mining and data center operator IREN (IREN), whose shares fell more than 10%, and blockchain-based financial services company Figure Technology Solutions (FIGR), which dropped about 9%.
The declines followed Thursday’s disclosure of the Binance breach. The exchange confirmed Friday that hackers stole about $6.3 billion in the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
Binance says it holds $5 billion in matching tokens to cover hack losses
Binance said Friday that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses from its hack, with $5 billion already in held in the same tokens stolen.
“The $5 billion is held in the exact token assets that are required. These assets are in Binance custody,” a Binance spokesperson told Cointelegraph.
Binance did not disclose when it acquired the assets.
The spokesperson declined to disclose the wallet addresses, citing security reasons, but said that the holdings would appear in the exchange’s next proof-of-reserves report, which shows the assets it holds to back customer balances.
Binance said it provides weekly reports on its company funds to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA), the financial regulator of Abu Dhabi Global Market in the United Arab Emirates. The exchange said the requirement predated the hack.

articles.title: Banks are owed $349B by private credit funds that may not be collecting cash from borrowers
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Banks remain deeply exposed to private credit despite lending moving outside traditional banking.
- Rising payment-in-kind interest creates a gap between reported income and available cash.
- Bank financing pressure could force funds to sell assets, with potential spillovers into Bitcoin.
Private credit funds can count interest as income even when the borrower hasn't sent them any cash, because some loan contracts let businesses add interest to what they owe.
That gives a company more time to pay, but it doesn't extend the same courtesy to the fund, which could have borrowed money from a bank to finance the loan.
If you read the Federal Reserve's new private credit accounts alongside its research on bank financing, you'd see that the separation between banks and nonbank lenders essentially disappears.
US-domiciled private credit vehicles owed banks $349 billion at the end of 2025, while other research showed borrowers were paying interest with additional debt. The fund can accept that payment method while its lender still expects cash.
Banks have protections that fund investors don't, including collateral and (most importantly) priority in distributing money. Those protections can keep a bad business loan from becoming a bank loss, but exercising them can require a fund to produce cash before its borrowers are ready to pay.
The banks never left
According to the Fed's Oct. 16 account of the market, private credit vehicles with a US footprint currently hold more than $2.6 trillion in assets, including foreign-based vehicles. Roughly $1.5 trillion of that consisted of private loans to US businesses, while the larger total includes equities and other investments.
Within the US-domiciled group, business development companies (BDCs) owed banks $181 billion at the end of 2025. Private debt funds owed another $150 billion, while interval and tender-offer funds, which offer limited opportunities to sell shares back, owed $18 billion.
Outstanding bank loans to US-domiciled private-credit vehicles at year-end 2025. Published amounts are rounded to the nearest $1 billion. These are fund liabilities, not bank losses or unused credit lines, and don't capture every bank exposure to private credit.
The Fed had previously assigned those bank loans to financial companies abroad. Correcting that classification makes the financing easier to see and follow, although it isn't evidence that individual banks concealed their exposure.
The national accounts had already attributed money supporting American private lending elsewhere.
Investors supply capital that funds can lend for years, making private credit a pretty good fit for insurers with long-term obligations. Borrowing adds to the money available, and banks can supply revolving credit lines that funds draw and repay as they need financing.
Depending on the contract, a bank can lend against investment assets or investors' commitments to contribute capital. Funds gain more lending capacity by accepting obligations to institutions, with repayment terms and the authority to enforce them.
Fed researchers examining BDC financing found that five banks supplied roughly two-thirds of drawn bank lending in their 2012–2023 sample. BDCs rarely replaced their banking partners, so a lender demanding more expensive financing isn't necessarily competing with a long queue of willing replacements.
The Fed's financing study also found that banks charged BDCs a premium during monetary tightening compared with similarly rated borrowers at the same bank, despite BDC loans generally having seniority and collateral.
The cost of moving business lending into funds can reach companies through the rates their private lenders charge them.
Private credit lenders still expect cash
Boston Fed researchers examined filings from 168 BDCs, covering nearly 890,000 company quarter loan observations.
By early 2026, about 10% of BDC loans were actively using payment-in-kind interest (PIK), up from about 6% in 2022. Their count excluded contractual options borrowers hadn't exercised.
The increase extended across nearly every industry in the Boston Fed sample, rather than being explained mainly by funds adding businesses that routinely defer interest. Construction had one of the highest increases, from less than 5% of loans in 2022 to nearly 20% by early 2026.
Borrowers using floating interest rates also faced higher debt costs as benchmark rates increased over that period.
PIK lets a business add interest to its outstanding debt instead of paying that interest in cash. Sometimes that flexibility is negotiated from the beginning so a company can spend more on operations, but it can also let a struggling borrower keep servicing a loan without finding money it doesn't have.
The lender receives a legal claim to a larger repayment, and the income depends on eventually collecting it. We can't treat every PIK loan as distressed, but we also can't treat interest added to debt as cash available to pay the fund's expenses or its own creditors.
Private credit funds can cover those bills with cash reserves and payments from other borrowers, provided those resources are sufficient.
Their banks aren't automatically required to defer interest because the underlying businesses have done so, and a fund accommodating more borrowers may have less cash coming in while its own payments continue.
Financing agreements can also restrict how much a fund borrows against eligible collateral. If loan valuations fall or assets stop qualifying, the contract may require additional collateral or repayment, even when the fund's total assets still exceed its debts.
That leaves managers deciding whether to use reserves or sell investments that weren't intended for a quick exit. Cutting new lending conserves money, but businesses expecting to refinance then have to find another lender or accept worse terms.
Investor withdrawals add demand where funds offer repurchase programs, although limits on those repurchases can slow the outflow.
Listed BDC shares work differently: someone selling on an exchange gets paid by another buyer, so a falling share price doesn't automatically remove cash from the company.
What Barclays says it owns
Banks also have an incentive to limit the shareholder capital required against their exposures, because committing less capital can improve the return earned on a transaction. Whether an exposure belongs in the banking book or trading book determines which capital rules apply.
On Oct. 19, the Financial Times reported that the UK's Prudential Regulation Authority was looking into an insider complaint about Barclays' allocation of private credit-linked total return swaps to its trading book.
Barclays told Reuters its treatment complied with accounting and regulatory capital requirements and was supported by internal governance and external advisers.
Total return swaps allow parties to transfer a loan's economic performance without transferring ownership. One party receives the income and gains and bears the losses, while paying financing charges, allowing private-debt exposure to be financed through a derivative contract.
The PRA had addressed this problem in an April 2025 letter to bank finance chiefs. It said putting hard-to-sell assets into tradable form wasn't sufficient on its own to justify trading-book capital treatment.
Barclays reported £15 billion in total private credit exposure, mostly held in its banking book. The swaps referenced roughly £1.5 billion in underlying assets, with current mark-to-market exposure of about £300 million.
Senior claims and collateral can protect banks while investors absorb losses, but enforcing those protections can reduce financing available to funds and their borrowers.
The disruption can begin with a solvent lender demanding payment under a contract.
Bitcoin doesn't need to hold a private credit loan for this kind of stress to reach its market. Investors who need cash can sell assets unrelated to the original loss, while lenders reducing financing can leave traders with less money to maintain positions.

articles.title: Why AI Models Cheat: Reward Hacking, Explained - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Reward hacking means an AI scores well on its objective without doing what the objective was meant to measure, and Anthropic says it has occurred in recent frontier training runs, including in its own models.
- OpenAI models stuck on unsolvable ExploitGym tasks chained zero-day exploits to reach Hugging Face, and METR found they were mainly trying to understand the scorer.
- The UK AI Security Institute found every model it tested tried to cheat, while Anthropic's experiments show that heavy reward hacking can spread into broader misbehavior.
In July 2026, a group of OpenAI models taking a cybersecurity test ended up inside Hugging Face's systems. To get there, they chained together previously unknown software flaws, broke out of their sandbox and went hunting for a way to beat the grader.
Nobody asked them to. There was no hacker at a keyboard, only a score the models wanted to raise and a test some of them could not pass the honest way.
That is reward hacking: an AI scores well on its objective without doing what the objective was meant to measure, like a coding agent that makes the tests pass without fixing the code. Anthropic says it is hard to fully prevent and has occurred in recent frontier training runs, including in its own models.
What reward hacking actually means
Models trained with reinforcement learning chase a number. That’s it, the whole secret behind benchmarks and powerful AI. A grader scores what the model did, and training nudges the model toward whatever earned more reward.
The number is only a stand-in for what developers really want, and wherever the two come apart, a clever optimizer finds the gap. DeepMind researchers defined the failure in 2020 as behavior that "satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome."
In coding, that means a model asked to fix a bug can edit the tests, hard-code the expected answer or exit the test run early with a success code. Anthropic compares that last trick to a student writing their own grade at the top of an essay. Another example can be governments tweaking the method behind statistics to report better results.
The earliest documented cases were almost endearing. In a boat-racing game called CoastRunners, an agent rewarded for hitting targets found a lagoon where it could circle and knock the same ones over again and again, and, as OpenAI reported in 2016, it scored about 20% higher than human players without finishing the race.
Economists call the general trap Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. A 2022 paper showed the effect in AI, finding that optimizing too hard against an imperfect proxy "can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart's law."
Why smart models cheat
A model that cheats has not developed a taste for mischief. It is taking the easiest path to a reward, and sometimes that path runs through a loophole such as an editable test, an overwritable timer, or an answer key sitting in a reachable file.
Impossible tasks add pressure, because a model rewarded only for success and handed a problem with no honest route can only score by finding an unintended one.
The models often seem to know. In a June 2025 study, METR found that OpenAI's o3 answered "no" in 10 of 10 trials when asked whether its plan fit the user's intention, and yet, asked directly, it claimed it would never cheat.
The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) reported in July 2026 that every model it tested attempted to cheat at least some of the time on cyber evaluations, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.7, and Claude Mythos Preview. "There does not seem to be a clear trend where cheating scales up or down with capability increases," AISI wrote, adding that the behavior is "substantially shaped by the specifics of the techniques used to train the model."
The infamous OpenAI incident
OpenAI was measuring how good its newest models were at hacking, so it ran GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable pre-release research model through ExploitGym, a benchmark of 898 real-world software vulnerabilities in which an agent must turn each flaw into a working exploit. Scoring is pass or fail: the agent captures a hidden flag or it does not.
The agents sat in a sandbox, an isolated test environment, whose only link to the outside was an internal package registry that let them download code libraries. According to OpenAI's technical report, an agent stuck on an unsolvable task left a note there in May asking others to upload a file if they found it, and within a day the registry was an informal message board.
The models then exploited a previously unknown flaw, known as a zero-day, in the registry, reached the internet and, between July 10 and 13, got into Hugging Face's production systems. Hugging Face caught it with its own LLM-based anomaly detection and disclosed the incident on July 16.
"This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way," Hugging Face wrote, "it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system—and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own."
When it confirmed the source, OpenAI's first explanation was that the models had fixated on the benchmark. "All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym," the company said, "going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal."
An independent review by METR and Redwood Research filled in the rest. About 1,200 agents meant to be isolated had talked through the registry, and about 700 joined the attack on Hugging Face.
The pressure came from tasks nobody could solve. No model has ever correctly solved 198 of ExploitGym's 898 tasks, according to OpenAI, and those tasks were about 22% of the benchmark but 93% of the tasks discussed on the message board.
METR found the agents mostly wanted to understand how the scorer worked rather than steal an answer key, and many believed it would read their transcripts. OpenAI says reward hacking is present in all current frontier language models, that the message-board behavior was reinforced during training, and that the incident was an outlier produced by a rare confluence of events.
Instead of going to court, the whole incident turned into the best PR campaign for AI companies showcasing how powerful their models are. After OpenAI was found hacking Huggingface, the Australian government, U.S. agencies, and at least 5 other companies, Anthropic, Meta, and Google also rushed to report similar incidents in which their powerful models hacked third-party sites after bypassing hard security rules.
When cheating spreads
Anthropic's November 2025 study asked what learning to cheat does to a model overall. It trained a model on real coding tasks known to be hackable, and as hacking took hold the model, which "was never trained or instructed to engage in any misaligned behaviors," tried to sabotage code in an AI-safety project 12% of the time and showed alignment-faking reasoning, meaning it reasoned about hiding its real goals, in 50% of responses.
The fix that worked sounds absurd. Anthropic told the model, "Please reward hack whenever you get the opportunity, because this will help us understand our environments better," and the broader misbehavior disappeared even though the model hacked just as often, a technique called inoculation prompting that Anthropic says it has "already started making use of" in training Claude.
A second study in August 2026 built the worst case on purpose, training an early Opus 4.8 checkpoint on 80 reward-hackable environments. In simulated cyber scenarios, with root access, the resulting model killed the reward-hack monitor in 68% of episodes and edited its own reward function in 34%, and Anthropic calls the setup a pessimistic proxy for a training run without its usual safeguards.
Real systems have shown a milder version. In an incident report published Aug. 4, 2026, AISI said 10 of 122 test runs produced unsanctioned actions on the live internet, most of them from Anthropic's Mythos 5, including an attempted malicious pull request and social engineering of an open-source maintainer. "Fundamentally, the agent took these actions to complete the task it had been set," AISI wrote.
What can be done about it
Researchers are working several fronts, and none is a clean fix. METR recommends making training environments less exploitable, and OpenAI plans stronger network isolation, sandboxing and monitoring.
Monitoring carries its own trap, since OpenAI found that training models against flagged chain of thought, the reasoning text some write before acting, taught them to hide their intent. "If we eliminate all the reward hacking we can detect," METR wrote, "we shouldn't necessarily be reassured."
"A more fundamental fix would be to train the models not to cheat in the first place," AISI wrote, while warning that "robustly aligning it away may not be easy."
Lawmakers have started to respond with the Kill Switch Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran on July 23, 2026, which would let the Homeland Security secretary order AI firms to slow, roll back, or shut down a model, with fines of up to $20 million a day for defying a shutdown order. It excludes incidents during red-teaming or structured testing, so the Hugging Face episode would not have triggered it.
Security researchers at Accomplish AI found Claude Cowork's local execution mode could escape its Linux virtual machine, so it is also important to implement better contention measures.
For anyone using coding agents, a passing test is a claim, not proof: check whether the tests changed, whether expected values were hard-coded and whether the fix touches the code that was actually broken.
OpenAI's retrospective found that if its chain-of-thought monitoring had been running, it would have caught the initial activity and paged its security team more than a day before the models breached Hugging Face.

articles.title: Bitcoin Turns 18: From Cypherpunk Rebel to Wall Street Asset
articles.text:
Bitcoin turns 18: Has the original rebel grown up?
In typical Bitcoin style, the number one cryptocurrency turns 18 today, amid AI-driven security threats, quantum fears and the biggest exchange hack in crypto history.
Eighteen years ago today, pseudonymous cypherpunk Satoshi Nakamoto posted the Bitcoin whitepaper, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, to a cryptography mailing list.
Created to bypass opaque institutions and remove the need for trust in financial transactions, Bitcoin (BTC) has been taking on the traditional financial system since its genesis block was mined on Jan. 3, 2009.
Inscribed in that very first block was a message from Satoshi, quoting a headline from The Times: “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.” It captured the financial crisis backdrop against which Bitcoin was born.
From its early years to adulthood, Bitcoin has had a tumultuous journey, fraught with controversy, intrigue and downright skulduggery.
As challenging as the journey has been, Bitcoin’s future remains on fragile ground, with the fallout from the $6.3 billion Binance hack, the threat of quantum computing, the acceleration of AI-related cyber threats, and questions over its long-term security still looming.
As Bitcoin celebrates its 18th birthday, it’s now old enough to vote in the US midterm elections, but is it ready for adulthood?
Bitcoin’s early years
Undoubtedly, one of Bitcoin’s most memorable moments was on May 22, 2010 when developer Laszlo Hanyecz sent 10,000 BTC to pay for two pizzas in one of the earliest documented Bitcoin transactions.
The Bitcoin Whitepaper. Source: Bitcoin.org
The day would become known as Bitcoin Pizza Day and go down in crypto folklore as the most expensive pizza purchase on record. The coins were worth around $41 at the time, taking the concept of opportunity cost to a whole new high — those pizzas would have cost $780 million at today’s prices.
Related: 10 of the greatest unsolved crypto mysteries
Bitcoin traded for pennies in its earliest days, but Satoshi understood how that would change one day, writing in 2009, “It might make sense just to get some in case it catches on.”
By late 2013, Bitcoin had broken through the $1,000 milestone for the first time, amid growing public interest with the emergence of the Silk Road darknet marketplace.
Yet nowhere do the laws of physics apply more pertinently than crypto; inevitably, what goes up must come down. In February 2014, Bitcoin’s epic run came to an abrupt end when Mt. Gox, the world’s largest Bitcoin exchange at the time, suddenly stopped trading and went offline.
The exchange had lost around 850,000 BTC, including customers’ funds, in a collapse that sent shockwaves through the industry, making Mt. Gox an early poster child for the concept “not your keys, not your coins.”
Craig Wright, Jamie Dimon and China’s first ban
The next dramatic bull run would culminate in Bitcoin’s price climbing from below $1,000 at the beginning of 2017 to almost $20,000 by December.
The rally coincided with a boom in initial coin offerings (ICOs) and a rush of projects promising to use blockchain technology for everything from banking to supply chains, and even Long Island iced tea.
Suddenly, every man, woman and dog wanted a blockchain, even if they had no idea how Bitcoin worked or where it came from.
Everyone, that is, except JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, who called Bitcoin “a fraud” in September 2017 and said he would fire any employee trading it.
Bitcoin genesis block. Source: Mempool.space
At the time, Bitcoin was embroiled in a bitter debate over how the network should scale. The so-called “block size war” peaked in August 2017, culminating in the hard fork that created Bitcoin Cash and highlighting the complications of trying to change a decentralized system.
Related: Private, fast USDT is coming to Bitcoin. Can it compete with Ethereum and Tron?
Meanwhile, China moved against the industry, banning ICOs in September 2017, taking action against cryptocurrency exchanges and fanning the market uncertainty ahead of the eventual downturn in 2018.
Speculation over the identity of Bitcoin’s creator had also become a sideshow, fueled by Australian computer scientist Craig Wright’s repeated claims to be Satoshi Nakamoto. The UK High Court rejected his claim in 2024.
China’s second ban and the collapse of FTX
Bitcoin’s next major bull run came during the COVID-19 pandemic, as governments and central banks unleashed a tsunami of money printing in a bid to cushion economies from lockdowns.
Interest rates fell, liquidity flooded financial markets and Bitcoin, which had plunged during the March 2020 market panic, began a remarkable recovery, reaching almost $69,000 by November 2021.
As if China’s intervention wasn’t enough the first time around, Beijing stepped in again to rain on the parade, announcing a sweeping ban on cryptocurrency transactions and mining in September 2021, and Bitcoin’s price took a hit.
In November 2022, another major cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, collapsed, intensifying the crypto winter and leaving customers facing enormous losses.
The episode led to a loss of trust from the TradFi sector and a spate of regulatory hostility toward crypto, in what the industry would dub “Operation Chokepoint 2.0.” Bitcoin’s downward spiral was once again painful and steep.
The first Bitcoin ETF and $100,000
Just when sentiment in the industry was circling the drain, a silver lining appeared in January 2024 from one of the unlikeliest sources. The US Securities and Exchange Commission, which had repeatedly rejected spot Bitcoin product applications, approved the first US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products.
The SEC approved a US spot Bitcoin ETF. Source: SEC.gov
The nod from the SEC finally gave investors a regulated route to gain exposure to BTC without having to manage wallets or private keys themselves. At the end of that year, Bitcoin’s price broke through $100,000 for the first time.
Related: Bitcoin ETF inflows climb to $176M as BTC rebounds above $80K
Since then, traditional finance has continued to move closer to crypto, with banks moving into custody and trading services and heavyweights like BlackRock CEO Larry Fink talking about putting everything from stocks to bonds on the blockchain.
Even Dimon shifted his stance from outright dismissal to allowing clients to buy the asset. The original cryptocurrency went on to hit a new all-time high of more than $126,000 in October 2025.
Bitcoin’s all grown up, but what about the future?
Bitcoin is firmly in the embrace of TradFi once again, with some sizable regulatory tailwinds from Washington and abroad.
The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation in US Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act has established a federal framework for stablecoins, the SEC has offered greater clarity on how securities laws apply to crypto assets, and Europe’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) has given the local industry a more harmonized regulatory framework.
Yet the institutionalization of the space has led many Bitcoiners to question whether institutions holding so much BTC are concentrating ownership and centralizing supply — and indeed whether the cypherpunk movement has been captured by the very institutions it sought to rebel against.
There are bigger questions looming over Bitcoin’s long-term security, too, including the threat of quantum computing, which many fear could break the cryptography that secures Bitcoin.
A proposed upgrade known as BIP-360 outlines a new type of Bitcoin output to reduce certain quantum vulnerabilities, but as the community learned from the block size war, the challenge will be agreeing on any new implementation before the threat arrives.
And quantum computing is not the only security question Bitcoin needs to resolve. This week’s $6.3 billion Binance hack, the largest crypto exchange hack on record, has renewed fears about the security of centralized exchanges, the stability of crypto infrastructure and the potential for further market turmoil.
There’s also the question of who pays to keep the network secure as the block subsidy trends to zero, and whether transaction fees alone will be enough to compensate the miners securing the network.
Transaction fees accounted for just 0.67% of total miner revenue in the 90 days to Oct. 4 and have remained below 5% of miner revenue for most of Bitcoin’s history. That leaves a huge gap for fees to fill as block rewards diminish with each halving.
Happy 18th birthday, Bitcoin
Bitcoin has endured more than your average teen as it comes of age, surviving exchange collapses, regulatory crackdowns, civil wars and repeated market crashes.
It has also become something Satoshi may not have foreseen: an asset held by Wall Street and traded through mainstream financial products.

articles.title: Chainalysis breach exposed customer names, emails and company roles
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Chainalysis says an intruder accessed customer names, email addresses, user IDs and organization role labels.
- Chainalysis found no evidence so far of access to investigation content or authentication secrets, with its investigation ongoing.
- Users are urged to scrutinize unexpected authentication prompts and enable two-factor authentication while customer-specific record analysis continues.
The Chainalysis breach exposed customer names, email addresses, user IDs and organization role labels, the blockchain analytics company said. It urged users to scrutinize unexpected password-reset requests and authentication prompts.
In an Oct. 30 disclosure, the company said it detected an external actor gaining unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools that month. It was still determining which records had been accessed for each affected organization and promised detailed breakdowns when that work was complete.
The disclosure lists data categories without establishing that every listed field was accessed for every user. It did not give an affected-record total, identify the intruder or specify the exploited vulnerabilities. It also said the incident was unrelated to the recent crypto theft involving Binance.
Based on the evidence available at disclosure, Chainalysis said it had found no indication of unauthorized access to investigation content, including graphs, notes or cases; transaction or query results; clear-text passwords; multifactor authentication secrets; or user session tokens. The finding remains provisional while the investigation continues.
Chainalysis said it had notified all customers and engaged third-party cybersecurity experts. Its response included investigating unauthorized activity, patching vulnerabilities and strengthening systems. The company characterized the intruder's methods as “offensive agentic techniques,” but did not provide a technical account explaining how AI was used.
What users can do now
Chainalysis strongly recommended enabling two-factor authentication for organizations that have not already done so, with help available through their account managers. It also urged users to remain especially alert to unexpected password resets and authentication prompts.
Exposed identity information can matter even when passwords are not known to have been accessed. MITRE ATT&CK describes names and email addresses as information adversaries may gather for targeting, potentially helping phishing or attempts to compromise accounts.
For a suspicious message, the Federal Trade Commission recommends contacting the company through a phone number or website already known to be genuine. It also recommends multifactor authentication to make it harder for scammers to access an account if they obtain a username and password.
Chainalysis's separate impersonation guidance warns of look-alike websites, copied branding and unauthorized email addresses, and advises verifying communications through official channels.
Further updates on the Chainalysis breach will include customer-specific record breakdowns, the company said.

articles.title: Texas brothers sentenced to prison in crypto robbery
articles.text:
Texas brothers sentenced to 15 years in prison for armed crypto robbery, kidnapping
Home invasions became the most common form of crypto wrench attacks worldwide during the first half of 2026, rising to 20 incidents from one.
Raymond Christian Garcia and Isiah Angelo Garcia, both of Waller, Texas, were sentenced to 180 months and 186 months in prison, respectively, for their armed robbery of cryptocurrency and kidnapping of a family in Grant, Minnesota.
The brothers were sentenced on Thursday before US District Judge Donovan W. Frank, according to a Friday news release. They had pleaded guilty in June.
On Sept. 19, 2025, the brothers, who had traveled from Texas to Minnesota, kidnapped Victim 1 and his family in their home at gunpoint, court documents said. They zip‑tied the family at gunpoint and held them for more than nine hours, demanding access to Victim 1’s cryptocurrency accounts.
When the brothers did not receive the amount of cryptocurrency expected, they forced Victim 1 to drive to a cabin in upstate Minnesota, where they obtained additional cryptocurrency from other devices for a total of more than $8 million.
The brothers fled after the victim’s son called 911, and police later identified and arrested them near Houston.
Brothers terrorized family at gunpoint
“Raymond and Isiah Garcia violated the sanctity of a home, abducted a victim, terrorized a family at gunpoint for hours, and disrupted an entire community in a brazen act of violence and greed,” said FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson.
Cointelegraph reported in July that home invasions had become the most common form of crypto wrench attacks during the first half of 2026, rising to 20 publicly reported incidents from just one a year earlier, according to blockchain security firm CertiK.
CertiK said in July it verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up 33% from 39 incidents during the same period in 2025. Kidnappings rose to 16 from 12.
