articles.title: Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver
articles.text:
Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Osaka Metropolitan University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that low testosterone and a high-fructose diet can work together to worsen fatty liver disease in mice. Unexpectedly, changes in gut bacteria appear to drive this harmful interaction, revealing a potential new target for preventing liver damage.
- Share:
Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.
Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.
How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver
To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.
The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.
To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.
A Dangerous Combination for Fatty Liver
The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.
When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.
The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.
These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.
Gut Bacteria Reveal a Hidden Mechanism
Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.
"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.
In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.
The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.
Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease
Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.
"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.
Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.
The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.
Story Source:

articles.title: Cận cảnh 4 con rồng komodo kịch chiến giành quyền thống trị
articles.text:
Video ghi lại cảnh 4 con rồng komodo khổng lồ, mỗi con dài tới 2m kịch chiến giành quyền thống trị trong vườn quốc gia trên đảo Komodo, Indonesia.
Video do cán bộ quản lý rừng Konstantinus Muga ghi lại. Muga cho biết, đầu tiên anh bắt gặp hai con rồng komodo trong rừng, chúng nhìn nhau trừng trừng suốt vài giây để đánh giá đối thủ trước khi bật dậy đứng bằng hai chân sau và bám vào nhau.
Cả hai con rồng đều cố gắng huy động tất cả sức mạnh cơ bắp để vật ngã đối thủ xuống đất. Màn đọ sức đang gay cấn thì đột nhiên xuất hiện thêm hai con rồng komodo khác kéo tới nhập cuộc khiến cuộc chiến giành quyền thống trị càng dữ dội.
Kết thúc cuộc chiến, con rồng komodo to nhất trở thành kẻ thắng trận, nó nằm đè lên ba đối thủ còn lại như một cách phô trương thành tích. Muga cho biết cuộc chiến kéo dài tổng cộng 10 phút.
Rồng komodo thường chiến đấu để thu hút sự chú ý từ con cái hoặc giành quyền thống trị lãnh thổ.
Rồng komodo nổi tiếng là loài thằn lằn lớn nhất hiện đang còn sinh sống trên Trái Đất và là những sinh vật đáng sợ, hung hãn. Chúng cũng là 1 trong những loài bò sát phàm ăn nhất Trái Đất. Rồng komodo có thể ăn thịt bất cứ sinh vật gì trong môi trường sống của mình thậm chí chúng còn ăn thịt chính đồng loại của mình.
Những con rồng Komodo trưởng thành có thể sẽ thịt những con rồng con non yếu. Chính vì vậy, những con non thậm chí phải trèo lên cây cao để tránh những con rồng lớn trong 8 đến 9 năm cho đến khi trưởng thành.

articles.title: Vì sao năm Mão của Việt Nam là mèo, ở Trung Quốc, Hàn Quốc là thỏ?
articles.text:
Sự khác biệt này được lý giải do trong quá trình tiếp nhận lịch Can - Chi, người Việt đã có sự biến đổi cho phù hợp với địa lý và văn hóa của mình.
Theo lịch âm, năm mới 2023 là năm Quý Mão. Tuy nhiên, điều thú vị là trong khi các quốc gia khác như Trung Quốc, Hàn Quốc và Nhật Bản, năm Mão đại diện bởi con thỏ, còn Việt Nam là quốc gia duy nhất có mèo là con giáp đại diện.
Ở Việt Nam, mèo là con vật đại diện cho năm Mão. (Ảnh: Wallpaper).
Theo sách "12 con giáp trong văn hóa người Việt", 12 con giáp có nguồn gốc từ lịch Can - Chi. Loại lịch này xuất hiện vào thời nhà Thương (1766-1122 TCN) ở Trung Quốc. Theo đó, 12 con giáp gắn với Thập Nhị Chi.
Theo đó, người Trung Quốc xưa đã chọn ra 12 con vật gắn liền với đời sống hoặc được con người thuần dưỡng sớm nhất để đưa vào lịch Can - Chi, theo thứ tự: Tý (Chuột), Sửu (Trâu), Dần (Hổ), Mão (Thỏ), Thìn (Rồng), Tỵ (Rắn), Ngọ (Ngựa), Mùi (Dê), Thân (Khỉ), Dậu (Gà), Tuất (Chó), Hợi (Lợn).
Còn trong văn hóa Việt Nam, theo sách "Chuyện Đông, Chuyện Tây" của tác giả An Chi, "con giáp" là một lối nói của phương ngữ Nam Bộ.
Mèo và Thỏ đều là con giáp thứ 4 trong lịch Can - Chi ở Việt Nam và Trung Quốc.
Con giáp là chu kỳ 12 năm âm lịch, gọi từ tên của 12 địa chi, từ Tý đến Hợi, cho ra một nghĩa rộng là chu kỳ thời gian từ một năm cho đến năm cuối cùng một chi với nó sau đó 12 năm.
Trong phương ngữ Bắc Bộ, "giáp" thoạt đầu vẫn được hiểu là một chu kỳ 60 năm, về sau lại được linh động hiểu thành chi kỳ 12 năm như hiện nay.
Khác biệt của 12 con giáp trong văn hóa của Việt Nam chính là con mèo được dùng thay thế cho con thỏ.
Có nhiều lý giải khác nhau về việc trong văn hóa Việt, mèo là con vật đại diện cho năm mão.
Trong tiếng Trung Quốc, hai từ này khác nhau về dấu, nhưng về ngữ âm thì "mèo" (măo) và mèo (máo) có cách đọc giống nhau, đều là mao. Trong "Việt Nam tự điển", chữ "mão" - nghĩa là con thỏ - lại được dùng để chỉ con mèo.
Sim Sang - Joon, Giám đốc Trung tâm Giao lưu văn hóa Việt - Hàn, cũng giải thích rằng mèo tuy không phải loài vật nằm trong Thập Nhị Chi nhưng lại được ghi âm chữ Hán giống với con thỏ (máo - âm Hán Việt là miêu).
Mèo là con vật thân thuộc trong đời sống người dân Việt Nam. (Ảnh: Kelvin Valerio/Pexels).
Dù đã tiếp thu Thập Nhị chi (12 con giáp) của Trung Quốc, song có lẽ do yếu tố môi trường tự nhiên này nên người Việt đã không tiếp thu y nguyên mô hình ở Trung Quốc mà biến cải cho phù hợp với môi trường sống của mình.
Ở Việt Nam, điều kiện môi trường thuận lợi cho loài mèo phát triển mạnh hơn hẳn thỏ. Vì Việt Nam là văn hóa thảo mộc chứ không phải văn hóa thảo nguyên.
Nếu thảo nguyên là môi trường có những đồng cỏ mềm mượt, mà các loài động vật có thể thỏa sức ăn thành từng bầy đàn, thảo mộc lại là môi trường phong phú đa dạng các thảm thực vật đan xen lẫn nhau.
Mặt khác, ở Việt Nam, thỏ vốn không phổ biến và thân thuộc, chỉ được coi là loài hiền lành, dễ thương. Trong khi mèo được mệnh danh là "tiểu hổ" và gần gũi với đời sống các gia đình.
Mèo còn xuất hiện trong ca dao, tục ngữ, các bài hát... Mèo cũng có tài bắt chuột, giúp ích nhiều cho các gia đình, đặc biệt trong nền kinh tế nông nghiệp.
Một lý giải khác cho rằng thay thế thỏ bằng mèo trong 12 con giáp đã được chấp thuận rộng rãi và hợp lý. Theo Reuters, thỏ là một loài gặm nhấm, chuột (Tí) cũng là loài gặm nhấm, trong khi 12 con giáp cần độc nhất và khác biệt.
Mèo còn tạo ra thế đối xứng với chó (Tuất). Theo thuyết âm dương, điều này tạo ra thế cân bằng, giúp giải quyết các mâu thuẫn, dung hòa các mặt đối lập và khiến vòng tròn hoàng đạo cân bằng hơn.

articles.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
articles.text:
Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.
- Share:
Medications are designed to treat diseases and relieve symptoms, but some can also produce unintended effects that put patients at risk. While side effects are common with many treatments, researchers have identified a particularly concerning possibility involving drugs used to control inflammation.
Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have discovered that a widely used class of anti-inflammatory medications may make it easier for certain viruses to infect cells and spread throughout the body.
"We have found a surprising and potentially serious side effect of a class of anti-inflammatory drugs. They can help viruses spread more easily in the body," says Denis Kainov, a professor at the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
Common Anti-Inflammatory Drugs May Help Viruses Spread
The medications at the center of the findings belong to a class called Janus kinase inhibitors, or JAKs. These drugs are widely prescribed to control inflammation, but their effects on the immune system may also leave the body more vulnerable to viral infections.
"Among the viruses that more easily affect the body with the help of these drugs are Rift Valley fever virus, influenza A, adenovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19," Kainov says.
These viruses can cause significant illness, making any treatment that potentially increases their ability to spread a serious concern.
Why Arthritis Drugs Can Weaken Antiviral Defenses
In a new study published in NAR Molecular Medicine, Kainov and his colleagues investigated how JAK inhibitors influence the body's ability to defend itself against viruses.
"JAK inhibitors are often prescribed for autoimmune diseases and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis," says Erlend Ravlo, a PhD research fellow at NTNU and first author of the article.
Although these medications can be highly effective at reducing inflammation, their benefits come with an important trade-off. By suppressing certain immune responses, they can also interfere with the mechanisms that normally protect the body from viral infections.
"In particular, the drugs suppress an important immune signalling pathway that helps protect healthy cells from viral attacks," Ravlo said.
This pathway plays a central role in coordinating the body's response when viruses attempt to infect healthy tissue.
Scientists Discover How JAK Inhibitors Disrupt Immune Protection
The research team found that JAK inhibitors, including the medication baricitinib, can reduce the activity of genes involved in fighting viral infections.
"These genes play a crucial role in the body's response to viral infections," said Aleksandr Ianevski, an NTNU researcher and coauthor of the new paper.
When JAK inhibitors interfere with this immune signaling system, they weaken an important layer of antiviral protection. Without the usual defensive response, viruses may find it easier to establish an infection and spread between cells.
To investigate these effects, the scientists combined advanced virology methods with gene expression analysis and organoid technology. Their experiments included cells from the lungs, eyes and brain, along with miniature organ models grown in the laboratory.
These approaches allowed the team to examine how the drugs affect antiviral defenses across different types of human tissue.
"Although JAK inhibitors are effective in the treatment of inflammation, this shows that they can pose a hidden risk for patients who have latent or active viral infections," says Ravlo.
What the Findings Mean for Patients and Future Treatments
The results highlight the importance of carefully considering the risks associated with JAK inhibitors, particularly when patients may already have a viral infection or when outbreaks are occurring.
Researchers suggest that healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing these medications during periods of increased viral transmission.
However, the same immune-suppressing properties that create potential risks for patients could also offer advantages in certain research settings. Under controlled laboratory conditions, these effects may help scientists develop vaccines or evaluate potential antiviral medications.
The researchers hope their findings will encourage greater awareness of how JAK inhibitors influence the immune system and support further investigations into their safest and most effective uses.
"We recommend further studies to better understand how the drugs can be used optimally, especially during virus outbreaks or pandemics," says Ianevski.
Professor Magnar Bjørås of the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine provided significant scientific expertise and secured most of the funding for the research. Additional financial support came from the Central Norway Regional Health Authority, the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.

articles.title: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.
articles.text:
Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.
In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.
Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.
Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.
In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?
In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.
James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie
Live Science Pro
This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.
Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.
They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.
This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.
It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.
It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.
Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.
Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'They cannot compete with the prices that fish factories will pay': How demand for fish meal takes priority over feeding people
- Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
- 'Parasites of human societies': How did we end up so close to cats?
Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.
The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.
A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.
Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.
This article is adapted from Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature by James O’Hanlon . Copyright © James O’Hanlon 2027, 2025 First published in Australia by NewSouth, an imprint of UNSW Press Ltd. Used by arrangement with Columbia University Press. All rights reserved.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.
James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

articles.title: Khỉ bay: Sinh vật bí ẩn trong rừng nhiệt đới, giống khỉ nhưng không phải khỉ, có thể bay mà không có cánh
articles.text:
Trong những khu rừng nhiệt đới, nơi ánh sáng mặt trời khó xuyên qua tán cây rậm rạp và không khí luôn đượm mùi đất ẩm và hương hoa, tồn tại vô số loài sinh vật độc đáo và kỳ diệu. Trong số đó, có một sinh vật đặc biệt mà sự hiện diện của nó luôn gợi lên sự tò mò và ngạc nhiên. Đó là "khỉ bay", một sinh vật không chỉ biết leo trèo mà còn có khả năng lướt qua không trung mà không cần cánh.
Dù mang cái tên "khỉ bay", loài sinh vật này thực tế không phải là khỉ, mà thuộc họ sóc gặm nhấm. Với tên khoa học là Cynocephalus, khỉ bay sở hữu ngoại hình giống một con sóc nhưng có vóc dáng thanh mảnh hơn. Điều đặc biệt khiến chúng trở nên nổi bật chính là màng da mềm mại nối giữa các chi, cho phép chúng lướt bay nhẹ nhàng qua không trung giữa các ngọn cây, giống như những vũ công điêu luyện của rừng già.
Có hàng chục loài khỉ bay sinh sống trong các khu rừng nhiệt đới, đặc biệt là ở Đông Nam Á. Chúng chủ yếu sống trên cây, ăn lá, trái cây, và đôi khi là côn trùng. Khả năng leo trèo của khỉ bay vô cùng xuất sắc. Chúng có thể di chuyển từ cành này sang cành khác một cách nhanh nhẹn, và khi cần di chuyển xa hơn, khỉ bay sẽ bật nhảy từ độ cao, mở màng da và lướt bay trên không trung, bay hàng chục mét mà vẫn hạ cánh chính xác lên mục tiêu.
Khỉ bay không thực sự biết bay như loài chim. Tên gọi này xuất phát từ khả năng di chuyển đặc biệt của chúng giữa các tán cây trong rừng.
Nhờ có màng da rộng nối liền các chi, khỉ bay có thể "lượn, lướt bay" từ cành cây này sang cành cây khác một cách uyển chuyển, tạo cảm giác như đang bay.
Khả năng lướt bay của khỉ bay không chỉ là một kỹ năng ngẫu nhiên, mà là kết quả của hàng triệu năm tiến hóa để thích nghi với môi trường sống phức tạp. Trong các khu rừng nhiệt đới, nơi cây cối mọc dày đặc và mặt đất thường ẩm ướt, khả năng lướt bay giúp khỉ bay dễ dàng di chuyển qua các chướng ngại vật và tránh các mối nguy hiểm khi phải đi trên mặt đất.
Thêm vào đó, khả năng lướt bay trên không cũng giúp chúng tiết kiệm năng lượng khi kiếm ăn, đồng thời nâng cao cơ hội sinh tồn trong môi trường khắc nghiệt này. Chúng không cần phải băng qua các khoảng cách dài bằng cách trèo hoặc đi bộ mà chỉ cần một cú nhảy, giúp tiết kiệm thời gian và giảm thiểu nguy cơ bị kẻ săn mồi phát hiện.
Màng da là đặc điểm phân biệt rõ nhất của khỉ bay. Màng da rộng, mỏng và có nhiều mạch máu, giúp chúng tạo ra lực nâng khi di chuyển giữa các cây.
Không chỉ có khả năng lướt bay độc đáo, khỉ bay còn có nhiều thói quen đặc biệt khác. Chúng thường hoạt động vào ban ngày và nghỉ ngơi trong các hốc cây vào ban đêm. Khỉ bay sống theo nhóm gia đình, nơi các thành viên trưởng thành cùng nhau chăm sóc và bảo vệ con non. Những khỉ con sau khi sinh sẽ nhanh chóng học cách lướt bay bay từ mẹ, và qua thời gian, chúng dần dần phát triển thành những cá thể thành thạo trong việc bay lượn qua rừng.
Điều đáng chú ý là khả năng sinh sản của khỉ bay khá ấn tượng. Mỗi năm, khỉ cái có thể sinh ra một vài con, và ngay từ khi mới sinh, những khỉ con này đã có thể lướt bay qua rừng cùng mẹ, học hỏi và thực hành kỹ năng sinh tồn trong môi trường rừng nhiệt đới đầy thử thách.
Khả năng lướt bay của khỉ bay là kết quả của quá trình tiến hóa thích nghi với môi trường sống trên cây. Nhờ khả năng này, khỉ bay có thể di chuyển nhanh chóng giữa các cây, tránh kẻ thù và tìm kiếm thức ăn hiệu quả hơn.
Trong hệ sinh thái phức tạp của rừng nhiệt đới, khỉ bay đóng vai trò quan trọng, vừa là động vật ăn thịt vừa là con mồi của các loài khác. Chúng tương tác chặt chẽ với nhiều loài thực vật và động vật khác trong khu rừng, góp phần duy trì sự cân bằng sinh thái. Khỉ bay không chỉ giúp duy trì sự đa dạng sinh học mà còn mang lại sự sống động và sức sống cho thế giới tự nhiên.
Hình ảnh khỉ bay lướt bay qua không trung với dáng vẻ duyên dáng, nhẹ nhàng chính là biểu tượng của sự kỳ diệu trong tự nhiên. Sự hiện diện của chúng nhắc nhở chúng ta về vẻ đẹp tuyệt vời và đa dạng của thế giới động vật, khiến ta thêm trân trọng và cảm nhận sâu sắc hơn về sự sống hoang dã.
Khỉ bay là loài động vật có khả năng thích nghi đặc biệt với cuộc sống trên cây. Khả năng lướt bay độc đáo của chúng đã khiến chúng trở thành một trong những loài động vật thú vị nhất trong thế giới tự nhiên.
Câu chuyện về khỉ bay không chỉ là một lời nhắc nhở về sự kỳ diệu của thiên nhiên mà còn là lời kêu gọi chúng ta cùng nhau bảo vệ và gìn giữ những di sản sinh thái quý giá này. Mỗi loài động vật trong tự nhiên đều có một vai trò quan trọng trong hệ sinh thái chung. Việc bảo vệ chúng cũng chính là bảo vệ môi trường sống của chính con người.
Chúng ta cần nhận thức rõ rằng, mỗi hành động nhỏ đều góp phần vào việc duy trì sự đa dạng sinh học trên hành tinh. Hãy chung tay bảo vệ những cánh rừng nhiệt đới – nơi không chỉ là ngôi nhà của loài khỉ bay, mà còn là nơi chứa đựng vô vàn phép màu khác của sự sống.
Khỉ bay, với khả năng lướt bay qua rừng mà không cần cánh, là minh chứng sống động cho sự đa dạng và sức sống mãnh liệt của thiên nhiên. Chúng ta nên trân trọng và bảo vệ những sinh vật kỳ diệu này, để chúng tiếp tục sống và phát triển, góp phần vào bức tranh đa dạng sinh thái của Trái Đất.

articles.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
articles.text:
James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered surprising evidence that a scorching planet covered in molten rock may be protected by a reflective layer of clouds that acts like a giant sunscreen. Scientists previously believed that the planet's extreme conditions would make it nearly impossible for an atmosphere to survive, but new observations suggest otherwise.
An international team of researchers, including Dr. Anjali Piette, an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham, reported the findings in The Astronomical Journal. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the scientists monitored a rocky exoplanet called TOI-561 b, located approximately 280 light-years from Earth. Over 37 hours, they observed nearly four complete orbits around its host star.
The observations indicate that TOI-561 b may be surrounded by a substantial atmosphere, although its conditions would be far too hostile for life as we know it. This atmosphere appears to help the planet reflect much of the radiation coming from its star. One possible explanation is a layer of highly reflective silicate clouds that prevents the surface from reaching the extreme temperatures expected on an exposed rocky planet. The atmosphere also appears to move heat from the permanently illuminated dayside toward the nightside, further reducing temperatures on the star-facing side.
A Lava Planet With an Atmosphere That Should Have Disappeared
Scientists still do not know exactly which gases make up the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. One possibility is a thick layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but under much hotter conditions. Another is an atmosphere dominated by sulfur dioxide, a gas released by volcanic activity on Jupiter's moon Io.
Dr. Anjali Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: "Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.
"Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere."
James Webb Reveals Why the Planet Is So Reflective
Earlier measurements revealed something puzzling about TOI-561 b. Its dayside was significantly cooler than researchers predicted for a dark, rocky planet orbiting so close to its star. That unexpected temperature suggested that much of the incoming energy was either being transferred to the nightside or reflected back into space before it could heat the surface.
To investigate, the team observed the planet throughout its orbit, allowing them to examine its nightside for the first time. Because the same side of TOI-561 b always faces its star, the nightside receives no direct starlight. However, the measurements showed that this darker hemisphere was not warm enough to explain all the missing heat.
The findings instead indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight reaching it, a remarkably high proportion comparable to Venus.
To determine what could produce such strong reflectivity, the researchers compared the telescope measurements with computer models of the planet's climate. Their simulations suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), may form over the dayside. If present, these clouds could reflect incoming radiation before it reaches the surface, functioning as a natural sunscreen.
Professor Lisa Dang, who led the project at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, said: "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere."
Could a Global Ocean of Lava Keep the Atmosphere Alive?
The new findings strengthen earlier evidence gathered by Professor Lisa Dang, Dr. Anjali Piette, and their collaborators that TOI-561 b has a thick atmosphere that may be continually replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.
That possibility could help explain how the planet has maintained an atmosphere despite enduring intense radiation from its star for billions of years. Rather than simply losing its gases to space, the planet's vast reservoir of molten rock may be constantly releasing new material into the atmosphere.
Researchers now hope to determine whether TOI-561 b is more like an extremely hot Venus or a much more intense version of the volcanic moon Io. Additional observations with JWST at longer wavelengths could reveal important details about the atmosphere's chemical composition and help resolve the mystery of its long-term survival.
Professor Dang added: "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of lo. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Birmingham. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Samuel Boucher, Lisa Dang, Alex McGinty, Johanna K. Teske, Raymond Pierrehumbert, Anjali A. A. Piette, Nicole L. Wallack, Angharad Weeks, Neil T. Lewis, Tim Lichtenberg, Mykhaylo Plotnykov, Emma Postolec, Daniel Huber, Timothy R. Bedding, Harrison Nicholls, Bo Peng, Mark Hammond, Diana Valencia. A Highly Reflective Atmosphere on the Lava World TOI-561b Revealed by JWST/NIRSpec Phase Curves. The Astronomical Journal, 2026; 172 (4): 239 DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae9763

articles.title: Chùm ảnh AI mô phỏng cuộc sống con người năm 2100
articles.text:
Trình tạo hình ảnh bằng trí tuệ nhân tạo Midjourney đã tạo ra những mô phỏng về cuộc sống của chúng ta vào năm 2100.
Midjourney cho thấy thế giới vào năm 2100.
AI giúp công việc của con người trở nên dễ dàng hơn nhiều trong việc viết nhạc, tạo văn bản có ý nghĩa và thậm chí chẩn đoán bệnh.
Midjourney có thể tạo ra những bức tranh, cách điệu theo tinh thần của những bộ phim nổi tiếng và tạo nên hình ảnh của những sinh vật trong truyện cổ tích.
Mạng thần kinh là một chương trình được thiết kế dựa trên nguyên tắc kết nối nơ ron trong não người.
Thuật ngữ mạng thần kinh xuất hiện lần đầu tiên vào giữa thế kỷ 20, khi các nhà khoa học quyết định cố gắng tạo ra một công nghệ có thể tái tạo bộ não con người.
Trong tương lai, rất có thể đây sẽ là một phần trong cuộc sống của con người.
Mạng thần kinh hiện đại có thể tự học, tìm lỗi trong công việc và áp dụng kinh nghiệm trước đó.
Ngày nay, mạng lưới thần kinh được sử dụng để giải quyết các vấn đề phức tạp đòi hỏi tính toán phân tích, giống như những vấn đề được thực hiện bởi bộ não con người.
Mạng thần kinh có thể phân phối dữ liệu theo các tham số, đưa ra dự đoán về tình hình hiện tại, chẳng hạn như kinh tế.
Theo Diễn đàn Kinh tế Thế giới, đến năm 2025, trí tuệ nhân tạo sẽ có thể thay thế các chuyên gia trong lĩnh vực nghệ thuật thị giác, điện ảnh, báo chí, lập trình và các lĩnh vực khác.
Midjourney có các thuật toán nâng cao có thể phân tích và bắt chước các phong cách và mẫu khác nhau, cho phép nó tạo ra nhiều loại nội dung trực quan độc đáo và được cá nhân hóa.
Midjourney là một công cụ mang tính cách mạng sử dụng công nghệ trí tuệ nhân tạo để tạo ra những hình ảnh tuyệt đẹp và có độ chân thực cao.
Khả năng của trí tuệ nhân tạo rất lớn.
Midjourney là một trong những mạng thần kinh chính để vẽ.
Midjourney có khả năng tạo ra những hình ảnh vô cùng sặc sỡ theo nhiều kiểu khác nhau từ các mô tả bằng văn bản.

articles.title: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie
articles.text:
'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie
Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.
Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.
Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."
Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.
James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).
Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?
James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?
And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?
OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?
JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.
OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?
JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.
I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?
There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.
OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?
JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.
OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?
JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.
OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?
JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.
Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.
OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.
JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.
OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?
JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.
OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?
JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.
OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?
JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.
As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?
A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.
OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?
JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.
It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.
We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- This psychologist has a new theory for why orcas keep attacking boats
- Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
- 'The Russians were the problem in the end': Sailor Matt Rutherford on being intercepted by the FSB while attempting to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo
OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?
JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.
You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.
OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?
JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.
This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.
Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

articles.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
articles.text:
Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
New model gives astronomers a powerful tool to understand discoveries from NASA's James Webb and Nancy Roman space telescopes.
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Smithsonian
- Summary:
- Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.
- Share:
Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever developed, offering a remarkable new way to explore how the cosmos evolved after the Big Bang. Known as "Lumina," the simulation was built by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian to help astronomers interpret observations from powerful instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope.
The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, reconstructs the universe's first 2 billion years by modeling the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation. By comparing Lumina's predictions with observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes, scientists can evaluate how well existing theories explain cosmic evolution and identify discoveries that might challenge their understanding of the universe's fundamental laws.
Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing explanations for the formation of stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. Modern supercomputers now make it possible to turn these ideas into detailed simulations that predict how the universe should behave. When telescope observations agree with those predictions, they strengthen confidence in current theories. Unexpected differences, however, may point toward physical processes that scientists have yet to fully understand.
"With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics," said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. "To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video."
Recreating the Universe's First 2 Billion Years
Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation hydrodynamics simulation ever produced. In simple terms, it uses powerful computers to calculate how gas, dark matter, and light influenced one another as the young universe developed. By following these interactions across the first 2 billion years after the Big Bang, researchers can examine how the earliest galaxies formed and how their activity changed the enormous clouds of gas surrounding them.
The simulation models a volume of space more than 100 times larger than those covered by earlier comparable projects. Its virtual universe spans a cube approximately 1.5 billion light-years on each side, providing a view of cosmic evolution on a scale comparable to the vast regions that today's most advanced telescopes can study.
Another major advance is Lumina's treatment of helium reionization, a process in which radiation strips electrons from helium atoms. For the first time, a simulation of this kind follows that transformation as it unfolds while simultaneously accounting for how it affects the surrounding universe. This allows scientists to study the relationship between evolving galaxies, radiation, and the gas that fills the space between them.
"We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina," said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. "For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation."
A Massive Supercomputer Powers the Virtual Cosmos
Recreating such an enormous portion of cosmic history demanded extraordinary computing resources. The team used more than 15,000 graphics processing units on Frontier, one of the world's fastest supercomputers, housed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.
That processing power enabled the researchers to simulate an exceptionally large region of the early universe without sacrificing the fine detail needed to investigate individual galaxies and other important structures. As a result, Lumina can capture the broader evolution of the cosmos while also tracking processes involved in the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes.
Testing the Mysteries of the Early Universe
Beyond recreating cosmic history, Lumina provides a powerful new framework for investigating how the universe developed. Researchers plan to use it to explore the movement of gas between galaxies, the influence of radiation left over from the Big Bang, and the emergence of regions where stars formed at especially high rates.
By placing these predictions alongside observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, and other instruments, scientists hope to build a more complete picture of the universe's earliest chapters. Any unexpected differences between the simulated cosmos and the real one could provide valuable clues, potentially revealing where current theories need to be refined or reconsidered.

- Oliver Zier, Aaron Smith, Xuejian Shen, Rongrong Liu, Rahul Kannan, Sonja M Koehler, Volker Springel, Rüdiger Pakmor, Mark Vogelsberger, Teodora-Elena Bulichi, Lars Hernquist. Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2026; 552 (4) DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag1469

articles.title: Are sharks really older than trees?
articles.text:
Are sharks really older than trees?
It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?
You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.
But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.
"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."
The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.
This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.
For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees — such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England — also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.
But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.
Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.
"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.
Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.
These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.
Related mysteries
Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.
There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.
"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

Alice Sun is a science journalist based in Brooklyn. She covers a wide range of topics, including ecology, neuroscience, social science and technology. Her work has appeared in Audubon, Sierra, Inverse and more. For her bachelor's degree, she studied environmental biology at McGill University in Canada. She also has a master's degree in science, health and environmental reporting from NYU.

articles.title: Lần đầu tiên NASA phải kêu gọi sự giúp đỡ từ công chúng, trong công cuộc khám phá sao Mộc
articles.text:
Tàu thăm dò Juno của NASA là tác giả của một trong số những bức ảnh đẹp nhất về sao Mộc trong những năm trở lại đây. Mới đây. cơ quan vũ trụ đã thành lập một dự án khoa học công dân để công chúng có thể giúp sức trong công việc xác định các đặc điểm khí quyển của hành tinh khí khổng lồ.
Dự án có tên Jovian Vortex Hunter và được dẫn dắt bởi các nhà nghiên cứu tại Đại học Minnesota và NASA, đặt mục tiêu phân loại các loại mây khác nhau trên sao Mộc. Các nhà nghiên cứu quan tâm đến việc xác định động lực học của chất lỏng cơ bản dẫn đến sự hình thành của các xoáy và cấu trúc hỗn loạn trên hành tinh này và kiểm tra các hình ảnh thu được bởi sứ mệnh Juno.
Sao Mộc là hành tinh khí khổng lồ lớn nhất trong Hệ Mặt trời
Sao Mộc chủ yếu chứa vật chất ở trạng thái khí và lỏng. Nó là hành tinh khí khổng lồ lớn nhất trong Hệ Mặt trời với đường kính 142.984 km tại xích đạo. Khối lượng riêng trung bình của hành tinh bằng 1,326 g/cm³, và có khối lượng riêng lớn nhất trong số bốn hành tinh khí khổng lồ.
Nhà nghiên cứu sau tiến sĩ vật lý và thiên văn học Ramanakumar Sankar, người đứng đầu dự án Jovian Vortex Hunter, cho biết: "Có rất nhiều hình ảnh mà nhóm nhỏ của chúng tôi sẽ mất vài năm để kiểm tra tất cả chúng".
"Chúng tôi cần sự giúp đỡ từ công chúng để xác định những hình ảnh nào có xoáy, chúng ở đâu và chúng xuất hiện như thế nào. Với danh mục các đặc điểm (đặc biệt là xoáy), chúng tôi có thể nghiên cứu vật lý đằng sau cách các đặc điểm này hình thành, và chúng liên quan như thế nào đến cấu trúc của khí quyển, đặc biệt là bên dưới các đám mây, nơi chúng tôi không thể quan sát trực tiếp chúng".
NASA cần mọi người giúp đỡ để xác định những hình ảnh nào có xoáy trên sao Mộc.
Vệ tinh Juno của NASA đã có mặt ở bên ngoài khí quyển của sao Mộc từ năm 2016 trong sứ mệnh khám phá hành tinh này. Đó là con tàu vũ trụ có chiều dài bằng 1 sân bóng rổ và quay quanh quỹ đạo của sao Mộc. Hiện vệ tinh này cùng kính viễn vọng James Webb là những công cụ quan trọng giúp NASA cung cấp nhiều cái nhìn chi tiết về sao Mộc, phục vụ việc nghiên cứu.
Các nhà nghiên cứu hy vọng sẽ trả lời được ba câu hỏi chính: Có sự khác biệt về sự đa dạng giữa các đặc điểm xoáy thuận và anticylonic, cấu trúc đám mây khác nhau có thể có là gì, và những khối màu nâu (xoáy thuận dài có màu nâu đậm) khác với các đặc điểm xoáy thuận khác như thế nào?
Trên sao Mộc, hầu hết các đám mây được tạo ra từ các chất hóa học không phải nước.
"Bầu khí quyển của sao Mộc rất giống với bầu khí quyển của chúng ta: có những đám mây có hình dạng và kích thước khác nhau", các nhà nghiên cứu của Jovian Vortex Hunter giải thích: "Trên sao Mộc, hầu hết các đám mây được tạo ra từ các chất hóa học không phải nước, và có thể có kích thước vài nghìn km".
"Một số đám mây cũng được tạo ra từ những cơn bão mạnh có chiều cao hơn 50 km hoặc thậm chí là hàng trăm kilomet. Việc tìm ra cách những đám mây này hình thành là rất quan trọng để hiểu được bầu khí quyển của sao Mộc, và các quá trình tạo ra những đặc điểm tuyệt vời mà chúng ta thấy".
Jovian đề cập đến loại đám mây mà nhóm chủ yếu quan tâm đến việc nghiên cứu.
"Các đám mây khác nhau trên sao Mộc hình thành trong các điều kiện khí quyển khác nhau (ví dụ như bão, lốc xoáy), tương tự như cách chúng ta nhận được các loại mây khác nhau khi bầu khí quyển tĩnh lặng hoặc có bão. Các loại mây trên sao Mộc cũng phụ thuộc nhiều vào hóa chất hình thành chúng. sao Mộc có ba lớp mây chính: những đám mây amoniac chủ yếu là những đám mây mà chúng ta có thể nhìn thấy vì chúng hình thành ở phía trên cùng, tiếp theo là một lớp amoni hydrosunfua và sâu trong bầu khí quyển (khoảng 150 km bên dưới các đám mây amoniac), có thể sẽ là những đám mây nước dày".
"Để hiểu được những đám mây khác nhau này hình thành như thế nào, chúng ta cần xem xét sự đa dạng của các đặc điểm đám mây trong khí quyển. Trong dự án này, chúng tôi sẽ tạo danh mục đó và nhóm các tính năng đám mây khác nhau từ hình ảnh JunoCam lại với nhau".
Jovian Vortex Hunter được phân loại là một dự án khoa học công dân, là sự hợp tác giữa các nhà khoa học và các thành viên quan tâm của công chúng.
| Sao Mộc là hành tinh lớn và nặng nhất trong Hệ Mặt trời. Bán kính trung bình của nó là 69.911± 6 km, lớn gấp 10,97 lần Trái Đất. Khối lượng sao Mộc là 1,8986.1027 kg, tương đương 317,8 lần Trái Đất. Mặc dù vậy, vì là một hành tinh khí, nó có mật độ vật chất nhẹ hơn vào khoảng 1,326 g/cm3. Bên cạnh đó, vì là một khối khí khổng lồ, sao Mộc không có một bề mặt thực sự. Nếu ai đó đứng trên nó, đơn giản là họ sẽ chìm và đi xuyên vào lõi rắn của hành tinh. Kết quả là lực hấp dẫn trên sao Mộc (được định nghĩa trên đỉnh đám mây khí) khoảng 24,79 m/s2, tương đương 2,528 g. |

articles.title: A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
articles.text:
A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - San Diego
- Summary:
- Scientists at UC San Diego have developed a surprising new way to store digital information using light instead of magnets, potentially paving the way for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient memory devices. By precisely shaping and shrinking an ultrafast laser beam, researchers demonstrated that they could switch magnetic states in a material, the basic process used to write digital data. The technique could potentially operate more than 1,000 times faster than conventional magnetic switching methods.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a new way to control magnetism using light, a breakthrough that could eventually make digital data storage faster, more compact, and more energy-efficient.
The research, conducted by engineers at the University of California San Diego, was published in the journal Nature Communications.
Modern hard drives and other storage systems rely on tiny magnetic regions to encode digital information as 1s and 0s. Writing new data usually involves applying an external magnetic field to change the orientation of these regions. However, this process consumes considerable energy and places limits on how quickly information can be recorded.
The UC San Diego team has demonstrated an alternative that uses light to change these magnetic states, a technique known as optical switching. Light can deliver energy in extremely short bursts and can be focused onto remarkably small areas, potentially allowing magnetic information to be written much faster and with less energy. According to the researchers, optical switching could achieve speeds more than 1,000 times greater than conventional methods that depend on external magnetic fields.
Shrinking Laser Light To Improve Data Storage
To make this possible, the engineers used a specialized ultrafast laser and carefully modified the shape and size of its beam. The resulting beam was dramatically smaller than those employed in earlier experiments, with the researchers describing a reduction of tens of orders of magnitude.
Such precise control over light could also make it possible to store significantly more information within a limited amount of space. By directing laser energy onto smaller magnetic regions, future memory devices could potentially hold more data without increasing their physical size.
"The smaller the size of the beam, the smaller and more dense the optical memory," said study senior author Abdoulaye Ndao, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.
Until now, optical switching faced two important restrictions. Earlier experiments had succeeded only with extremely thin magnetic structures containing no more than three magnetic layers. The process also required light with a particular polarization, meaning its electromagnetic waves had to be oriented in a specific way.
"Past experiments had found that increasing the material's thickness beyond three layers suppressed optical switching," Ndao said. "That put a constraint on the overall thickness of the magnetic material and thus, its ability to retain memory in the long term."
These restrictions limited the potential usefulness of optical memory, particularly because thicker magnetic structures can help preserve stored information over extended periods.
Scientists Overcome a Major Magnetic Memory Barrier
By carefully reshaping and reducing the size of the laser beam, Ndao and his colleagues found a way around both obstacles.
They successfully demonstrated optical switching in a substantially thicker magnetic structure containing nine alternating layers of platinum and cobalt. The researchers also showed that the process worked without requiring a particular polarization of light.
"We've optically engineered the light to change the physics that's happening in the material at the micro- and nanoscale," said study first author Muhammad Waleed Khalid, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student in Ndao's research group.
The technique works by concentrating laser energy into an extremely small region and delivering a sequence of ultrafast pulses.
The first pulses briefly heat a localized area of the magnetic material, causing a small region to reverse its magnetic orientation. Additional pulses gradually enlarge that reversed region until the new magnetic state becomes stable.
This carefully controlled sequence allows the researchers to manipulate magnetism in ways that had not been achieved using conventional laser beams.
"Working with a specialized laser allowed us to optically engineer the beam to have a certain shape and size," Khalid said. "That gave us the room to explore more fundamental physics, which cannot be done with conventional beam lasers."
An Unexpected Discovery That Required Repeated Testing
The unusual results initially proved difficult to establish within the scientific community. Because the effects differed so greatly from what earlier experiments had suggested was possible, the researchers needed extensive additional testing to confirm their observations.
"The effects we were seeing were so new and unusual that we had a difficult time convincing others in the field that our discovery was not a one-time fluke. We spent a lot of time and effort repeating and verifying our experiments to substantiate our work to the optics community," Khalid added.
The breakthrough emerged from a collaboration between researchers specializing in two areas that do not often intersect: optics, which focuses on light, and magnetic materials.
Ndao's optics research team worked with Eric Fullerton, an expert in thin-film magnetic materials at UC San Diego. Fullerton is a professor of electrical and computer engineering and of chemical and nano engineering, as well as the Endowed Chair Professor of the university's Center for Memory and Recording Research.
Combining these areas of expertise allowed the team to investigate an established problem in magnetic memory from a different perspective. Rather than developing a magnetic material with new properties, the researchers focused on changing how light interacts with an existing material.
"Instead of designing a new material to enable optical switching, we redesigned the light itself and showed new properties that were not previously thought to be possible," Ndao said.
The Next Challenge for Ultrafast Computer Memory
Although the results point toward promising possibilities for future storage technologies, significant technical obstacles remain before optical switching could be used in everyday electronic devices.
One major challenge is the specialized ultrafast laser required for the experiments. Current versions are not easily incorporated into computer chips, making practical integration difficult.
The researchers are considering other ways to achieve similar results, including identifying magnetic materials that could respond to laser systems more suitable for integration into electronic hardware.
They are also attempting to reduce the laser beam's size even further, with a target of just a few hundred nanometers. To accomplish this, the team is exploring optical structures capable of concentrating light into progressively smaller regions.
These efforts are aimed at understanding how precisely engineered light can manipulate magnetism at extremely small scales. If the remaining engineering challenges can be overcome, the approach could help enable a new generation of compact, high-density memory devices capable of writing digital information at much greater speeds.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Muhammad Waleed Khalid, Sheena K. K. Patel, Koffi-Emanuel Sadzi, Mohammed Salah El Hadri, Sergio A. Montoya, Stéphane Mangin, Eric E. Fullerton, Abdoulaye Ndao. Optical beam shaping induced reconfigurable magnetic domains. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77572-3
