articles.title: Keyboards of The Verge
articles.text:
What is a keyboard if not the original brain-computer interface? You can tap on a touchscreen or talk to the computer, but if your work involves getting information out of your head and into the computer, you’re probably spending a lot of time using a keyboard.
Keyboards of The Verge
From the strictly utilitarian to the ergonomic to the obsessive, these are the keyboards we use every day.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
We’ve written about many keyboards over the years, from the legendary Optimus Maximus to the ultra-luxe Seneca to even stranger fare. But I wanted to know what my coworkers actually use. As I’d hoped, there’s a wide range. Some of us are strictly utilitarian, optimizing for ergonomics or functionality. Others obsess over every detail of feel, sound, layout, and looks. Still others — maybe the most enlightened — just use whatever’s in front of them.
NuPhy came up a lot. So did Keychron. The Apple Magic Keyboard has its stalwarts. The Kinesis Freestyle split is surprisingly well represented. And there are other, odder entries.
These are the keyboards of The Verge.
Jay Peters, senior reporter
I currently use the Kinesis Freestyle Pro, and I’ve used it for so long that I’ve forgotten when I first got it. In the late 2010s, I had wrist pain that led me to try a lot of ergonomic keyboards so I could keep using computers. The Freestyle Pro — with its optional tenting add-ons that give the keyboard a significant angle and the palm rest accessories — just feels the best under my hands. If this keyboard broke, I’d buy another one the same day.
Kallie Plagge, senior copy editor
For work, I use a simple Keychron K2. But for my gaming PC, I use the Logitech G713 wired mechanical keyboard — the one that comes with the cloud wrist rest. Did I mostly buy it for the wrist rest? Perhaps. But I do love the tenkeyless layout. My previous gaming keyboard had a number pad and two rows of programmable keys, which was cool, but I mostly used the number pad to type the alt code for em dashes. The G713, on the other hand, meets my gaming requirements without taking up half my desk. I’m not playing anything competitive on my PC that requires adjustable actuation points, so the GX red linear switches do the trick. (And they’re the right amount of clicky, unlike the overly loud ones on my K2.) So yeah, maybe I bought it for the sleek all-white look and the cute wrist rest, but it’s also a great keyboard, too.
Danielle Steussy, product manager
I’m using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with the numeric keypad. Some version of Apple’s keyboard has been on my desk for over 20 years, starting with the Apple A1048 that came with my first Mac in college. I loved that keyboard (the sound of my fingertips hitting the keys — swoon!) and I wore it down to the point of keys falling off. Since then, I’ve stuck with Apple’s wireless keyboards. Honestly, it’s a pretty keyboard, but otherwise unremarkable, and blends in with my desk setup (which also is kind of the point, right?). My biggest complaints are that the key legends wear off faster than I’d like and the Bluetooth connection isn’t totally reliable. It’s not my favorite Apple product (by far), but after two decades of muscle memory, I’m not switching anytime soon.
David Pierce, editor at large
I really want to be a mechanical keyboard guy. I love typing on mechanical keyboards! I love the clackiness, the way they look on my desk, the huge personality upgrade that comes with them. But then I start typing notes during a call, and someone goes, “Sorry, what’s that noise in the background?” and I bail on my mechanical keyboard. I used Logitech’s MX Keys S for the last few years, and love that keyboard, but recently replaced it with an Apple Magic Keyboard (black keys, number pad) because I got tired of typing my 1Password password all the time. I bought a $200 keyboard for the Touch ID button. Ugh.
Jacob Kastrenakes, executive editor
My keyboard is probably the single dumbest thing I have ever spent money on, but it brings me joy every time I look at it. The setup matches a Boop Redux case with the GMK Dots keycaps and Silent Bluish White (V2) switches. I didn’t so much want to get deep into the mechanical keyboard hobby as I wanted to have this exact keyboard after I saw images of the Dots keycaps on the (original) Boop case floating around in around 2022. It looks cool, right? (Right?) From a practical standpoint, this is fully a downgrade from the Apple Magic Keyboard I was using before: It’s bigger and louder, with fewer keys, and I probably type a bit slower on it, too, owing to the longer key strokes. It’s also a few hundred dollars more expensive. But you know what? I think it looks really cool.
Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer
Since I review laptops and occasionally mechanical keyboards, I’m constantly changing what I type on. But one of my personal keyboards that remains close to my heart is my TM680 (aka the Gamakay LK67). It’s a cheap bare-bones 65-percent kit I bought from AliExpress in 2021. I was inspired by the video that YouTuber Scott “Keybored” Kim did on it, so I dabbled in modding it.
I started with basic Gateron Milky Yellow linear switches and some crummy knockoff Evangelion keycaps, but I later upgraded to a much nicer MT3 3277 keycap set. I then spent hours individually lubricating and adding switch films to each of the Gaterons, lubing the stabilizers, inserting some foam into the base of the chassis, and adding layers of painter’s tape to the bottom of the PCB. This combination made my basic build sound and feel much better, and it shaped my preference for deeper, “thockier”-sounding boards that I still have today.
My old TM680 is easily outdone by just about any budget board these days. Many switches now arrive pre-lubed from the factory, and even a sub-$100 keyboard can sound and feel nicer right out of the box. But doing the mods myself felt special. I doubt I’ll ever bother with all that work again, because lubing and filming switches is just too tedious and time-consuming, but I’m glad I at least experienced it once. And no matter how many new keyboards I test, I intend on keeping my TM680.
TC Sottek, former senior editor
I used to buy pretty expensive gaming keyboards that I can’t even name now without digging deep through email archives for receipts. I know I once spent nearly $200 on a full-size Razer mechanical keyboard with a numpad that took up a ton of desk space. The key travel felt amazing and it had a great sound. But what I really remember was knocking over a full glass of water on it. Oops! Farewell, keyboard.
Unfortunately, this happened not once, not twice, but three times for me with relatively expensive keyboards over the years. Yes, I should have learned to contain liquids in bottles on my desk. But now I’ve settled for cheap–but–still-good options the same way I’ve done with the several pairs of earbuds I’ve ruined over the years. (Former serial AirPods Pro user here, now fully on board the Nothing Ear train.)
I’m currently rocking a Keychron K2 with a 75-percent layout. It took me a minute to get my 120-plus WPM back on a cramped keyboard, but now it works just fine and I like the look. I’ll probably splurge again someday on a really compelling set of keycaps.
Meredith Haggerty, senior reports editor
I use the laptop that is attached to the M2 MacBook Air I was issued by my employer. It’s right there whenever I need it, but I think they should make a version that’s covered in way fewer crumbs.
Emma Roth, news writer
I have a toxic relationship with my keyboard, a Corsair K55 RGB Pro that I picked up for half the price at a thrift store a few years ago. It’s a decent, budget-friendly keyboard that’s fine to use for gaming and writing. But recently, it’s been getting on my nerves. The keys no longer light up when I turn my computer on, and it sometimes doesn’t sync properly with my Corsair iCUE software. I can’t see what I’m pressing unless the keyboard is lit up (the keys are translucent), so I’ve had to resort to unplugging the keyboard and plugging it back in when I turn on my computer, which usually does the trick. The issue is probably software-related, but I might just get fed up enough to buy myself a fancy new mechanical keyboard.
Andrew J. Hawkins, transportation editor
NuPhy Air75 V3
The latest version of a Verge favorite, this low-profile mechanical keyboard has long battery life, tri-mode wireless, hot-swappable low-profile switches, and remappability.
I have never been a keyboard guy. I was content to use the one attached to my laptop or whatever wireless Apple version I could get for cheap. But I changed when a coworker turned me on to the NuPhy Air75 mechanical keyboard. The keys feel great, the “clack-clack” sound is so satisfying, and the overall design is retro without seeming outdated. That big yellow spacebar, the delightfully orange Enter button, the subtly aquamarine Escape key — chef’s kiss. Connectivity is robust and the battery lasts for days before needing to be recharged. It took some getting used to, but I chalk it up to not being able to use my left ring finger while typing since breaking it in a freak scooter accident years ago. But that’s a different story.
Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor
A 65 percent gasket-mounted wired mechanical keyboard kit. Use the Design Lab to customize its top, bottom, switchplate, and accent colors, plate materials, and mechanical or electrocapacitive PCBs. (Switches, stabilizers, and keycaps sold separately)
These days I mostly swap between a Leopold FC660C and a couple of Omnitype Bauer Lites. The Leopold is a Topre board I’ve had since 2017; I’ve modified it a fair bit over the years, with silencing rings, a new controller board, and Ursa keycaps. I fell in love with the unbeatable tactility of Topre switches early, but I love the customizability of regular mechanical keyboards too, so I’ve spent a lot of time over the past decade trying to find something that combines the best of both.
I got most of the way there with my first Bauer Lite a couple years ago; its Kailh Deep Sea Silent Islet switches are linear, but they’re the closest to Topre I ever found in an MX-compatible switch. (They’re basically identical to the ones in the HHKB Studio). It’s also fluorescent orange, which just makes me happy. I built another one recently with DynaCap electro-capacitive switches and MTNU Space Cadet keycaps. Do I need three wired 65-percent keyboards with very similar layouts and pretty similar typing feel? Probably not. But I have them anyway. Also several other keyboards.
Stevie Bonifield, news writer
I love trying out new mechanical keyboards (and have reviewed dozens of them), but for the last year straight I’ve been using a NuPhy Halo75 V2 as my daily driver. I’ve built several custom mechanical keyboards over the years, but I haven’t changed anything on this one yet. I may swap out the switches and keycaps at some point. NuPhy’s tactile Mint switches are fairly good, but I miss the Leobog Juggle V2 switches I have on a wired keyboard that used to be my daily driver.
I’ve been pretty happy with how the Halo75 sounds and feels out of the box. I also appreciate that the design’s simple enough to not be distracting while still having a few pops of color. The battery life could be a bit better, but there’s not much to complain about overall — the build quality feels solid, the keycaps and switches have held up well over months of heavy typing, and the Halo75 works smoothly with both Mac and Linux. It also has Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, which was a must-have for me since I like to hop between multiple devices from the same keyboard.
I’ve had a great experience with the Halo75 so far, but I’d recommend it mainly for Mac users — macOS is where it really shines. It works fine for gaming, but I’d suggest configuring it with linear switches if you want to use it for gaming, rather than the tactile switches I went with.
Brad Bourque, commerce writer
I started building mechanical keyboards a few years ago, and have a few in my quiver, but the one I use most often is a NovelKeys NK65 in white. This 65-percent keyboard is sturdy and compact, with just enough extra buttons for work or surfing the web, and arrow keys in case I want to sneak in some gaming. It’s a hot-swap board, so I change up the setup occasionally, but it’s currently equipped with SA Mizu keycaps and C3Equalz x TKC Dragonfruit tactile switches, with a matching desk pad and metal Escape key.
Adi Robertson, senior tech & policy editor
I’ve upgraded my writing equipment since 2021, when I proudly displayed an Apple Magic Keyboard on top of a piece of cardboard on top of a MacBook with several nonfunctional butterfly keys. And as much as I love collecting dedicated typing machines — I’ve got a Freewrite, a 1990 Smith Corona word processor, a beautiful 1930s Underwood manual typewriter, and an impressively awful faux-vintage one from the zombie-brand era of Royal, among others — I discovered my perfect work setup is low-profile mechanicals: clicky enough to be satisfying, short enough travel to not hamper my typing speed. (I’m still slightly faster on a chiclet keyboard, but I’ll take the hit.) I spent a few years with a NuPhy Air75, but fell victim to its fairly well-known swollen battery issues, so I’ve since switched to the Iqunix MQ80 — which has less of a fun retro color scheme, but a more satisfying heft. I love the idea of giving it a cool custom keycap makeover someday, but for now I’m too cheap and lazy, and perfectly satisfied with its Mirror’s Edge-y sci-fi white.
Sean Hollister, senior editor
Keychron V1 Max
Keychrons are the equivalent of Toyotas in the mechanical keyboard world, offering reliability and a great value for the money. The 75-percent V1 Max features RGB backlighting, USB-A and USB-C 2.4GHz dongles, and modifier keycaps for both Windows and Mac. Plus, it offers simple customization that lets you remap any key to your favorite macro command.
I noped out of mechanical keyboards for years because they were too clicky! No good for my shared office space. Then, Verge alum Dan Seifert clued me into the near-silent Boba U4 switches, which I installed in a Keychron V1 (love the small size, love the QMK programmable lighting, love the volume dial!) and I almost never looked back.
I did have to re-spring and lube all the switches to get a familiar level of spring action, which was easy enough. Some of the switches have spontaneously stopped working over the past four years, but it only takes seconds to hot-swap another one in. And a family member bought me 8BitDo’s awesome Nintendo-themed wireless mechanical numpad, so I’m covered there too.
But I don’t think it’s endgame. When I switch back from my laptop, I often miss the faster, more effortless typing I can do on its lower-profile keys. Maybe it’s time for something new.
Robert Hart, AI reporter
I should preface this by saying I know absolutely nothing about keyboards. My standards for what I want are pretty modest: It should work, move easily around my desk, and not hurt my wrists. Looking cool doesn’t hurt.
I’ve cycled through a few over the years, mostly geometric oddities — sorry, ergonomic — like the Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Desktop and Logitech Ergo K860, which were rather unwieldy. I also tried ordering the Kinesis Freestyle Pro Jay uses, but gave up after the supplier tried to pass off clearly damaged kit (read: tangled hair clogging everything) as brand-new.
I’ve been using the Keychron K2 Pro for a few years now. It’s compact, looks great, and holds a charge well. It has no number pad, but that keeps things nimble, and it handily switches between multiple computers I use on the go. There are also fancy lights, though I usually turn them off. The main downsides are having to regularly Google the key commands needed to control it — a pain when those lights won’t stop strobing like a hyperactive Christmas tree. It supports key remapping, so I may attempt a new layout like Dvorak sometime soon.
Elizabeth Lopatto, senior internet typist
First of all, keyboards should be clacky. I want to sound like I am firing a machine gun while I write. Second, due to assorted repetitive stress injuries, my keyboard needs to be split. So I am typing with a light-up gaming keyboard — the lights are optional, I just like them — called the Kinesis Gaming Freestyle Edge RGB. Do I game? Uh, well, I do crossword puzzles. But the Cherry MX Blue switches guarantee I sound fucking productive while I do them.
Nilay Patel, editor-in-chief
Very boring Apple keyboards. Every five years the right side of the spacebar stops working and I buy a new one. Full-size. Numpad for life.

articles.title: Claude Max 20x đổi tên thành Ultra, bỏ giới hạn 5 giờ
articles.text:
Giá và hạn mức theo tuần không đổi, nhưng cái tên mới đặt lại câu hỏi "20x" thực chất là gấp bao nhiêu lần gói Pro.
Ngày 30/10, Anthropic thông báo đổi tên hai gói cao cấp của Claude dành cho cá nhân. Max 5x trở thành Max, giữ mức 100 USD mỗi tháng, tương đương khoảng 2,6 triệu đồng. Max 20x trở thành Ultra, giữ mức 200 USD, tương đương khoảng 5,3 triệu đồng. Người đang đăng ký được chuyển sang tên mới tự động, không cần thao tác gì.
Thay đổi đáng kể hơn nằm ở cách tính hạn mức. Trước đây, người dùng gói cao cấp của Claude chịu hai lớp giới hạn: một "phiên" 5 giờ, dùng hết là phải chờ phiên làm mới, và một hạn mức tính theo tuần. Với Ultra, lớp thứ nhất bị bỏ đối với tài khoản đã xác minh. Người dùng chỉ còn bị tính theo tuần, ở mức 10 lần gói Pro (gói Pro giá 20 USD mỗi tháng, hơn 520.000 đồng). Thay đổi này có ích nhất cho người chạy Claude Code hoặc giao cho Claude những tác vụ dài, vốn dễ bị ngắt giữa chừng khi cạn phiên 5 giờ.
Ultra không phải gói "không giới hạn". Anthropic cho biết hạn mức tuần vẫn áp dụng cho mọi mô hình, có thêm một hạn mức tuần riêng cho dòng mô hình Fable, và hãng có thể đặt thêm các giới hạn khác để đảm bảo công bằng giữa người dùng. Hạn mức tuần của Ultra giữ nguyên so với Max 20x.
"Tài khoản đã xác minh" do Anthropic tự quyết định, dựa trên các yếu tố như lịch sử tài khoản và thanh toán. Tài khoản mới đăng ký vẫn bị giới hạn tạm thời cho đến khi được xác minh, và hãng sẽ gỡ tự động. Xác minh số điện thoại lúc thanh toán là một bước khác, không giúp gỡ giới hạn này. Để kiểm tra, người dùng vào Settings > Usage: nếu không thấy thanh "Current session" thì tài khoản đã được xác minh. Việc gỡ giới hạn triển khai theo từng đợt, bắt đầu từ ngày 30/10 với phần lớn người đăng ký hiện hữu, và người dùng sẽ nhận email khi giới hạn được dỡ.
Anthropic giải thích lý do đổi tên khá cụ thể. Khi ra gói cao nhất hồi tháng 4/2025, Claude chỉ có đúng một giới hạn là 5 giờ, ở mức 20 lần gói Pro, nên gói được gọi là Max 20x. Sau đó hãng bổ sung hạn mức tuần và đặt ở mức 10 lần gói Pro, trong khi giới hạn 5 giờ vẫn giữ 20 lần. Giờ giới hạn 5 giờ bị bỏ, con số còn lại trên gói 200 USD là 10 lần mỗi tuần, nên cái tên "20x" không còn mô tả đúng thứ người dùng nhận được.
Cách đặt tên này từng bị chất vấn. Ngày 14/6, người dùng Karl Kahn nộp đơn đề nghị công nhận vụ kiện tập thể lên tòa liên bang ở bắc California. Đơn này cho rằng khi tính cả hạn mức tuần, Max 20x chỉ tương đương khoảng 6 đến 8 lần gói Pro thay vì 20 lần, còn Max 5x khoảng 3,5 lần thay vì 5 lần. Anthropic từng mô tả hệ số "20x" tính theo từng phiên 5 giờ, còn hạn mức tuần là giới hạn riêng. Vụ kiện chưa được công nhận là kiện tập thể và chưa có phán quyết nào. Hiện chưa có thông tin cho thấy việc đổi tên liên quan đến vụ kiện này.
Tính theo các con số Anthropic công bố trên trang giá, gói Pro là 1 lần, Max là 5 lần và Ultra là 10 lần hạn mức tuần, ứng với mức giá 20, 100 và 200 USD. Nói cách khác, mỗi gói đều có đơn giá quanh 20 USD cho mỗi "tuần Pro", và Ultra đắt gấp đôi Max cho hạn mức tuần gấp đôi. Điều này khác với ấn tượng "gấp 4 lần" mà cặp tên 5x và 20x từng gợi ra.
Hai lớp giới hạn này vốn đã giằng co nhau. Ngày 22/10, đơn vị nghiên cứu SemiAnalysis đo hai tài khoản Max 20x trong cùng một ngày, dùng cùng mô hình, và thấy một tài khoản có cửa sổ 5 giờ lớn hơn khoảng 19% nhưng hạn mức tuần nhỏ hơn khoảng 20%. SemiAnalysis cho rằng Anthropic có vẻ đang thử nghiệm chia nhóm người dùng. Đây mới là quan sát từ bên ngoài.
Đổi tên cũng đưa Claude về gần cách gọi của đối thủ. Google bán gói AI Ultra ở hai bậc: 99,99 USD (khoảng 2,6 triệu đồng) cho mức gấp 5 lần và 199,99 USD (khoảng 5,3 triệu đồng) cho mức gấp 20 lần hạn mức của AI Pro. OpenAI có ChatGPT Pro ở ba bậc 100, 200 và 500 USD, và cho biết hiện các gói Pro không áp giới hạn 5 giờ trong Codex và ChatGPT Work. Việc Anthropic bỏ giới hạn 5 giờ ở gói cao nhất đi cùng hướng với OpenAI.
Với người dùng hiện hữu, trước mắt chưa cần làm gì. Người dùng Max giữ nguyên quyền lợi, còn người dùng Ultra sẽ thấy giới hạn 5 giờ biến mất dần khi tài khoản được xác minh. Một số màn hình tài khoản cũ có thể vẫn hiển thị dòng "gấp 20 lần Pro" trong giai đoạn chuyển tiếp. Ultra hiện chỉ bán theo tháng, mức 200 USD áp dụng cho đăng ký qua web, còn đăng ký qua ứng dụng di động có thể có giá khác.

articles.title: Doanh thu không quá 10 tỷ đồng/năm, được giảm 30% thuế thu nhập cá nhân
articles.text:
Cá nhân kinh doanh doanh thu không quá 10 tỷ đồng được giảm 30% thuế
Chính phủ ban hành Nghị định số 398/2026/NĐ-CP quy định chi tiết Nghị quyết số 43/2026/QH16 về giảm thuế thu nhập cá nhân (TNCN), thuế thu nhập doanh nghiệp (TNDN) đối với cá nhân và doanh nghiệp.
Theo đó, Nghị định quy định giảm 30% số thuế TNCN phải nộp của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026 và năm 2027 đối với thu nhập từ kinh doanh của cá nhân cư trú có mức doanh thu hằng năm của năm 2026, năm 2027 không quá 10 tỷ đồng.
Cụ thể, việc giảm thuế quy định tại Điều này áp dụng đối với cá nhân cư trú có hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh, bao gồm cả cá nhân đăng ký thành lập hộ kinh doanh hoặc người được các thành viên hộ gia đình ủy quyền làm người đại diện hộ kinh doanh (cá nhân kinh doanh).
Số thuế TNCN được giảm của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 được tính trên số thuế TNCN phải nộp phát sinh từ toàn bộ thu nhập từ hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh của cá nhân kinh doanh, không phân biệt phương pháp tính thuế TNCN.
Doanh thu năm làm căn cứ xác định cá nhân kinh doanh thuộc đối tượng được giảm thuế TNCN thực hiện theo quy định tại Điều 4, Điều 5 Nghị định số 68/2026 quy định về chính sách thuế và quản lý thuế đối với hộ kinh doanh, cá nhân kinh doanh (được sửa đổi, bổ sung bởi Nghị định số 141/2026).
Kê khai giảm thuế: Cá nhân kinh doanh dự kiến doanh thu trong kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 nếu không quá 10 tỷ đồng thì kê khai giảm thuế TNCN theo Mẫu số 01 tại Phụ lục kèm theo Nghị định và nộp cùng hồ sơ khai thuế quý, 6 tháng đầu năm, 6 tháng cuối năm, năm.
Tổ chức, cá nhân thực hiện khấu trừ, khai thay, nộp thay thuế TNCN cho cá nhân kinh doanh, căn cứ doanh thu nếu không quá 10 tỷ đồng thuộc phạm vi khấu trừ, khai thay, nộp thay và quy định tại Điều này, tổ chức, cá nhân thực hiện giảm 30% số thuế TNCN phải khấu trừ, khai thay, nộp thay theo tháng, quý hoặc theo lần phát sinh, kê khai theo Mẫu số 02 tại Phụ lục kèm theo Nghị định này và nộp cùng Tờ khai TNCN của tổ chức, cá nhân thực hiện khấu trừ, khai thay, nộp thay thuế TNCN cho cá nhân kinh doanh.
Căn cứ tổng doanh thu thực tế của toàn bộ hoạt động kinh doanh, cá nhân kinh doanh xác định số thuế TNCN phải nộp và được giảm theo quy định tại Điều này.
Trường hợp tổng doanh thu thực tế trong năm vượt quá 10 tỷ đồng thì không được áp dụng mức giảm thuế và phải nộp bổ sung số thuế TNCN đã được giảm, kê khai điều chỉnh theo Mẫu số 03 tại Phụ lục kèm theo Nghị định và nộp cùng hồ sơ khai thuế của kỳ phát sinh doanh thu lũy kế tính từ đầu năm trên 10 tỷ đồng.
Số thuế TNCN phải nộp bổ sung do xác định lại điều kiện giảm thuế theo quy định này không tính tiền chậm nộp đến thời hạn nộp hồ sơ khai thuế theo quy định của kỳ phát sinh doanh thu lũy kế trên 10 tỷ đồng.
Trường hợp đã kê khai thuế TNCN nhưng chưa kê khai số thuế được giảm theo quy định tại khoản 1, khoản 2, khoản 3 Điều này thì được khai điều chỉnh, bổ sung hồ sơ khai thuế đã khai hoặc xác định giảm thuế khi quyết toán thuế năm theo quy định.
Trường hợp cá nhân kinh doanh nộp thuế theo thuế suất trên doanh thu nếu nộp thừa thì cuối năm được bù trừ, hoàn trả, hoàn trả kiêm bù trừ thu ngân sách theo quy định đối với số thuế nộp thừa.
Trường hợp cá nhân khai bổ sung hồ sơ khai thuế TNCN của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 hoặc theo quyết định, kết luận, thông báo kết quả thanh tra, kiểm tra, kiểm toán của cơ quan thuế, cơ quan có thẩm quyền làm tăng số thuế TNCN phải nộp thì số thuế tăng thêm được giảm 30% theo quy định của Nghị định này nếu cá nhân vẫn đáp ứng điều kiện được giảm thuế.
Trường hợp cá nhân khai bổ sung hồ sơ khai thuế TNCN của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 hoặc theo quyết định, kết luận, thông báo kết quả thanh tra, kiểm tra, kiểm toán của cơ quan thuế, cơ quan có thẩm quyền làm giảm số thuế TNCN phải nộp thì điều chỉnh giảm số thuế TNCN được giảm theo quy định của Nghị định này và xử lý số tiền thuế nộp thừa (nếu có).
Doanh nghiệp phải nộp bổ sung nếu doanh thu vượt ngưỡng 10 tỷ đồng
Nghị định cũng quy định về việc giảm 30% số thuế TNDN phải nộp của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026 và năm 2027 đối với thu nhập của doanh nghiệp, tổ chức được thành lập theo quy định có mức doanh thu hằng năm của năm 2026, năm 2027 không quá 10 tỷ đồng.
Cụ thể, việc giảm thuế TNDN quy định tại Điều này áp dụng đối với người nộp thuế TNDN là doanh nghiệp, tổ chức được thành lập theo quy định, bao gồm: Doanh nghiệp được thành lập theo quy định của pháp luật Việt Nam; hợp tác xã, liên hiệp hợp tác xã được thành lập theo Luật Hợp tác xã; đơn vị sự nghiệp được thành lập theo quy định của pháp luật Việt Nam; tổ chức khác được thành lập theo quy định có hoạt động sản xuất kinh doanh có thu nhập.
Việc giảm thuế TNDN không áp dụng đối với các doanh nghiệp được thành lập theo quy định của Luật Doanh nghiệp hình thành từ việc chia, tách doanh nghiệp sau ngày Nghị quyết số 43/2026 có hiệu lực, mà tổng doanh thu hằng năm của năm 2026, năm 2027 của các doanh nghiệp sau chia, tách trên 10 tỷ đồng.
Số thuế TNDN được giảm của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 được tính trên toàn bộ thu nhập của doanh nghiệp có kỳ tính thuế theo năm, không phân biệt phương pháp tính thuế TNDN, bao gồm cả các khoản thu nhập quy định tại khoản 3 Điều 18 Luật Thuế TNDN.
Số thuế TNDN được giảm được tính trên số thuế TNDN phải nộp của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027.
Trường hợp doanh nghiệp đang được ưu đãi thuế theo quy định của Luật Thuế TNDN hoặc các luật, nghị quyết khác của Quốc hội thì số thuế TNDN được giảm quy định tại khoản này tính trên số thuế TNDN phải nộp sau khi đã trừ ưu đãi thuế.
Doanh thu năm làm căn cứ xác định doanh nghiệp thuộc đối tượng được giảm thuế TNDN bao gồm doanh thu từ hoạt động bán hàng, cung cấp dịch vụ (không bao gồm các khoản giảm trừ doanh thu), doanh thu từ hoạt động tài chính và thu nhập khác.
Trường hợp kỳ tính thuế năm đầu tiên đối với doanh nghiệp mới thành lập hoặc kỳ tính thuế năm cuối cùng đối với doanh nghiệp chuyển đổi loại hình doanh nghiệp, chuyển đổi hình thức sở hữu, hợp nhất, sáp nhập, chia, tách, giải thể, phá sản mà có thời gian ngắn hơn 3 tháng và doanh nghiệp được cộng vào kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 để hình thành một kỳ tính thuế TNDN thì việc xác định doanh thu và số thuế được giảm áp dụng đối với 12 tháng của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027.
Trường hợp doanh nghiệp có đơn vị phụ thuộc, địa điểm kinh doanh thì doanh thu trong kỳ tính thuế TNDN bao gồm doanh thu của đơn vị phụ thuộc, địa điểm kinh doanh thể hiện trên báo cáo tài chính tổng hợp năm.
Việc xác định tổng doanh thu hằng năm của các doanh nghiệp sau chia, tách quy định tại khoản 1 Điều này là tổng cộng doanh thu của tất cả các doanh nghiệp được hình thành từ quá trình chia, tách doanh nghiệp ban đầu trong kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027.
Kê khai giảm thuế
Doanh nghiệp dự kiến doanh thu trong kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 nếu không quá 10 tỷ đồng thì tự xác định số thuế được giảm khi tạm nộp thuế TNDN hằng quý.
Trường hợp tổng doanh thu thực tế trong kỳ tính thuế vượt quá 10 tỷ đồng thì doanh nghiệp thực hiện kê khai, nộp thuế TNDN theo quy định.
Doanh nghiệp phải nộp đủ số tiền thuế thiếu so với số phải nộp và việc xử lý tiền chậm nộp thực hiện theo quy định tại khoản 3 Điều 24 Nghị định số 252/2026 quy định chi tiết một số điều và biện pháp để tổ chức, hướng dẫn thi hành một số điều của Luật Quản lý thuế.
Trường hợp doanh nghiệp khai bổ sung hồ sơ khai thuế TNDN của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 hoặc theo quyết định, kết luận, thông báo kết quả thanh tra, kiểm tra, kiểm toán của cơ quan thuế, cơ quan có thẩm quyền làm tăng số thuế TNDN phải nộp thì số thuế tăng thêm được giảm 30% theo quy định của Nghị định này nếu doanh nghiệp vẫn đáp ứng điều kiện được giảm thuế quy định.
Trường hợp doanh nghiệp khai bổ sung hồ sơ khai thuế TNDN của kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027 hoặc theo quyết định, kết luận, thông báo kết quả thanh tra, kiểm tra, kiểm toán của cơ quan thuế, cơ quan có thẩm quyền làm giảm số thuế TNDN phải nộp thì điều chỉnh giảm số thuế TNDN được giảm theo quy định của Nghị định này và xử lý số tiền thuế nộp thừa (nếu có) theo quy định.
Nghị định này có hiệu lực thi hành kể từ ngày 29/10/2026 và áp dụng cho kỳ tính thuế năm 2026, năm 2027.

articles.title: Sam Altman is upset at you for hoarding RAM in your own computer - Engadget
articles.text:
Sam Altman is upset at you for hoarding RAM in your own computer
He says it's 'terrible' to have 'a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM' sitting in people's PCs.
AI data centers have gobbled up so much of the world's RAM supplies that prices of the memory units — and all electronic devices that have them — have skyrocketed as a result. So when OpenAI chief Sam Altman sat for an interview with YouTuber Cheeky Pint and Stripe, the conversation naturally turned to the RAM shortages affecting the whole tech industry. His opinion? He thinks it's "quite terrible" for people to have "a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer" and using it five percent of the time.
He added: "Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." Now, to be fair, he was specifically talking about local inference, which is what you call when you run AI models on your own computer.
Perhaps it shouldn't come as a surprise that he would hold that opinion and talk from a "global allocation perspective," as the head of one of the biggest AI companies on the planet today. But he also shouldn't be surprised if people call him tone-deaf, seeing as OpenAI has tied up roughly 40 percent of the world's RAM output through various agreements.
In addition, he's not taking into account that people buy and use RAM for more than just local inference. People who game on their PC, do live streams, edit high-definition videos and do other resource-heavy tasks, need more RAM than the ordinary user. With the AI industry monopolizing the world's RAM supply, everyone else has to deal with shortages. Since most electronics have some form of RAM inside them, their manufacturers pass on higher memory prices to consumers by raising their prices, as well.

articles.title: Alexa for Shopping hits 400m users after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse
articles.text:
Few people shop through outside AI agents yet, because the experience is not good enough, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy told analysts on Thursday. He expects Amazon’s own assistant, Alexa for Shopping, to be the main agent people use to buy from the store.
Jassy spoke on Amazon’s third-quarter earnings call. About a month ago, the company blocked Meta’s Muse agent from its site. He did not name Muse, Fortune reported.
“Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet, as the experience is still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly to research or one-click order there,” Jassy said.
Alexa for Shopping’s numbers
More than 400 million customers used Alexa for Shopping in the past 12 months, Amazon said in its results. Customer interactions grew 570% year on year. US customers who use it spend 50% more per order than those who do not, Jassy said.
“Though we anticipate working with horizontal agents, we believe Alexa for Shopping is going to be the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon,” he said.
Horizontal agents are general assistants that work across many shops, such as Muse. Jassy argued that Amazon’s assistant already knows a customer’s purchase history, shipping address and payment details.
Amazon has added more than 100 capabilities to the assistant. US customers can now ask it to create and edit shopping lists and gift registries, Amazon said in a blog post on the day of the results. It can also update delivery instructions, answer questions about charges and refunds, and pause or change recurring deliveries.
Ads, and the case for Muse
Advertising revenue grew 11% in the quarter, below analysts’ forecasts. Jassy said outside agents were not the cause, and he expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the holiday quarter.
Some analysts see Muse as a test for Amazon. Bank of America’s Justin Post made the point in a research note this week, Axios reported.
“Muse traction will likely drive questions on Amazon’s agentic strategy,” Post wrote.
Meta has signed up Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy as Muse partners. More than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up the agent, Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said last week. Shopping is its most common use, he said. Muse shoppers poured in so fast that Meta had to ask Stripe to raise its limits. Walmart has also said it will let AI agents shop for its customers.

articles.title: The Keurig Alta Brewer Replaced My Barista
articles.text:
Ahead of my virtual taste-test briefing for the new Keurig Alta brewer, it was 9:50 am and I was panicking. Pesky time zones be darned; the meeting I thought was taking place in two hours was actually in 10 minutes. That led to the first of many positive interactions with this machine—I had it fully set up, connected to my Wi-Fi, and ready to brew in less than seven minutes. That's about as intuitive a setup process as one could hope for with a first-of-its-kind coffee machine. (We won't talk about the amount of packaging scattered all over my kitchen floor during the aforementioned meeting.)
The Keurig Alta looks like something straight out of a design convention. It almost looks like spaceship decor with its curved white lines and sleek components (it also comes in black and stainless steel). Whereas some inexpensive Keurigs—the kind that sell for $50 during shopping holidays—can feel cheap and plasticky, this machine feels high-end from top to bottom. The cup holder is metal, the cup and whisk for the steam wand are magnetic, and the reservoir bin is slim and reversible. Both drip trays tuck away seamlessly without adding extra bulk.
The top of the machine has two compartments. On the right side, you'll find the standard Keurig K-Cup basket, with the typical needle at the bottom to pierce the cup. On the left, though, is a new compartment for the brand-new Keurig AltaRounds ($11 for a box of 8). These little pucks are the latest in Keurig's coffee technology and are like nothing I've seen before. The whole package comes at a high price point, but compared to in-home espresso makers, it's not unreasonable.
In Bloom
If you've ever used an espresso machine or watched a barista pull shots, you'll be familiar with the process of filling a portafilter with ground coffee and tamping it down. The Keurig AltaRounds look similar to this puck of coffee. Each puck is coated in a substance derived from seaweed, and that layer of “glue” holding the AltaRounds together allows them to bloom inside the machine. They're available in four varieties right now: dark roast, medium roast, a caramel blend, and double-shot espresso, with light-roast coffee and single-shot espresso varieties coming soon. The AltaRounds are stamped with a QR code that the machine reads in a split second when you insert them into the left touchscreen compartment.

articles.title: Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’
articles.text:
After hackers stole a shocking $6.3 billion from Binance customers in a record-breaking crypto heist, the company’s CEO says that 90 percent of the funds have been replaced, and the company plans to cover the remaining 10 percent as well. Binance is covering the stolen funds directly, and the remaining 10 percent consists of “less liquid” tokens, which the company says may take longer to acquire.
Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’
Most of the $6.3 billion in crypto stolen from Binance users has been restored.
The company also said in a post on X that, while withdrawals remain paused, they’re on track to be enabled on Sunday.
Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions.
Our next milestone in focus is resuming the withdrawal services for users. We remain on track to reopen withdrawals within our previously stated timeframe (on Sunday, 2026-11-01) and will provide a further update as soon as details are confirmed.

articles.title: 5 Samsung One UI features you won't get with other Android phones - Engadget
articles.text:
5 Samsung One UI features you won't get with other Android phones
From deep customization to seamless multi-device computing, there's a lot that makes One UI stand out from other Android variants.
Samsung's Galaxy smartphones are the world's most popular Android smartphones, which means that a huge chunk of Android users' experience of the OS is through Samsung's One UI software. But that's not a bad thing: One UI has a slew of unique features you can't get elsewhere, and once you find the most useful features for you, it can be hard to switch to another brand.
Some of Samsung's exclusive features in One UI 9, the most recent version of its skin built on Android 17, can help you use your devices together more easily. Others protect your phone against security threats and advanced malware. But some of the most charming features involve audio. As the owner of brands like Harmon Kardon, Denon, and JBL, Samsung is a major player in the audio space, and its Android skin reflects that with features that let you share and control your music more easily.
All of these features were tested on devices running this year's feature-rich One UI 9 and One UI 8.5, but not every Samsung phone will update to that software. But don't fret: all of these features are also available on One UI 8, which some older devices support.
Multi Control lets you use the same mouse and keyboard with multiple devices
Switching between multiple Galaxy devices — or a Galaxy device and a Windows PC — can be cumbersome. That's where Multi Control comes in, allowing you to connect a mouse and keyboard to one device and use them on the others. Multi Control lets you move your inputs between any combination of Galaxy devices and a Windows PC and use them to control the native Android interface. You can also type in text boxes on all connected devices and even drag files between them.
Other manufacturers have similar features — Lenovo as part of Motorola Smart Connect and Oppo/OnePlus within the O+ Connect suite — but the crucial difference is that those features require a PC to sit in the middle of the connection. Only Multi Control lets you share a mouse and keyboard between a phone and tablet without a PC in the mix. As someone who uses a Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Ultra as my primary "laptop," this means I can pop my phone on a kickstand, fold out my tablet's keyboard case, and use the keyboard and trackpad to control both devices. It essentially turns my phone into a miniature second monitor, perfect as an always-on Spotify window or a dedicated screen for a calendar or to-do list.
Until recently, Multi Control on PC was locked to Samsung computers such as Galaxy Books. However, as of this writing, Samsung has opened the functionality up to work with any PC. As I write this, my tablet sits alongside my PC monitors, happily accepting the PC's cursor on its screen. My phone sits below the tablet, and I can move my cursor between them seamlessly.
Separate App Sound lets you DJ a party while watching TikTok
Have you ever been in charge of the music on a road trip or at a party and accidentally blasted the beginning of a TikTok or Instagram video over the Bluetooth speaker? If so, Samsung has a feature that will prevent those embarrassing moments.
Android generally wants to play from just one audio source at a time and only to a single output. Playing a video pauses your music, for example, and both will play via the same pair of earbuds. Samsung's Separate App Sound lets you tweak that behavior. You can route apps to specific outputs, so TikTok and Instagram can be set to play through the phone's built-in speaker, even when you're connected to your car's Bluetooth, preventing that road trip faux pas.
To configure Separate App Sound, open Settings > Sounds and vibration > Separate app sound. You will be prompted to pick an app and select an accompanying output device. To go a step further, you can download Good Lock from the Galaxy Store and install the Sound Assistant module. Inside Sound Assistant, you will find the Multi sound setting, which lets you choose which apps can play audio at the same time as other apps. Alternatively, select the "All apps" option to prevent apps from pausing other apps' audio system-wide, essentially forcing Android to handle audio like a desktop OS.
Music Share lets your friends DJ the road trip without diving into Bluetooth settings
We've all been in a situation where a friend wants to take over the car radio to play some of their own music. As eager as you may be to oblige, though, connecting their phone requires fiddling with the inscrutable Bluetooth menus in your car's head unit, which isn't easy while you're parked, let alone while careening down the highway, so you say "no."
Music Share is a Samsung Galaxy feature that solves this exact issue. It allows other devices to connect to your phone and piggyback on your Bluetooth connection. After connecting your Galaxy device to a Bluetooth speaker and enabling Music Share from the Quick Panel, the speaker will show up on other people's phones as "[speaker name] via [your name]." Friends who connect to that device are actually connecting to your phone, which then routes their audio forward to the speaker.
Not just anyone can use your phone as an audio router. By default, Music Share only allows pairing requests from contacts and requires you to approve the connection. You can change these in Music Share settings by long-pressing the Music Share tile in the Quick Panel. Additionally, Music Share will disconnect a device if no audio is played from it for 10 minutes. You can change that duration to five minutes, 30 minutes or never. And, of course, you can kick someone off your Music Share, making it easy to shut a guest DJ down if they abuse your generosity by playing Nickelback.
Good Lock is an embarrassment of customization riches
Nearly every time the topic of Galaxy-exclusive features comes up, so does Good Lock, Samsung's suite of customization tweaks. Good Lock is where Samsung lets its engineers go nuts with features that might overwhelm a basic user. Samsung is already infamous for stuffing its phones to the gills with features and settings most people will never use, so you can get a sense of just how extra Good Lock's additions are. And instead of being a single app, Good Lock is a container for downloadable plugins — 23 at the time of writing — that each enable a bundle of settings.
Home Up, for instance, lets you customize your home screen, while Camera Assistant adds options to the camera app and MultiStar improves multitasking features. Most people have never wanted to replace their home button with a GIF, but Good Lock's NavStar module will let you. Similarly, you may never have thought of setting a longer screen-off timeout for specific apps, but Good Lock has that option tucked away in Display Assistant. Turn app icons on your home screen sideways or make them take up the whole screen? Good Lock can do that. Manually select which camera lens to use? That too. It even lets you reorder your settings menu. Rattling off everything you can adjust in Good Lock would take an entire workday, really.
The best way to approach Good Lock is to download it from the Galaxy Store and start poking around. It's not the most intuitive app, with some functions not clearly labeled and incorrect English copy here and there. But it has a human touch that's often missing from modern tech, and it's clear some features are Samsung engineers' passion projects. The suite is a confusing and expansive tangle of options, but if you love endless customization, it's utterly glorious.
Auto Blocker is an extra layer of security against hackers
Lastly, Samsung includes a suite of security features called Auto Blocker that harden your Galaxy device against the most advanced forms of malware. There is some overlap between Auto Blocker and Google's Advanced Protection suite commonly available on newer Android devices, but Auto Blocker is unique enough to stand on its own. The most security-conscious users should enable both.
Auto Blocker prevents your phone from installing apps sourced from outside the Play Store. While installing apps from anywhere on the internet is one of Android's strengths, those apps can pose risks and contain malware. Auto Blocker also prevents USB commands from reaching your phone. Some attackers use a rubber ducky, a USB stick that executes commands automatically when plugged in. Similarly malicious tools can be hidden in USB ports or cables, which is why you should never use a USB port charger at an airport or other public location. If you do, though, Auto Blocker should make any attack less likely to succeed.
Another feature is protection against malware delivered through a messaging app. With zero-click malware (which doesn't require you to click anything to execute an attack) on the rise, this is another excellent addition to Samsung's security umbrella. Auto Blocker can also turn on automatically after you disable it, keeping you protected even if you turn it off temporarily to install an APK, for example.
If all that isn't enough, Auto Blocker includes another suite of protections in its Maximum Restrictions submenu. When enabled, Maximum Restrictions blocks device admin apps that could remotely execute commands, prevents all USB connections beyond charging, and blocks automatic connections to insecure Wi-Fi networks that could make you more vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. It also blocks 2G network connections, which can be spoofed by law enforcement tools such as Stingrays.

articles.title: Mở rộng không gian đô thị công nghiệp sinh thái tại cửa ngõ Tây Nam TP.HCM
articles.text:
Giải mã “Khu công nghiệp sinh thái”
Theo Tổ chức Phát triển Công nghiệp Liên Hợp Quốc (UNIDO), Khu công nghiệp (KCN) sinh thái (Eco-Industrial Park - EIP) là mô hình hướng tới ba mục tiêu: nâng cao hiệu quả kinh tế, cải thiện hiệu quả môi trường và tạo ra những giá trị xã hội tích cực. EIP thúc đẩy sự kết nối giữa doanh nghiệp và hạ tầng trong cùng khu vực, từ chia sẻ nước, năng lượng, nguyên vật liệu đến tận dụng các dòng phụ phẩm, qua đó giảm tài nguyên tiêu thụ và chất thải phát sinh.
Hiệu quả mô hình được thể hiện qua Chương trình KCN sinh thái toàn cầu (GEIPP) do UNIDO triển khai với sự hỗ trợ của SECO. Tại Việt Nam, các giải pháp giai đoạn 2020-2024 giúp tiết kiệm mỗi năm 14.378 MWh điện, 264.127 GJ nhiên liệu hóa thạch, 278.690 m³ nước và 22.180 tấn nguyên liệu, hóa chất, đồng thời giảm khoảng 138.994 tấn CO₂ tương đương và mang lại 2,33 triệu EUR giá trị tiết kiệm tài chính mỗi năm.
Trên thế giới, Kalundborg Symbiosis (Đan Mạch) là mô hình cộng sinh công nghiệp tiên phong, nơi 17 doanh nghiệp và tổ chức kết nối để trao đổi vật liệu, nước và năng lượng, giúp cắt giảm khoảng 635.000 tấn CO₂ và tiết kiệm 3,6 triệu m³ nước mỗi năm. Trong khi đó, tại Singapore, CleanTech Park phát triển theo mô hình eco-business park, kết hợp sản xuất, nghiên cứu với hạ tầng xanh và sử dụng tài nguyên hiệu quả. Khoảng 10% diện tích dành cho Jurong Eco-Garden, trong đó 65% lượng nước mưa được thu giữ và tái sử dụng; hệ thống điện một chiều tại CleanTech One giúp giảm tới 45% điện năng chiếu sáng.
Những kết quả này cho thấy một khu vực có hoạt động công nghiệp không nhất thiết phải đồng nghĩa với việc đánh đổi môi trường sống xung quanh. Điểm khác biệt nằm ở cách KCN được quy hoạch và vận hành, khi không gian xanh, quản lý nước và sử dụng năng lượng được tính toán như một phần của hạ tầng ngay từ đầu.
Cửa ngõ Tây Nam TP.HCM: Mô hình cộng sinh giữa không gian sản xuất và chốn an cư
Nhìn một cách khách quan, chất lượng môi trường sống quanh một KCN vì thế không đơn thuần được quyết định bởi khoảng cách địa lý xa hay gần. Đó là kết quả của sự tích hợp quy hoạch bài bản: từ cách KCN vận hành tài nguyên, xử lý chất thải cho đến cách khu đô thị lân cận tổ chức mảng xanh, mặt nước và các khoảng đệm. Khi cùng phát triển theo triết lý sinh thái, ranh giới giữa “nơi sản xuất” và “nơi cư trú” có thể trở thành một vùng chuyển tiếp hài hòa.
Tại cửa ngõ Tây Nam TP.HCM, mô hình này được cụ thể hóa qua kết nối giữa cụm KCN Tandoland - Prodezi 650 ha và Đô thị Dragon Eden 146,8 ha do Tandoland đầu tư và Mai Bá Hương phát triển. KCN Prodezi hướng đến kinh tế tuần hoàn với năng lượng tái tạo, tái chế nước, công trình xanh và đa dạng sinh học, trong khi Tandoland định hướng sản xuất sạch và logistics hiện đại. Ở phía đô thị, Dragon Eden đóng vai trò là khoảng đệm sinh thái hoàn hảo. Điển hình như phân khu River rộng 30 ha nằm kế cận kênh Thầy Mười rộng 40m, kết hợp cùng công viên ven kênh 1,1 ha và Eden Park 2,1 ha, tạo thành những lớp không gian xanh giúp giảm cảm giác tiếp giáp trực diện với khu vực có cường độ hoạt động cao.
Trong bối cảnh ESG trở thành tiêu chuẩn đầu tư toàn cầu, việc quy hoạch đồng bộ hạ tầng kỹ thuật và cảnh quan sinh thái là lợi thế chiến lược giúp cụm KCN - đô thị Dragon Eden thu hút dòng vốn FDI chất lượng cao, đồng thời kéo theo nhu cầu lưu trú lâu dài của chuyên gia, kỹ sư và lao động trình độ cao. Đây cũng là điểm giao giữa công nghiệp và bất động sản. articles.title: Amazon Q3 earnings: customers ‘gobbling’ up AI capacity, Jassy says
articles.text:
Amazon’s free cash flow fell to minus $42.4bn over the 12 months to September. Spending on AI drove most of the drop, the company said on Thursday. A year earlier it was a positive $14.8bn.
The Amazon Q3 earnings showed revenue up 12% to $201.9bn and operating income up to $28.1bn, from $17.4bn a year earlier. Its operating margin of 13.9% was the highest Amazon has ever reported. Purchases of property and equipment rose by $94.8bn over the 12 months, mostly for AI, the company said.
Shares fell as much as 7% in extended trading on Thursday, Reuters reported. Revenue and earnings per share came in below analysts’ forecasts of $202.3bn and $1.96, CNBC reported.
AWS grows at its fastest rate in almost five years
Revenue at Amazon Web Services rose 39% to $46bn, and its operating income climbed to $17.8bn from $11.4bn. The cloud unit now has an annual revenue run rate of $184bn and a backlog of $578bn, Jassy said.
“We’re installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up,” Jassy said on the call.
He expects AWS revenue to grow more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Late in 2027, Amazon also plans to start selling its Trainium AI chips outside AWS, he said. Earlier this month it released TorchNeuron for Trainium, so developers can run PyTorch code on the chips.
“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” Jassy said in the results statement.
Cash, capex and the stores business
Amazon spent $77.3bn on property and equipment in the third quarter, against $35.1bn a year earlier. It still expects about $220bn of cash capital spending this year, a figure it set in July’s results. It raised $48.1bn of long-term debt in the quarter. A filing after the results showed it can now borrow up to $80bn against the AI hardware it buys.
Jassy told analysts that Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” in 2027, with what he called a clear line of sight to attractive returns.
“We can fund this plan,” Jassy said.
The retail side grew more slowly. Online store sales rose 2% to $68.5bn, and advertising revenue rose 11% to $19.6bn. Prime Day moved into the second quarter in most large countries this year. That cut about four percentage points from total growth, Amazon said. Jassy said Prime Video now has a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars and is profitable.
For the holiday quarter, Amazon expects revenue of $240bn to $247bn and operating income of $28.5bn to $33.5bn. Its rivals reported the day before: Google Cloud revenue doubled, while Alphabet shares had their worst day on record.

articles.title: Are Memories Transferable? Meet the Scientists Replicating an Infamous Study to Find Out
articles.text:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
It was the dead of winter in Boston. The surface of the Charles River was frozen solid. But Zachary Kelso braved the biting cold to finally put to rest a mystery that has haunted neuroscience labs for over half a century.
To do that, Kelso, a research assistant in the Harvard lab of the neuroscientist Sam Gershman, needed some worms. Specifically, planarians: arrow-headed flatworms, which are among the simplest creatures to possess a brain and a nervous system with bilateral symmetry like ours. Normally, labs order these widely used model organisms from biological supply companies. But the mail-order worms weren’t up to snuff. So Gershman had dispatched Kelso to the Charles’ icy banks to catch some wild ones. “I thought, ‘I’m going to look crazy because I’m using a hammer to beat through the ice,’” Kelso recalled. “So I wore the more business end of business casual.”
It wouldn’t be the last time Kelso found himself in this situation. The Charles River planarians, it turned out, didn’t cut it either. Neither did the worms he sourced while stream-hopping around Eugene, Oregon, in March 2025. Nor did the ones he fished from Michigan lakes that June—this time in thigh-high waders—while picnicking families gawked from shore. Kelso diligently turned over rocks, angled with bits of meat tied to a string, and even followed maps from a vintage guidebook called The Fresh-Water Triclads of Michigan. But his adventure was fruitless. Sure, he caught plenty of planarians. But back in Gershman’s lab, none of them would do what they were supposed to do.
In the 1960s, an eccentric behavioral psychologist named James McConnell convinced the scientific establishment that planarian worms, like Pavlov’s dogs, could be classically conditioned—and that memories of this training could be transferred from worm to worm through cannibalism. These bizarre findings were replicated by other scientists, and worm training became a staple of high school science fairs. Now, 60 years later, the worms have stopped learning, and nobody knows why.
I first learned about this scientific mystery while reporting another piece about what a cell can remember. As I dug into the historical literature on memory research, I kept coming across McConnell’s strange worm experiments, which captivated a generation of scientists before disappearing entirely. Planarian memory had itself been forgotten. I was content to dismiss it as a fluke of history until Gershman mentioned, in passing during an interview, that in addition to their work with the unicellular ciliate Stentor coeruleus, his lab was attempting to reproduce some wacky worm experiments from the 1960s. Had I heard of them?
Gershman, I learned, was keen to pick up where McConnell had left off. As part of a growing cohort of cognitive scientists looking beyond the brain for clues to the origins and basis of memory, he’s fascinated by any creature that seems to remember without the benefit of neural, synaptic networks. Little Stentor coeruleus, for example, can modify its behavior based on previous experience—quite a feat for a single-celled creature that can’t possibly have a neuron. Planarian worms, if McConnell’s findings were to be believed, might be the next great model organism for memory research.
The trouble was, it wasn’t going well. In fact, no matter how hard Gershman tried to train them, none of his planarians would learn a thing.
Can a worm learn? When McConnell posed the question in the early 1950s, the notion that memory had something to do with synaptic associations between neurons in the brain was just beginning to gain currency. McConnell, then a graduate student in psychology at the University of Texas, reasoned that planarians—among the simplest creatures with true neurons—should therefore be able to learn.
His early worm experiments were not particularly novel. He simply substituted worms for rats in what were, at the time, standard classical conditioning studies: repeatedly shocking the worms while exposing them to a bright light. After a period of this training, the worms came to associate the light with the shock and scrunched their bodies in anticipation whenever the light flashed. Voilà: worm learning!
Planarians have stranger features to offer for experiments. If a planarian is chopped in half, both halves will regrow into a new worm—the tail will grow a new head, and the head will grow a new tail. A fragment as small as 1/279 of the original worm can regrow into a completely normal adult worm in a matter of weeks, a regenerative capacity so powerful that, as one early naturalist put it, planarians are effectively “immortal under the edge of the knife.” For McConnell, this ability begged the question: When you chop a worm in half, do both halves remember?
This is where the real worm torture began.
In the ’60s, McConnell, by then a young professor at the University of Michigan, started beheading his trained planarians. The worms that grew back from the severed heads behaved as the originals had, associating the light with the shock—a result he expected, given the preservation of their primitive brains. What surprised McConnell was that the worms that regenerated from headless tails remembered, too. This meant that whatever form the worms’ memories took, they weren’t the exclusive purview of the brain. “It appeared that the memories were laid down throughout the animal’s body,” McConnell later reflected.
Thrilled, McConnell pushed his experiments further. He cut the worms into smaller and smaller pieces; each time, the regenerated segments retained the memory. He stitched the heads of trained worms onto untrained tails, but they kept falling off. He pureed trained worms and injected them into naïve recipients, a delicate process that the historian Larry Stern has compared to “impal[ing] a prune with a javelin.” Finally, remembering that some planarians are cannibals, he fed trained-worm puree to their brethren. In subsequent trials, the “cannibal” worms picked up the light response right away, as though they were remembering, rather than learning, what to do.
If McConnell’s experiments appear gruesome, his line of inquiry was of his time. The discovery of the DNA helix in the 1950s had revealed just how much information is packed into proteins and nucleic acids. The notion that the physical traces of memories, or “engrams,” might have some chemical basis seemed plausible enough to many scientists. Could McConnell’s cannibal worms have eaten an engram? McConnell certainly thought so. He was convinced that their memories were encoded in the structure of their RNA—and could be transferred from worm to worm.
“In the jargon of computer engineering, information is always ‘fed’ into a computer,” the journalist Arthur Koestler later wrote in an appreciative survey of McConnell’s work. “Here the metaphor became flesh.”
These were sensational findings, and McConnell took every advantage of the media attention they generated. Before becoming a scientist, he had had a brief career in radio, and he knew how to repackage nuanced ideas as pithy soundbites. In magazines such as Time and Esquire, he spoke grandly of a future of memory consumption—of “piano lesson pills” and “professor burgers.” He brought his trained worms onto The Steve Allen Show, and, belying his clean-cut hair and horn-rimmed glasses, dubbed himself “McCannibal.”
Students began writing to McConnell’s lab at the University of Michigan to ask for worm-training tips for their school science fairs, and McConnell shared advice. Science, he believed, should be for the people; he saw himself as a latter-day David pitching stones at institutional Goliaths. This made him one of the most famous public scientists of his era, but it did not endear him to more serious peers. It also didn’t help that he published all his research in The Worm Runner’s Digest, a countercultural journal he distributed from his lab.
The Worm Runner’s Digest was “sort of Mad Magazine meets a serious scientific journal,” Gershman told me recently. At its peak, it had some 2,500 subscribers around the world. The hand-drawn shield on its cover featured a two-headed planarian and the Latin motto ignotum per ignotius, which roughly translates to “the unknown explained through the even more unknown.” Its 1959 inaugural issue consisted of only 14 mimeographed pages about the care and feeding of planarians, but it quickly grew. In addition to publishing dozens of memory transfer papers and related scholarship, McConnell welcomed humor and printed science fiction stories, rousing editorials, student-drawn planarian cartoons, spoof articles, and poems.
While the Digest is now something of a cult classic, the mix proved confusing for many readers. McConnell eventually cut the publication in half, not unlike a planarian worm, and renamed the serious half The Journal of Biological Psychology (no relation to the current peer-reviewed journal Biological Psychology, founded in 1973). But McConnell’s reputation as a heretic and prankster was well established.
The wheels started to come off in the mid-1960s. Although McConnell enjoyed a period of fame and funding—including an accelerated path to tenure at the University of Michigan—attempts to replicate his memory transfers yielded inconsistent results. While many apparently succeeded, the failures were more visible. In 1965, the Nobel Prize–winning biochemist Melvin Calvin tried to replicate McConnell’s worm experiments and failed, even with the help of some of McConnell’s former assistants and using the same device. His high-profile publication of the results sparked an acrimonious debate about, among other things, proper worm handling.
By the 1970s, the planarian memory fad had come and gone. Scientists had moved on to rats, cats, goldfish, and even praying mantises. Researchers showing successful memory transfers in rats—by injecting brain RNA from one animal to another—had published their findings in prestigious journals such as Nature and Science, making the planarian model seem unimpressive in comparison. But when further experiments proved inconclusive, interest in the question of memory transfer petered out. As the science historians Harry Collins and Trevor Pinch put it, “memory transfer was never quite disproved; it just ceased to occupy the scientific imagination.”
McConnell closed his laboratory in 1971, and his long period of subsequent obscurity was broken only once, in 1985, when he became a victim of the Unabomber. (He lost his hearing temporarily after the blast.) He died in 1990. If a younger generation of scientists is familiar with his cannibal planarians, it’s as “a cautionary tale that neuroscientists tell to their students at bedtime to scare them away from ill-fated projects,” Gershman said.
Still, McConnell’s unconventional work and contrarian attitude has lingered in neuroscience lore, and the idea of memory transfer remains a subject of private fascination. What if McConnell really did manage to feed a memory to a worm? For Gershman, who is searching for a way to study memory at a molecular level and connect it to observable behavior, the question was an itch that had to be scratched. He decided to settle the matter once and for all.
It all seemed straightforward enough. In the spring of 2025, Gershman and Maddie Snyder, one of his postdocs, set out to reproduce the worm-training protocol of one of McConnell’s students, Alan Jacobson. Jacobson’s papers were the most rigorous of the planarian memory transfer era, and Gershman and Snyder followed them to the letter. “We wanted a behavioral basis to be able to study the circuits that are driving memory in these extremely unstable animals,” Snyder said. “Are those circuits at all being used for memory consolidation or storage? Because if you lose your head and all those circuits are gone, then what is the mechanism of storing memory?”
Despite their best efforts, however, they couldn’t do what Jacobson, McConnell, and so many others had done back in the 1960s: condition the worms to scrunch their bodies in response to light. (They reported the results on biorxiv.org in April 2026.) “I was really scratching my head about this,” Gershman said. He’d assumed that the memory transfer would be the dodgy part of the experiment—not getting the worms to form a memory in the first place.
They talked to other planarian labs. They tried different stimuli. They ran the planarian footage through a machine-learning pipeline. In desperation, Kelso and Snyder even visited the Harvard Science Museum to examine a vintage “inductorium,” an electric-shock contraption used in midcentury worm science. But it offered no clues.
Kelso searched for any of McConnell’s former collaborators who might still be alive, and through a stroke of luck he found contact information for Daniel Kimble and his wife, Reeva, who had both worked in McConnell’s lab. Now in their nineties, they live in Eugene, Oregon. When Kelso called them, he discovered that not only did they run many of McConnell’s experiments in the 1960s, but they’d also kept the entire print archive of The Worm Runner’s Digest in a box in their basement.
Kelso and Snyder bought tickets to Eugene. Over the course of two days, while consuming plates of homemade cookies and countless cups of tea, they absorbed everything they could from the Kimbles. On breaks from hand-scanning back issues of the Digest, they went stream-hopping nearby and filled casserole dishes with silty fresh water. Back at the Kimbles’ kitchen table, the two generations of scientists watched the silt settle to see what worms might emerge.
This, after all, is what McConnell did. Rather than using laboratory strains of planarians, he sourced his from a lake near the University of Michigan. And so, not wanting to leave any stone unturned, Kelso made one final trip to McConnell’s former fishing grounds in Michigan. He returned with plastic tubes full of worms, but not a single one was a learner. “At some point, we had like 12 different strains of planaria, none of which showed any learning,” Gershman said.
As Snyder tells it, the Kimbles were absolutely convinced that their conditioning experiments in the 1960s had worked. The worms learned—they were sure of it. The literature of the era seems to support their certainty; at least 36 labs reported similar results. So why is it that when the exact same experiments are done today, using the same laboratory protocol and even the same worms, fished from the same Michigan waters, planarian worms are utterly uneducable?
One explanation, Snyder said, is that McConnell, the Kimbles, and all the other “worm runners” were inconsistent in how they scored the planarians’ behavior and may have misinterpreted more anodyne worm “turns” for the definitive “scrunch” of the light reaction. Every scientist is a product of their time, after all, influenced in myriad, often invisible ways by sociological conditions, funding pressures, and, in this case, a highly charismatic leader. This interpretation made Snyder hyperaware of her own potential biases. “Throughout this entire project,” she told me, “I was like, ‘What are the things that I am taking for granted now in our models of neuroscience, and our assumptions of what is known and unknown, that I should really notice?’”
A more remote possibility is that planarian worms themselves have somehow changed over the last six decades—falling victim to pollution or genetic drift. Gershman finds this scenario unlikely. “What are the chances that a bunch of researchers just happened to do these studies at the particular time when this phenomenon happened?” he asked, incredulous. “They just got extremely lucky, in the millions of years of planarian evolution? And then our luck ran out?”
No matter the reason, in 2026, despite their nervous system and simple brains, planarians don’t learn. From an evolutionary perspective, this might actually make sense. “The reason that we learn associations, to some degree, is so that we can predict danger and avoid it,” Snyder said. But planarians have a different relationship to danger. Their regenerative physiology, so key to McConnell’s experiments, protects them from blunt trauma. Bitten in half, they simply grow back. What use is memory to such a creature? “That’s a whole other philosophical conundrum,” she said.
It’s a great time to be wrestling with such conundrums. Planarian learning may be a dead end, but memory transfer experiments with other organisms are back in scientific vogue—and those experiments appear to be working. In 2018, the neuroscientist David Glanzman of the University of California, Los Angeles, performed a memory transplant on the sea slug Aplysia californica, a darling model organism for memory research owing to its relatively simple nervous system and gigantic neurons. After training the slugs to respond to a shock to their tails, Glanzman was able to transfer the sensitization from one slug to another via a direct injection of genetic material. This suggested that some aspect of the memory was stored in RNA, which was McConnell’s contention.
Then, in 2021, the Princeton University geneticist Coleen Murphy found that Caenorhabditis elegans worms—microscopic roundworms with 302 neurons to their name—could learn to avoid a pathogenic bacterium by eating, or even just swimming around in, pureed worms who had learned the hard way. Murphy’s group identified a retrotransposon, a jumping segment of genetic material, called Cer1, that appears to “carry a memory” between individuals, she said. A few years later, a group at the Indian Institute of Science published a paper suggesting that trained C. elegans worms release extracellular vesicles—small lipid particles containing genetic information—that can impart their training to their naïve counterparts.
None of these researchers are half as flashy as McConnell was, but their work indicates that he may have been right about worm memory after all. He just bet on the wrong kind of worm—and doubled down on it, despite inconsistent evidence. In the end, he lost his reputation, but his sheer gusto sparked the curiosity of another unconventional scientist. Fortunately, this one’s following the evidence.
At Harvard, Gershman is shifting his focus from the inscrutable planarian to the more legible C. elegans. It may not regenerate when it’s cut in half, but C. elegans is a long-standing model organism in neuroscience—and it’s been consistently shown to learn. With new experiments underway, Gershman is cautiously optimistic. “I just hope we’re not going down another rabbit hole,” he told me. A wormhole, on the other hand—that’s for certain.

articles.title: Happy Pikmin Day Eve
articles.text:
This morning, Nintendo announced that tomorrow, November 1st, would be the first annual Pikmin Day. As part of the short Pikmin Day Direct, Shigeru Miyamoto shared new info about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, as well as an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and announced the Hello! Pikmin series of shorts.
Happy Pikmin Day Eve
Nintendo is celebrating the first annual Pikmin Day by debuting a new series of short films.
Players will be able to use the Switch 2’s built-in microphone to issue voice commands to Oatchi, the space dog. Pikmin 4 will also have a Dandori Academy mode that will test players’ skills in specific challenges. There will be limited tests on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, complete with leaderboards where players can compare stats. Pikmin Bloom will be getting a new feature called Secret Caves, where players can win treasure by battling enemies and exploring said caves.
Lastly, Miyamoto showed the first installment of a new series of shorts called Hello! Pikmin. A second episode will premiere tomorrow, with a third later in November. The series will then debut one short per month starting in December. The shorts build on the success of Close to You, a Pikmin animation released last year.

articles.title: 29 ngân hàng giảm lãi suất huy động, có nơi giảm tới 0,7 điểm phần trăm
articles.text:
Theo thống kê của VietNamNet dựa trên các biểu lãi suất được công bố trong tháng 10/2026, có 29 ngân hàng điều chỉnh giảm lãi suất huy động ở ít nhất một kỳ hạn hoặc một hình thức gửi tiền.
Danh sách gồm: LPBank, VietBank, BVBank, Bac A Bank, BaoViet Bank, OCB, HDBank, KienlongBank, Nam A Bank, NCB, Sacombank, TPBank, VPBank, ABBank, MBV, PVcomBank, SHB, MB, SeABank, Techcombank, PGBank, Saigonbank, GPBank, MSB, VietABank, Agribank, BIDV, Vietcombank và VietinBank.
Phần lớn ngân hàng điều chỉnh giảm lãi suất huy động ở các kỳ hạn từ 6 tháng trở lên, với mức giảm phổ biến 0,5 điểm phần trăm. Tuy nhiên, mức điều chỉnh có sự khác biệt giữa các ngân hàng và từng kỳ hạn.
Về hình thức gửi tiền, một số ngân hàng chỉ điều chỉnh lãi suất niêm yết tại quầy, trong khi các ngân hàng khác áp dụng mức giảm đối với cả tiền gửi trực tuyến và tại quầy.
Riêng nhóm ngân hàng quốc doanh (Agribank, BIDV, Vietcombank, VietinBank), HDBank, PGBank và BVBank chỉ giảm lãi suất tiết kiệm tại quầy.
Đáng chú ý, trong khi phần lớn ngân hàng giảm lãi suất tối đa 0,5 điểm phần trăm, Ngân hàng Quốc Dân (NCB) giảm tới 0,6 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiết kiệm các kỳ hạn từ 6 tháng, Ngân hàng SeABank giảm tới 0,7 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiết kiệm tại các kỳ hạn 18-36 tháng.
Trong khi đó, Techcombank giảm 0,1 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiền gửi kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng, giảm 0,5 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiền gửi kỳ hạn từ 12 tháng.
Tương tự, Ngân hàng MB giảm 0,4 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiết kiệm kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng và giảm 0,5 điểm phần trăm lãi suất kỳ hạn từ 12 tháng.
VPBank giảm 0,4 điểm phần trăm lãi suất huy động kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng, giảm 0,3-0,5 điểm phần trăm lãi suất các kỳ hạn từ 12 tháng.
Trong tháng 10, Ngân hàng Nhà nước (NHNN) đã yêu cầu các tổ chức tín dụng (TCTD) triển khai đồng bộ các giải pháp nhằm giảm mặt bằng lãi suất.
Trước mắt, yêu cầu các TCTD điều chỉnh giảm tối thiểu 0,5 điểm phần trăm/năm đối với lãi suất tiền gửi niêm yết ở các kỳ hạn từ 6 tháng trở lên; đồng thời, giảm lãi suất cho vay đối với khách hàng, tập trung giảm từ 1,5-2 điểm phần trăm/năm đối với lĩnh vực sản xuất, kinh doanh và các lĩnh vực ưu tiên.
NHNN cũng yêu cầu các TCTD tuyệt đối không chạy đua tăng lãi suất huy động, gây cạnh tranh không lành mạnh và bất ổn thị trường tiền tệ.
NHNN cho biết sẽ theo dõi việc thực hiện thông qua hệ thống báo cáo thống kê. Trường hợp ngân hàng không tuân thủ chỉ đạo, cơ quan quản lý có thể áp dụng biện pháp xử lý, trong đó có việc xem xét giảm hoặc giao thấp chỉ tiêu tăng trưởng tín dụng.
