articles.title: Why you should never point a laser pointer at any aircraft - Engadget
articles.text:
Why you should never point a laser pointer at any aircraft
Unfortunately, some people need to hear this.
Aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft is a terrible idea. Contrary to popular belief, pilots are not, in fact, cats. Nor are they here for your PowerPoint presentation. They're humans performing a difficult, high-stakes job, and laser beams can interfere with their vision, risking lives for what amounts to juvenile mischief.
Hopefully, you don't need a lecture explaining the ins and outs of laser physics to understand the danger. But curious minds might want to learn a bit more about how a tiny beam from a $10 gadget can ruin a pilot's night and land the perpetrator in prison.
From tiny beam to windshield-sized flash
At normal distances, laser beams look like they stay perfectly narrow, but they spread out gradually as they travel. After a mile or two, what began as a tiny dot a few feet away may have grown to several feet across.
It's easy to imagine pilots seeing an annoying but harmless dot in the cockpit. But the reality is much scarier. Between the beam's increased size and the aircraft's scratched and curved windshield, the pilot might see a window's width of light glowing and cascading across their field of view. An imperfect analogy would be driving toward an intense desert sun that's low in the sky. Now imagine trying to land a plane like that, with the lives of hundreds of passengers in your hands.
These incidents also tend to happen at the worst time. Handheld lasers mostly hit low-flying planes, which are taking off or landing. Plus, they usually happen at night, when the pilot's pupils are already dilated. A laser lighting up the cockpit can cause flash blindness for a few seconds or longer, right when there's the least room for error.
Helicopters arguably have it worse. Police, medical and news choppers often fly low over neighborhoods, including at night, making them a prime target for anyone with a laser pointer and questionable judgment.
So yeah, don't be that person.
Why flashlights don't pose the same risk
A laser keeps its light concentrated for miles, expanding only gradually. Even a weak pointer can mess with a pilot's vision from about two miles away. A flashlight, on the other hand, spreads in a wide cone from the moment it leaves your hand.
Point your average flashlight at a plane all you want. It won't do much.
If nothing else, there's self-preservation
Unfortunately, plenty of people still point lasers at aircraft. Pilots reported nearly 11,000 laser strikes to the FAA in 2025 alone. The agency considers that number progress, since it dropped by 14 percent from the previous year. At the time of publication, nearly 6,000 have been reported in 2026.
Given the danger to everyone on board a laser-struck aircraft, the law takes this seriously. Aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft has been a federal crime in the US since 2012, punishable by up to five years in prison and fines of up to $250,000. The FAA can add civil penalties of more than $30,000 per violation, and states can levy their own penalties.
But who's going to get caught, right? Well, it's not as much of a long shot as you might think. Police helicopters carry infrared cameras that can trace a beam back to its origin. After all, lasers draw a bright line pointing right back to the person holding them. Just this year, a New York man was sentenced to 18 months in prison for pointing a laser at a Delta flight, and an Arizona resident got 10 months for pointing one at US Air Force F-35 jets. In that case, an FBI surveillance plane captured video of the laser strikes coming from his residence.
So, for crying out loud, keep your laser pointer limited to cat-play, presentations and science demos. And if you must act like a doofus, there are plenty of ways to get that out of your system that don't put lives at risk.

articles.title: Theranos whistleblower says AI lab NDAs are ‘likely illegal’
articles.text:
Tyler Shultz helped expose the blood-testing fraud at Theranos. He now says AI is hard to vet, and investors need to do real due diligence. Few laws govern AI, he added, which makes it hard for people inside AI companies to blow the whistle.
Shultz spoke to Theo Baker on The San Francisco Standard’s PST podcast. Baker was sitting in for the host, Emily Dreyfuss. The interview comes as a new film has put Elizabeth Holmes back in the news. “You Can See Everything”, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows the Theranos founder’s last weeks before prison.
Easy to fake
Baker asked whether the flood of money into AI raises the risk of another Theranos. Shultz said capabilities a company does not have, or may never have, are not hard to fake.
“It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is like something truly unique and new versus like a ChatGPT wrapper,” Shultz said.
Anyone who wants to deceive people has a great opportunity now, he said. Investors need to keep their guard up.
“I think the days of having a 30-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over,” he said.
Holmes took that model and scaled it to $100m, raising what Shultz called the biggest angel round of all time. On paper, the Theranos investors were the victims, he said. In his view, they were also enablers. Their lack of due diligence handed her power she should never have had.
NDAs and AI whistleblowers
The Theranos whistleblower also spoke about people at AI labs who raise safety concerns. The topic is live: this week twenty House Democrats wrote to OpenAI about its fired safety researchers. OpenAI had checked their phones for Signal chats, The Wall Street Journal reported. This month, former lab insiders gave evidence at a New York City hearing on AI.
“The NDAs and the non-disparagement agreements that many of these tech workers have signed are so incredibly overbearing and I would say likely illegal even,” Shultz said.
At Theranos, he signed several frightening NDAs. He thought he could not talk to a lawyer or a regulator, he said. He used a fake name and a fake email address to contact regulators. Workers need to know they can go to regulators and lawyers, he said. Some lawyers take whistleblower cases on contingency. He said he is now working to make those resources easier to reach.
Holmes back in the news
Shultz worked at Theranos as a scientist and raised concerns with managers, executives and a regulator before helping a Wall Street Journal reporter. Holmes and Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani went to prison about three years ago, on sentences of more than 11 years and nearly 13 years.
He called the film a masterpiece but said it was not a documentary, because it pursued ambiguity rather than truth. He also said Holmes is preparing a second act. Haemanthus, the blood-testing start-up run by her partner Billy Evans, says Holmes has no role in the company, Fortune reported.

articles.title: Pope Leo wants to disarm AI: ‘machines are tools, not persons’
articles.text:
Pope Leo XIV called on Friday for artificial intelligence to be “disarmed”. Decisions on human life, freedom and the use of force must always stay under human oversight, he said.
In an address published by the Vatican, he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to move towards banning lethal autonomous weapons. He spoke in the Consistory Hall of the Apostolic Palace. His audience was taking part in a meeting on the future of AI, which the Pontifical Academy for Life and the Future of Life Institute ran together.
Machines are tools, not persons
The pope set out five points. First, the future of AI depends on the choices people make. People have a duty to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its uses, he said.
“The decisive question, then, is not simply ‘What can AI do?’ but rather, ‘What purpose should it serve?’” he said.
He warned that treating AI as a race to be won risks forgetting the people left behind. A reliable system that serves people is worth more than a very powerful one, he said, if nobody can foresee or control its effects.
His second point was that machines are tools, not persons. He rejected proposals to give AI systems rights or legal personhood.
“Such an approach risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity,” he said.
Third, people must never hand some decisions to machines. He gave two examples: a target list and a border control database. A person on either risks becoming a mere data point, he said. This is where his call to disarm AI came in.
Institutions, not more principles
Fourth, AI must serve the common good and not the interests of a privileged few. The fifth point, perhaps the most urgent in his view, was about institutions. The world already knows many of the ethical principles, he said. What the world needs now are effective international bodies that can put them into practice.
“This calls for shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability,” the pope said.
States discuss lethal autonomous weapons under the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. Its Seventh Review Conference meets in Geneva from 16 to 20 November, according to Reaching Critical Will.
A position the pope keeps returning to
The pope also recalled the words of Pope Francis to the G7 in 2024. No machine should ever choose to take a human life, Francis said then. Each of Friday’s five points cites Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical Leo published in May.
He has made the case before. In May he called AI-directed warfare a spiral of annihilation. In September he said AI safety fears were not fake news. Not everyone in the industry agrees. Mistral’s chief executive, Arthur Mensch, has rebutted the pope on AI in warfare.

articles.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

articles.title: Tổng Giám đốc đơn vị thành viên của TKV bị khởi tố: Thu nhập 100 triệu/tháng, công ty lãi khủng
articles.text:
Theo thông tin Tổng công ty Khoáng sản TKV - CTCP (Vimico - mã: KSV) công bố ngày 30/10, doanh nghiệp đã nhận được quyết định của Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Bộ Công an về việc khởi tố bị can đối với ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ để điều tra về tội "Nhận hối lộ", theo Điều 354 Bộ luật Hình sự.
HĐQT Vimico cũng đã thông qua nghị quyết miễn nhiệm chức vụ Tổng Giám đốc đối với ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ kể từ ngày 29/10/2026.
Ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ sinh năm 1972, có trình độ Kỹ sư điện khí hóa - cung cấp điện. Ông bắt đầu công tác tại Tổng công ty Khoáng sản từ năm 1992.
Trong quá trình công tác, ông Tuệ từng đảm nhiệm nhiều vị trí quản lý tại Công ty Mỏ tuyển đồng Sin Quyền và Công ty Luyện đồng Lào Cai trước khi được bổ nhiệm làm Phó Tổng Giám đốc Tổng công ty vào tháng 8/2015.
Đến tháng 3/2018, ông chính thức được bổ nhiệm giữ chức Tổng Giám đốc Vimico, bắt đầu đảm nhiệm vị trí cao nhất trong bộ máy điều hành doanh nghiệp.
Tháng 4/2025, ông Tuệ tiếp tục được bầu giữ chức thành viên HĐQT nhiệm kỳ 2025-2030.
Tính đến thời điểm bị khởi tố, ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ có hơn 30 năm công tác trong ngành khoáng sản và hơn 8 năm giữ chức Tổng Giám đốc Vimico.
Đáng chú ý, thời điểm ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ được bổ nhiệm Tổng Giám đốc (năm 2018), Vimico có quy mô doanh thu mỗi năm khoảng 5.000-6.000 tỷ đồng. Lợi nhuận sau thuế khoảng 200 tỷ đồng.
Dưới thời ông Tuệ, quy mô doanh thu và lợi nhuận của Vimico liên tục được cải thiện qua các năm. Riêng năm 2025, doanh nghiệp ghi nhận doanh thu thuần hợp nhất 14.554 tỷ đồng, lợi nhuận sau thuế hợp nhất 1.908 tỷ đồng. Đà tăng trưởng tiếp tục được duy trì trong 9 tháng đầu năm 2026, trong bối cảnh giá bán nhiều sản phẩm khoáng sản chủ lực tăng mạnh.
Theo số liệu được công bố, riêng trong quý III/2026, doanh thu thuần của Vimico đạt hơn 9.453 tỷ đồng, tăng 144%; lợi nhuận sau thuế đạt gần 2.566 tỷ đồng, tăng 332%.
Lũy kế 9 tháng đầu năm 2026, Vimico ghi nhận doanh thu thuần 14.686 tỷ đồng, tăng 35% so với cùng kỳ. Lợi nhuận trước thuế đạt 4.340 tỷ đồng, tăng 149%, trong khi lợi nhuận sau thuế đạt 3.462 tỷ đồng, gấp hơn 2,5 lần cùng kỳ năm 2025.
Theo báo cáo tài chính riêng giữa niên độ năm 2026 đã được soát xét của Vimico, trong 6 tháng đầu năm, ông Trịnh Văn Tuệ được ghi nhận tổng thu nhập từ tiền lương, thưởng và thù lao hơn 603,3 triệu đồng, bình quân khoảng 100,6 triệu đồng/tháng. Con số này cao hơn 35,9% so với cùng kỳ năm 2025, khi tổng thu nhập được ghi nhận là 444 triệu đồng.
Vimico là đơn vị thành viên của Tập đoàn Công nghiệp Than - Khoáng sản Việt Nam (TKV), hoạt động trong lĩnh vực khai thác, chế biến khoáng sản và luyện kim.
Các sản phẩm chủ lực của doanh nghiệp gồm đồng, kẽm, thiếc, vàng cùng nhiều sản phẩm khoáng sản và hóa chất phục vụ sản xuất công nghiệp.
Trong đó, mỏ tuyển đồng Sin Quyền và các cơ sở luyện đồng tại Lào Cai là những mắt xích quan trọng trong chuỗi khai thác, chế biến và sản xuất kim loại của Vimico.
Ngày 30/10, HĐQT Vimico ban hành nghị quyết thông qua việc triệu tập và tổ chức ĐHĐCĐ bất thường năm 2026. Ngày đăng ký cuối cùng để thực hiện quyền tham dự đại hội là 20/11, thời gian tổ chức dự kiến ngày 15/12.
Theo nghị quyết, cuộc họp sẽ xem xét các nội dung thuộc thẩm quyền của ĐHĐCĐ theo Luật Doanh nghiệp và điều lệ Tổng công ty. Tuy nhiên, Vimico chưa công bố cụ thể các vấn đề sẽ trình cổ đông tại cuộc họp.

articles.title: How to improve audio quality on your Android phone with Bluetooth or wired headphones - Engadget
articles.text:
How to improve audio quality on your Android phone with Bluetooth or wired headphones
There are multiple ways to adjust the audio output on your Android phone.
A great pair of headphones or in-ear monitors alone isn't enough to get the best sound quality your Android phone can deliver. Digital audio is deceptively complex — you're essentially turning sound waves into code and then back into sound waves — but once you have a handle on the basics of how it works, you can eke better sound out of your devices.
To that end, it's important to understand how Android directs audio to your ears, and which layers in between can alter that signal. We'll also cover how to choose an app that supports lossless audio, as well as how to EQ your headphones for either a neutral sound or a profile of your choosing. Ultimately, you'll be able to choose whether you'd like to go the extra mile for full, audiophile-grade sound or simply get the best results from your music streaming app.
How Android handles audio (and why it matters)
There are some quirks to the way Android handles audio. Just plugging in your headphones won't automatically translate to the highest quality. Android's signal chain — the path audio follows through the system before reaching your ears — flows from the audio source (the app you're using to play your media) to the operating system, where a service called AudioFlinger passes it off to other layers like the mixer, where it might have effects applied or duck for a notification sound. This is where things get funky for audio enthusiasts, since we're looking for the pure sound signal in as unaltered a form as possible. After going through the mixer, audio is passed to the interface, technically known as the hardware abstraction layer (HAL), which transmits it to your hardware (wired or Bluetooth playback devices or your phone's speakers).
While all this is taking place, AudioFlinger is also sampling and downmixing the audio. By default, everything is processed in 32-bit floating point, which is to say, far higher quality than even a true lossless file is likely to need. Audio is then output at a sample rate of 48kHz with either 16 or 24 bits of depth. Since most lossless audio available to consumers tops out at 24-bit, and since human hearing sits below a 48kHz threshold, most people will be satisfied. But that behavior also means that the Android system is almost always making adjustments to audio. The average listener truly should not care about this and can skip forward a couple of paragraphs. But for those who want to go above and beyond in search of true, mathematical precision, things get a bit messy.
Mathematical precision in audio is also known as bit perfection, which means audio that remains untouched by mixing, resampling or other alterations along the audio chain. If the file you hear is mathematically identical to the one in your player, it is bit-perfect. While bit-perfect audio played from a lossless file is the gold standard for audiophiles, it actually cuts against another important aspect of achieving good sound quality that we'll cover later: EQing your headphones, which by definition alters the audio signal before it reaches your ears. However, because your phone may be applying its own changes to your audio before it reaches your ears, we need to get rid of any preexisting processing so that we can apply our own, custom tuning.
This is where lossless USB audio comes in. Starting in Android 14, an app can now address the mixer directly to tell it whether audio should be passed through the mixer as usual or sent directly through the audio framework to the HAL. But that only works if every layer of your audio stack is on board. Your phone maker must have implemented lossless USB audio, your player app must have done the same, your DAC must natively support the sample rate of your files, and so on.
That's a lot of information, but the steps you can take to act on it are simple. First, turn off any extra processing your phone is doing to your audio. That means an EQ in your device settings, any kind of Dolby or other spatial enhancements and anything else that may affect the audio signal.
Wired audio is the easiest path to perfection
Wired headphones don't need to bother with finicky Bluetooth codecs, which makes wired audio the easiest way to achieve the highest possible audio quality on any device, including your Android phone. That doesn't mean all wired headphones sound good, but rather that even the crappiest pair of wired headphones receives every bit of the audio signal without losing any data due to wireless compression. Whether they can reproduce that detail is a different matter.
You probably don't have a phone with a 3.5mm headphone jack. That's unfortunate, since if you did, you could plug the headphones right in and call it a day. Instead, you'll need a digital-to-analog converter, more commonly referred to as a DAC. It takes the digital signal your phone sends through its USB-C port and converts it into an analog signal your headphone cable can understand. In any system with a headphone jack, you can assume the DAC is inside the device, so the primary benefit of a standalone DAC is that you get to choose it yourself.
DACs don't have to be entire boxes that sit on your shelf. Not only are there portable DACs, but even a USB-C-to-headphone jack dongle is technically a DAC. What actually matters is how capable the DAC chip doing the actual audio conversion is. Ideally, you want high-resolution decoding at up to 32-bit, 96kHz. Some USB-C-to-3.5mm adapters are active and do the audio conversion themselves, while others are passive and connect to the latent DAC inside your phone, which may be present even if a headphone jack isn't. Look up whether your particular Android device has an internal DAC and whether it's any good before choosing a passive adapter.
Some DACs are expensive, but you don't have to pay through the nose. Many audio enthusiasts strongly recommend the Apple USB-C-to-3.5mm headphone jack dongle available from practically every tech retailer as a basic, no-frills DAC. Of course, you can spend hundreds on a DAC if you so desire. You can also check out our list of the best DACs for lossless streaming in 2026.
Bluetooth is lossy but can still deliver great audio quality
Bluetooth is widely reviled among audiophiles because it trades quality for convenience. There has traditionally been no such thing as lossless Bluetooth because the protocol does not have the bandwidth to support it. Currently, there is a single caveat to that rule we'll cover further down. With that said, some Bluetooth connections can deliver audio quality good enough that no human ear would notice the signal loss it introduces in a normal listening environment.
The standard Bluetooth codec, the thing that compresses and reads back the wireless data your phone transmits to your headphones, is Sub-band Codec (SBC). It is extremely lossy and tops out at 320 kilobits per second (kbps), or about as high-quality as an MP3 file can be, though it becomes much more stable at an even lossier 192 kbps. The other most common codec, Advanced Audio Coding (AAC), is notably used on iPhones but also many Android devices and tops out at 250 kbps. That's good enough for most people with most headphones to enjoy, but not great if you're interested in high fidelity.
However, there are high-resolution Bluetooth codecs, most notably Qualcomm's aptX and Sony's LDAC, each of which can push Bluetooth quality much higher than the norm. Because they are proprietary, you'll need to check whether your Android phone and headphones support them. There are multiple versions of aptX, including aptX LL, aptX HD and aptX Adaptive, the latter of which contains the aptX Lossless mode (Qualcomm, this is getting out of hand), which is capable of providing the highest audio quality of the bunch at up to 16 bits of depth and at 44.1kHz. While aptX Lossless is technically bit-perfect at that specific quality, it falls back to a lossy delivery at higher qualities, is only supported on a handful of phones that are mostly not available in the US and falls back to lossy if there are other wireless devices nearby.
Sony contributed its proprietary LDAC codec to the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which comprises the core of any Android device's software, giving it broad compatibility with headphones that support it. It can deliver audio with up to 32-bit internal processing to match Android's mixer, but its actual output tops out at 24-bit, 96kHz.
Because Samsung has the lion's share of the market, it's worth mentioning that Samsung Galaxy phones support aptX on some models, but more widely support LDAC. Samsung also has its own codec, Samsung Seamless Codec (SSC), which is used to provide 24-bit, 96kHz streams on devices like the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.
As you may suspect, you'll need headphones that support one of those codecs in order to benefit from high-resolution Bluetooth. If yours don't, you're out of luck and will be stuck with SBC or AAC. Many of the best earbuds for Android have at least one such codec. Some enthusiast wireless headphones, like the recent Sennheiser HDB 630, are doing innovative things with high-res wireless dongles that work similarly to those that come with wireless computer mice.
You'll also need to make sure that Android isn't fighting your hi-res codec. If your headphones have a companion app, the toggle for aptX or LDAC may be buried in that app's settings. Yet another toggle is in Android's Bluetooth settings, found by tapping the gear icon next to the listing for a connected pair of headphones. Lastly, if you're sure your phone and headphones both support a high-resolution Bluetooth codec, and it's not working, you may need to enable developer settings on your phone and toggle it on. My own device, a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, has a toggle in developer settings for HD audio, as well as a Bluetooth audio codec menu where LDAC can be selected while using my Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones. I have another three menus for sample rate, bits per sample and LDAC quality (for this, Best Effort is usually the best, but Optimized for Audio Quality will risk some connection stability issues in order to push the quality as high as possible).
Player apps are the heart of an Android audio setup
The most consequential decision you'll make while trying to maximize your audio quality on Android, aside from your choice of playback device, is your player app. If you're not aiming for bit-perfection (which most people aren't, especially since it can't be achieved over Bluetooth), the most popular music streaming apps are all fair game.
Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal, Qobuz and more all support lossless audio, with Spotify providing the lowest quality ceiling of the pack at 24-bit, 44.1kHz, while Tidal and Qobuz host tracks at up to a respectable 24-bit, 192kHz. Use your favorite pair of wired headphones or hi-res Bluetooth cans and jam out.
For the true audio freaks who want bit-perfect audio, only Tidal and Qobuz can satisfy, as both can hook into a third-party player to bypass the Android mixer. The latter also has an a la carte high-resolution music store, so you can easily grab local files of your favorite songs.
Which brings us to local players. You'll need one to play your actual music files in the highest quality. The two most robust apps for Android audiophiles are USB Audio Player Pro and Poweramp. Which you prefer will come down to what your priorities are. Both have a bit-perfect mode which also happens to work with Android 13 and earlier, as each app uses its own method to achieve bit-perfect outputs rather than relying on the Android 14 implementation.
My own preference is USB Audio Player Pro. The app also costs $9 at filing time, which could be a deal-breaker for some, and is probably only worth it if you know you'll use its advanced features. Poweramp will let you use some of its features for free, but an $8 in-app purchase unlocks the full version. Both paid apps focus on their own enthusiast features. Poweramp has plenty of DSP tweaks, including the ability to see your entire audio chain visualized and make adjustments. Where USB Audio Player Pro strikes a solid win is in its ability to stream from internet sources including Tidal and Qobuz, but also Dropbox, UPnP and DLNA servers, self-hosted OpenSubsonic servers, and network-attached storage. If you'd prefer not to manually move audio files to your phone in order to play them back, these streaming features provide an easy alternative.
EQing your headphones trades bit-perfect audio for personalized sound
The very last step in your Android audio journey is EQing. As noted earlier, the quest for bit-perfect audio is in tension with digital signal processing, or DSP. The term simply refers to making changes to a digital audio signal, and it encompasses everything from equalizing your audio mix to making time alignments with multiple speakers. If you touch the signal deliberately, you're using DSP, and if nothing touches it at all, it's bit-perfect. If you want a pure signal, you can ignore EQing.
However, EQing is important, especially in consumer audio. Most consumer headphones aren't going to sound the way you like right out of the box, as everyone's taste and sense of hearing are different. The best of both worlds, then, is to apply targeted DSP to an otherwise bit-perfect stream in order to achieve a consistent result.
When EQing, you'll choose one of two goals. Some people aim for a flat, neutral sound, meaning complete bit-perfection with no adjustments to the way the source file naturally sounds. Others want a sound profile customized for them. For example, if you like exaggerated bass, you can boost those frequencies. This is where making sure Android audio is otherwise bit-perfect pays off, even for those who don't want a bit-perfect listening experience, since we can now make precise EQ changes to an otherwise unaltered signal.
If you're going all in, you've got USB Audio Player Pro installed and are using bit-perfect mode with wired headphones. That means you'll need to use the app's built-in tools to EQ your headphones, or else use an external hardware device. More likely, you have no reason to care about bit-perfection and are sticking with something like Spotify that runs through the system mixer with no other effects applied. Either way, you need to build an EQ preset.
You could EQ manually and should feel free to do so. However, these days, it's much more fashionable to let the professionals handle things. Head to autoeq.app and use the search box at the top to find your pair of headphones or in-ears. Select them, then you'll see some frequency graphs. Select your EQ app from the drop-down menu under those graphs, then save as a text file. Import that file into USB Audio Player Pro's Parametric EQ if you're using that app. AutoEQ even has exportable settings for Spotify's built-in equalizer. However, many audio enthusiasts on Android are currently using Wavelet, which will run in the background and apply a consistent EQ to all of the audio from your phone when connected to headphones. Remember that you'll need a separate EQ preset for each different pair of headphones.
All that's left to do now is kick back, throw on some jams and enjoy the best sound quality Android has to offer.

articles.title: White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green
articles.text:
The realm of stars resembles a fairy tale. In it, we find giants, supergiants, and also many dwarfs. Rather like the flames of a fire, most stars’ colors are based on temperature. Cooler stars look orange, sun-like stars appear white, and the hottest ones shine light blue. However, there are exceptions, and astronomers have recently discovered some among the class of stars known as white dwarfs.
At the end of their lives, stars with a mass similar to the sun expand and turn into red giants. Subsequently, they shed their gaseous envelope, creating a planetary nebula that we can admire through telescopes. In place of the star, a white dwarf remains—a highly condensed object the approximate volume of the Earth but the mass of the sun.
Initially, white dwarfs have extremely high temperatures, and so the first ones discovered shone from white to light blue. That’s how they got their name. But according to a new study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, the world of white dwarfs is actually far more colorful—with some stars turning pink, green, and even purple.
The researchers posit that density is the deciding factor. The atmospheres of the coolest white dwarfs can reach a density of approximately 1 gram per cubic centimeter. That’s roughly the same density as water, which may not sound like much, but it’s packed for a star, this being about a million times denser than the sun’s atmosphere. Under these conditions, any trace elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors.
Material from ancient planetary systems also plays a role. The closest planets can perish in the fiery embrace of the red giant phase. Other planets, and especially asteroids, begin to collide and migrate toward the dead star. Fragments of these bodies then integrate into the white dwarf's atmosphere.
Through a hobbyist’s telescope, a white dwarf looks just like any other faint star. However, if observed up close, their colors would be much more varied. Carbon-rich white dwarfs tend to be pink or purple. According to calculations, white dwarfs whose atmospheres have been enriched with material from shattered asteroids or other bodies will exhibit yellow and, in some cases, green shades. The coolest white dwarfs are often a baby blue, which is caused by hydrogen and helium atoms colliding in their extremely dense atmospheres.
One example is the star WD J1330+6435. With a temperature of around 4,000 degrees Celsius, it has accumulated rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium. These elements give it a light chartreuse color, making it the first known green star in our galaxy.
Another white dwarf, WD J1011+2845, has a massive amount of carbon in its atmosphere. Almost all of its radiation is concentrated at wavelengths exceeding 600 nanometers, giving it a salmon-pink color. Meanwhile, the white dwarf WD J902-2010 leans toward the more bubblegum end of the spectrum.
However, there’s no reason to expect white dwarfs to start getting renamed, because most of these stars are, in fact, white. For this study, the authors examined 152 white dwarfs located within 65 light-years of Earth. Only five of them showed unusual coloration, suggesting that approximately one in thirty white dwarfs in the universe shines with unusually colored light.
This might seem like an expected result, but scientists previously assumed that white dwarfs were predominantly blue. That assumption may reflect bias in sampling the night sky. The hottest white dwarfs are also typically the brightest and can, therefore, be seen from greater distances. Because they’re easier to observe, many studies end up over-representing blue stars.
While you won’t be able to see the nearest white dwarf with the naked eye either, you can at least look in its direction. Sirius B is the companion to the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. During winter, Sirius is easy to spot shining brightly above the eastern horizon. Sirius B belongs to the group of “more boring” white dwarfs—its temperature hovers around 25,000 Kelvin, giving it a light blue color.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

articles.title: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
articles.text:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode.
Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
The latest Windows Insider builds revamp search with filters, actions, and phone controls.
The search improvements are quite comprehensive. You can now filter results for files, actions, or web results. You can also use the search box to perform actions like changing the screen brightness or volume, and even perform actions on a connected phone, including making calls. Results can also offer much more detail, like when a file was last modified and its author, or pull in charts for stock prices and weather forecasts. And you can train Windows 11 search by clicking inline thumbs-up or thumbs-down icons to help it improve over time.
For the full list of changes, check out Microsoft’s blog post. Beta Build 26220.9836 and Experimental Build 26340.9843 are both available now to Windows Insiders.

articles.title: What happens when AI starts self-replicating? - Engadget
articles.text:
What happens when AI starts self-replicating?
Anthropic warns that future is soon, but the threat is less novel than it seems.
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team recently published research suggesting that small AI models may be only months away from replicating and spreading across insecure devices, creating slow but hard-to-kill autonomous botnets. AI companies are no strangers to playing up the world-ending potential of their products as a form of marketing, but in this instance, experts Engadget spoke to broadly agree small AI models could become capable of self-replicating in the near future. However, the actual threat they pose may be less novel than it appears.
"It's maybe a little earlier than I would have said. I would have predicted something more like summer of next year as the time I'd be really worried about this," says Chris Canal, the CEO of EquiStamp, a company that works with AI labs, safety organizations and governments to verify and evaluate models. "Anthropic very likely has employees with information about the frontier of research that I don't have access to. So they very well could be making better predictions." Canal attributes the recent pace of model advancement to the fact that employees at Anthropic and other frontier labs are using their own AI tools to do machine learning research.
"I think [self-replicating models] are in the future. I think they're real. I think we'll see them," says Michael Bailey, a professor at the School of Cybersecurity and Privacy at Georgia Tech. "Whether they'll take on the exact form and shape, and have the same consequences, that [Anthropic] is pitching is a completely open question."
Bailey has been studying internet worms since the early 2000s, and more recently, botnets. In 2017, he co-wrote Understanding the Mirai Botnet, which Anthropic cites as part of its own research. Mirai allowed a group of cybercriminals to create a large botnet of IoT devices they later used to carry out a DDoS attack against Sony's PlayStation Network. In the process, they ended up affecting Dyn, one of the largest DNS providers in the US. In turn, the attack broke much of the internet in 2016, knocking Amazon, GitHub, PayPal, Reddit and Twitter offline for many users across the US and parts of Europe. The financial fallout of the attack was significant, with Sony estimating it lost about $2.7 million in net revenue.
"What Mirai showed is that you could compose these botnets — and have them be useful — out of everyday devices: cable routers, IP-enabled cameras, these kinds of things," says Bailey. "We thought those devices weren't useful to an adversary, either as targets or as sources of computation for launching attacks. In fact, they're actually quite effective at doing those kinds of things."
A decade later, Anthropic argues AI worms could represent a meaningful evolution of Mirai and other hard-coded botnets like Kimwolf because they could figure out unfamiliar devices on their own. Bailey says adaptability itself isn't new. Mirai already worked across "heterogeneous" devices, from routers to IP cameras running on different chip architectures. But that adaptability was finite: each new architecture required human work, at minimum recompiling the malware. What's novel, Bailey says, is the prospect of AI automating that work, though he doesn't think Anthropic demonstrated it "in a compelling way."
As a result, Bailey suggests more capable AI models will "redistribute" who does the work of creating botnets. "It's not going to do new stuff," he says. "It's going to change the economics between attackers and defenders." While Anthropic showed that a model could hop between devices and set up inference on each, it did so in an emulated network where the "exploit" involved was trivial. Additionally, Bailey takes issue with Anthropic's self-replicating claim.
"The framing is somewhat of a misnomer, because they're doing things like sharding. Not that that's bad, but it's not like a worm or a virus. It's not full propagation," he says. Instead, Bailey argues a real-world AI botnet might work more like a dropper, a type of malware that gets a foothold on a device and installs other code. Rather than copying itself wholesale onto every machine it compromises, the botnet would install a small coordination tool that takes instructions from elsewhere in the network.
"The idea that the malware itself is self-replicating, like existing internet worms, where I'd copy an exact copy of my code to the new architecture and it would start running a new agent — that's not really what's happening here," says Bailey. He also notes worms can be polymorphic, meaning they can change both their signature and behaviors. For an AI botnet to do that, he says, it would need to retrain its own models, something Anthropic didn't attempt. The closest it came was showing that copies of a model could pass notes to their successors and get better at setting up inference over time.
As with any warning to come out of an AI lab, it's worth asking if Anthropic published this research as a form of marketing, especially with the company officially filing for an IPO so soon after. "I think what's more likely is that the companies are worried about other AI companies being reckless," Canal says. "They realize they're incentivized to make the best model and deliver it to market faster so they can have market share, and they know the other companies have the same incentives."
Regardless of whether this novel threat vector is truly a worm, and how far in the future it might actually be, Anthropic's own suggestions for how to mitigate its harms are surprisingly old school. It suggests ISPs notifying customers of an infection and then limiting their internet access to a short list of safe websites — a strategy deployed during Mirai to great effect. The company also suggests regulation as a potential solution, pointing to the UK, where easily guessable default passwords on IoT devices are now banned under the PSTI Act.
To that point, Bailey argues the appropriate response to AI worms "looks a lot more like what we've been doing in systems security for a very long time, as opposed to something particularly unique to the AI space." In fact, according to Canal, it would be difficult to add safeguards to an open-weight model that would prevent it from acting as a worm. "There are lots of ideas, but there's nothing robust so far," he says. In work with FAR.AI, an AI safety research non-profit, EquiStamp found that "basically any strategy you Google for removing safeguards from a model works."
But as Bailey points out, "even misbehaving agents are going to have a hard time if they're up against hardened devices." If there's a single takeaway from Anthropic's research, he says, it's that we consistently fail to remember all the safety lessons we've learned in the past. Security in the era of AI worms will probably look a lot like it does now. "It looks like paying attention to patching these devices, paying attention to isolation, paying attention to good passwords and good hygiene," says Bailey. Those solutions are easy to describe and notoriously difficult to implement, but if AI truly makes these sorts of attacks more prevalent we may not have a choice.

articles.title: Hơn 30 năm mua vé số, nhà thầu Malaysia trúng Jackpot tương đương 64 tỷ
articles.text:
Một nhà thầu cải tạo công trình 54 tuổi tại bang Sarawak, Malaysia, vừa trúng giải độc đắc Toto 4D Jackpot 1 trị giá hơn 10,16 triệu Ringgit.
Theo tờ The Borneo Post và Utusan Borneo, giải thưởng đến từ kỳ quay số ngày 26/9/2026. Hai dãy số giúp người đàn ông trúng giải là 8622 và 5765, vốn xuất hiện trong một giấc mơ của ông.
Tổng số tiền ông nhận được là 10,16 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 64 tỷ đồng), cộng thêm 672 Ringgit (khoảng 4,2 triệu đồng) nhờ vé được mua theo cách chơi hệ thống (System Play) - hình thức bao nhiều bộ số để tăng cơ hội trúng.
Trước khi trở thành triệu phú, ông là khách hàng trung thành của công ty xổ số lớn nhất Malaysia Sports Toto trong hơn 3 thập kỷ, duy trì thói quen chi khoảng 50 Ringgit (khoảng 315.000 đồng) mỗi tuần để mua vé Toto 4D Jackpot.
Ông kể rằng hai dãy số 8622 và 5765 xuất hiện trong một giấc mơ. Khi đang ăn trưa gần một công trình cải tạo do mình phụ trách, ông nhận thấy một điểm bán vé Sports Toto nằm ngay cạnh nhà hàng.
Nghĩ đến hai bộ số trong giấc mơ hôm trước, ông quyết định mua dựa theo trí nhớ. “Lúc mua, tôi thậm chí còn chẳng dám chắc mình có nhớ đúng những con số đã mơ hay không. Chính tôi cũng không ngờ chúng lại mang đến cho mình khoản tiền thưởng lớn đến vậy”, ông chia sẻ.
Sau khi kiểm tra kết quả trên trang web chính thức của Sports Toto, ông đến trụ sở STM Lottery tại thủ đô Kuala Lumpur để nhận giải.
Dù khoản tiền hơn 10 triệu Ringgit có thể mở ra nhiều lựa chọn mới về nhà cửa, công việc và cuộc sống gia đình, nhưng người đàn ông này chưa công bố kế hoạch mua sắm hay đầu tư cụ thể.
“Tôi dự định quản lý số tiền một cách thận trọng và dành riêng một phần cho tương lai của các con. Cần lên kế hoạch cẩn thận trước khi đưa ra những quyết định lớn là rất quan trọng”, ông nói.
‘Giấc mơ’ và ‘con số đời thường’ trong văn hóa xổ số Malaysia
Câu chuyện của nhà thầu ở Sarawak không phải là trường hợp cá biệt. Trong các thông tin công bố về người trúng thưởng tại Malaysia, những con số gắn với giấc mơ, ngày sinh, giấy tờ gia đình hay biển đăng ký xe thường xuất hiện trong lời kể của người thắng giải.
Tháng 2/2026, một phụ nữ 72 tuổi ở Penang trúng giải Supreme Toto 6/58 trị giá khoảng 40,12 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 254 tỷ đồng). Bà mua vé Lucky Pick, tức lựa chọn số ngẫu nhiên, trong một lần ghé điểm bán vé khi đi mua sắm.
Tháng 6/2026, một người bán hàng về hưu 62 tuổi ở bang Perak trúng khoảng 11,8 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 74 tỷ đồng) trong trò Toto 4D Jackpot 1. Hai dãy số trúng thưởng được ông chọn dựa trên thông tin ghi trong giấy khai sinh của các cháu.
Cùng tháng, một người đàn ông 66 tuổi ở Kuala Lumpur, làm nghề tài xế riêng, trúng 23,95 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 151 tỷ đồng) với dãy số tượng trưng cho số con, số cháu và ngày cưới của vợ chồng ông.
Tháng 7, một nữ thợ massage ở Kuala Lumpur trúng 4,87 triệu Ringgit bằng biển số xe của chị gái và một người bạn thân.
Sang tháng 8, một bà nội trợ 50 tuổi ở Perak trúng 12,9 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 81 tỷ đồng) - lần thứ hai trong vòng 3 năm, sau khi từng trúng khoảng 1,4 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 8,8 tỷ đồng) trước đó.
Những câu chuyện này cho thấy một điều: ở Malaysia, xổ số gắn với niềm tin rằng những con số xuất hiện trong giấc mơ, trong giấy tờ gia đình, hay trong những sự kiện nhỏ của đời sống có thể mang lại vận may.
Xổ số vẫn là trò chơi có tính may rủi. Việc mua vé trong thời gian dài, chọn số theo giấc mơ hay sử dụng hình thức chơi hệ thống không bảo đảm người chơi sẽ trúng giải. Những khoản thưởng hàng chục triệu Ringgit chỉ là kết quả hiếm gặp, bên cạnh rất nhiều tấm vé không mang lại giải thưởng.
Năm 2025, tổng doanh thu gộp từ xổ số hợp pháp tại Malaysia ước khoảng 2 tỷ USD, với dự báo tăng lên 2,3 tỷ USD trong năm 2026.
Tháng 1/2025, Sports Toto ghi nhận giải độc đắc cao nhất lịch sử Malaysia: 121,7 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 771 tỷ đồng), được chia cho 60 người trúng.
Trong số đó, một doanh nhân 30 tuổi nhận gần 35 triệu Ringgit (khoảng 221,7 tỷ đồng) với một tấm vé System 12 - hình thức bao 12 bộ số để tăng cơ hội trúng so với vé thông thường.
Theo The Borneo Post, Utusan Borneo, WeirdKaya

articles.title: ChatGPT teen safety: limits apply ‘regardless of a user’s age’
articles.text:
ChatGPT will stop giving teenagers practical information about weapons and security systems, even when a question looks harmless, OpenAI said on Friday. The limit applies to teen accounts with no sign of violent intent.
OpenAI announced the change in a blog post, alongside a promise to publish a Community Safety Report on violence prevention. It made more than 200 referrals to law enforcement in the third quarter, the company said. The new safeguards will start rolling out in the next few weeks.
Less detail on past attacks, for everyone
For all users, ChatGPT will give less detail about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, even when that detail is available elsewhere online. It will not reconstruct an attack, including which weapons the attacker used and how they got them. It will also avoid detailed comparisons of how much harm attacks caused.
“These limits apply regardless of a user’s age or reason for asking,” OpenAI wrote.
People can still ask how such events affected victims and communities, and how to spot warning signs, OpenAI said.
When a chat shows signs that someone is fixating on violence or on seriously harming another person, ChatGPT will be able to end it automatically. If ChatGPT ends several chats for that reason, OpenAI may pause the account for a time.
Teens, age checks and parents
OpenAI said it has strengthened its age prediction system, which estimates from signals such as behaviour whether a user is under 18. It now keeps checking new signals and moves users into the teen experience when it sees fit. Adults placed there by mistake can confirm their age through Persona, OpenAI’s age verification partner.
Since July, parents with linked accounts get an alert if OpenAI deactivates a teen’s account over violence. OpenAI said it is working on alerts for when it pauses a teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence.
“Developing effective violence safeguards in AI systems requires solving novel problems in recognizing risk and responding appropriately,” OpenAI wrote.
The first report in early 2027
The first Community Safety Report will come out in early 2027 and cover the second half of 2026, with updates every six months. It will explain how OpenAI detects and responds to safety issues, with anonymised examples and data, the company said.
The update adds to the ChatGPT teen safety measures OpenAI launched in August. Earlier this month, Common Sense Media said ChatGPT for Teens is unsafe for under-18s. Eight US states have sued OpenAI over harm to children, and Texas has sued the company and Sam Altman.

articles.title: The pros and cons of using an all-in-one desktop computer - Engadget
articles.text:
The pros and cons of using an all-in-one desktop computer
Be willing to trade flexibility for simplicity.
All-in-one (AIO) PCs pack an entire computer into a monitor, so you don't need a tower, extra cables or the desk clutter of a traditional desktop setup. They're not the same as mini PCs, which are small boxes you still connect to a separate display. AIOs are their own category, a halfway point between a laptop and a desktop.
That simplicity has made AIOs appealing to anyone who wants a clean modern-looking setup without much fuss. Thanks to their sleek design, they've become a staple of corporate offices and school computer labs. But the same design limits them. Squeezing every component into a slim chassis means sacrificing the upgrade flexibility and repairability you'd get from a traditional desktop.
So is an all-in-one the right choice, or would a traditional desktop or laptop serve you better? The answer depends on how you plan to use the machine, your budget and how much you value upgrading your own hardware.
What are the advantages of an all-in-one desktop computer?
The big draw of an all-in-one PC is simplicity. The central unit combines the actual computer and the monitor. Most bundles you find online, such as the Apple iMac, also include a keyboard and mouse. Just unbox it, plug in one cord and start working. Because they're ready-to-use systems that don't require getting tangled in a million wires, AIOs are a great fit for non-technical users.
With everything integrated into the display, AIOs take up very little space, especially when compared to a tower-and-monitor combo. This makes them particularly suitable for smaller apartments, dorm rooms and home offices. And let's not forget how good they look. Design may not be the top priority, but a sleek, minimalist setup has real appeal.
While an all-in-one isn't portable like a laptop, it's much easier to move than a traditional desktop. Need to clear out your home office because a friend is crashing for a few days? All you need to do is carry a single unit to another room instead of unplugging and hauling a tower, a monitor, and a tangle of cables.
What are the downsides of an all-in-one PC?
The biggest tradeoff of an AIO's compact design is flexibility. All-in-one PCs are tightly packed, and many of their components are fixed in place to keep the chassis thin. Upgrading the processor or graphics card is nearly impossible on most models. Some AIOs let you upgrade RAM and storage, but with high RAM prices, it may not be worth it.
What you can upgrade depends on the model. Newer iMacs are very much what-you-see-is-what-you-get, while the Dell Pro 24 65W lets you add more storage and RAM. Check a specific model's specs before assuming you'll be able to upgrade it.
The design also makes repairs harder and more expensive. When something fails, technicians often have to work around glued-together parts that are hard to reach.
The right choice depends on what you need. If you mostly browse, work on documents and take video calls, the convenience of an all-in-one is hard to beat. If you game, edit video or want a system you can upgrade in a few years, a traditional PC gives you more room to grow.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 31/10: Thế giới tăng cao, dầu diesel vượt 30.000 đồng/lít
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (30/10) tăng mạnh.
Ở phiên giao dịch 30/10, theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, giá dầu Brent chốt phiên ở mức 113,4 USD/thùng, tăng 2,37% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI đóng cửa phiên 30/10 ở mức 104,1 USD/thùng, tăng 2,08% so với phiên liền trước.
Tính chung trong cả tháng 10 này, giá dầu Brent tăng 13,6%, còn dầu WTI tăng 15,2%.
Giá dầu thế giới tăng mạnh trong phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này khi giới đầu tư lo ngại xung đột Mỹ - Iran có thể leo thang sau cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ tại Mỹ.
Giá dầu tăng nhanh sau vụ tấn công tàu chở dầu ở eo biển Hormuz làm nổi bật rủi ro về nguồn cung.
Cơ quan Điều phối Thương mại Hàng hải Anh (UKMTO) thông báo một tàu chở dầu hoạt động tại eo biển Hormuz đã bị tấn công bằng thiết bị nổ gắn trên thân tàu. Tuy nhiên, hiện chưa xác định được lực lượng nào đứng sau vụ việc này.
Trong khi đó, ngày 30/10, Đại sứ quán Mỹ tại Riyadh thông báo, Washington đã yêu cầu các nhân viên chính phủ không làm nhiệm vụ khẩn cấp cùng gia đình rời Saudi Arabia kể từ ngày 23/10, do những rủi ro an ninh liên quan đến các cuộc tấn công của lực lượng Houthi (vốn được Iran hậu thuẫn) nhằm vào sân bay dân sự và cơ sở hạ tầng trọng yếu.
Trước đó, lực lượng Houthi tuyên bố đã tập kích một số địa điểm ở Saudi Arabia, bao gồm nhà máy lọc dầu Ras Tanura, nhà máy lọc dầu Rabigh và một cơ sở sản xuất ở Abqaiq thuộc tập đoàn dầu khí quốc gia Saudi Aramco.
Còn liên minh quân sự do Saudi Arabia dẫn đầu cho hay đã đánh chặn một tên lửa hành trình do Houthi phóng về phía khu vực miền Tây nước này.
Những diễn biến an ninh tại Trung Đông tiếp tục làm dấy lên lo ngại các cơ sở năng lượng trong khu vực có thể trở thành mục tiêu tấn công, đe dọa hoạt động khai thác, vận chuyển và xuất khẩu dầu thô.
Bên cạnh những diễn biến quân sự, các nỗ lực ngoại giao nhằm tìm kiếm thỏa thuận giữa Mỹ và Iran vẫn đang được duy trì.
Theo nguồn tin của Reuters, các nhà trung gian hòa giải Qatar đã trở lại Tehran hôm 30/10 để tiếp tục nỗ lực làm cầu nối giữa Washington và Tehran.
Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump cho biết, Phó tổng thống JD Vance đã liên hệ với Iran nhằm hỗ trợ nước này tiếp cận các nguồn cung vật tư y tế. Thông tin này được đưa ra sau khi truyền thông Mỹ đưa tin ông Vance đã gửi thư cho quan chức an ninh cấp cao của Tehran nhằm thúc đẩy nối lại các cuộc đàm phán hòa bình.
Hãng thông tấn bán chính thức Tasnim của Iran thông tin, Tehran đã nhận được thư của ông Vance nhưng chưa đưa ra phản hồi. Tasnim cho biết Iran muốn Mỹ đáp ứng các điều kiện do nước này đưa ra, đồng thời nhấn mạnh mọi lập trường đi ngược lại khung điều khoản đó đều không thể chấp nhận.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (31/10) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 29/10, giá bán của các loại xăng dầu đều được điều chỉnh tăng so với kỳ điều hành liền trước.
Cụ thể, giá bán lẻ xăng E5RON92 không cao hơn 26.027 đồng/lít, tăng 666 đồng/lít.
Giá xăng E10RON95-III cũng được điều chỉnh tăng 521 đồng/lít, lên mức tối đa 25.734 đồng/lít.
Cùng xu hướng, giá dầu diesel 0.05S tăng 696 đồng/lít, lên mức không cao hơn 30.246 đồng/lít.
Còn giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 223 đồng/kg, lên mức tối đa 23.596 đồng/kg.
Dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.

articles.title: OpenAI whistleblowers and ‘a slew of cybersecurity incidents’
articles.text:
Twenty House Democrats have asked OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to promise not to fire OpenAI whistleblowers who share safety information. They also want OpenAI to keep its pause on its most capable models until independent oversight is in place.
Representative Greg Casar of Texas led the letter, dated 29 October. It asks OpenAI to answer 11 sets of questions by 13 November.
“We are writing to express concern over your decision to fire apparent whistleblowers at your company for sharing information with an outside AI safety group, even as your company continues to experience a slew of cybersecurity incidents,” the lawmakers wrote.
The three fired researchers
The letter names the researchers as Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang. OpenAI reportedly fired them after it checked their personal phones. It found disappearing messages turned on in their Signal chats with Ryan Greenblatt, then a researcher at Redwood Research. TNW covered the firings last week.
OpenAI has said it fired them for breaking its rules on sensitive information, not for raising safety concerns, the letter notes. The researchers say they never shared OpenAI’s confidential information with anyone outside the company.
The lawmakers ask what the three shared, with whom, and why that was a fireable offence. They also ask whether OpenAI has fired anyone else for raising safety concerns. The question also covers staff who talked to safety groups or oversight bodies.
Hugging Face and the pause
Two OpenAI employees warned executives months before the Hugging Face breach, the letter says. They said OpenAI was not monitoring its newest models properly in testing. Executives replied that the tests had to move fast so the models could ship on time, the letter says, citing The New York Times. OpenAI’s 31 August reply to an earlier letter from Casar did not mention those warnings, the lawmakers wrote.
“These incidents appear to stem from alignment issues with your models,” the lawmakers wrote.
According to the letter, OpenAI has paused training, testing and tool use for its most capable models. OpenAI has said it will resume only when it is confident that more safeguards are in place, the letter says. The lawmakers ask which models the pause covers and when testing will resume.
They also want a list of every security incident OpenAI is investigating. And they ask whether OpenAI can stop its models when they act without permission.
What OpenAI published the same day
Also on 29 October, OpenAI published a post on how it now monitors its frontier models. It said it had replayed the Hugging Face incident with its expanded monitors in place. In that test, the monitors alerted its security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the breach at Hugging Face.
“We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services,” OpenAI wrote.
Alerts can page staff at any hour for frontier training runs, but only in business hours for most other work, OpenAI said. OpenAI has switched paging off for internal Codex traffic. An outside review by METR and Redwood Research found weak spots in the system in July and August. OpenAI said it has fixed most of them and one fix is still in progress.

articles.title: Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
articles.text:
Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced single “Down On My Luck”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Maybe you know him from his roles on The Chi or Bel-Air. Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence (peeling oranges and waxing poetic), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show.
Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.
Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.
Point is, the man wears many hats. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Just capture those ideas before they disappear.
What is your most indispensable tool?
Voice Memos. Everything starts there for me. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. Just press record before the thought disappears.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
Instagram, for better or worse. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. Instagram can be a circus, obviously, but it’s also a very valuable tool for connection.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Maybe Meta glasses. Them motherfuckers seem like they’re being used for evil.
What creation are you most proud of?
Probably my upcoming album right now. It’s the first album that I’ve really taken myself completely seriously as a producer. The surrounding art, videos, design, clothing, and world I’m building around it is something that really excites me as well.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I either do my Shambhavi Mahamudra meditation that I learned from Sadhguru or the Wim Hof breathing method. Ideally, I’ll do the Wim Hof breathing method in the steam room and then the meditation.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Live from the contradiction.
What is the last GIF or meme you used?

articles.title: AI training opt-out: publishers ‘should not have to choose’
articles.text:
Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic will honour one shared AI training opt-out in robots.txt. It lets a website keep its content out of generative AI training with a single rule. Today, a site that wants to say no has to write separate rules for each company’s crawler.
The shared signal comes from an IETF draft by Kevin Kelley of Anthropic, published on Friday. The same day, Google, OpenAI and Microsoft announced they would support it. Kelley announced the draft on the IETF’s AI preferences mailing list.
It works through robots.txt, the file sites already use to tell crawlers what they may fetch. A site adds a group for a new “policy token”, __usage_ai-training. It then lists the paths it does not want used for training. The draft’s example blocks a whole site except its press kit.
“Publishers should not have to choose between being discoverable in Bing and deciding how generative models use their work,” Krishna Madhavan, principal product manager for Microsoft Bing, wrote.
Who starts when
Anthropic has already started work on it, Kelley wrote. He said it would complement Anthropic’s existing crawler controls rather than replace them.
“It’ll take us some time to add support across our services and work through the inevitable complications and edge cases that I’m sure we’ll discover,” Kelley wrote.
OpenAI said it aims to implement the signal “in the coming months”. Its existing crawler controls, such as GPTBot, will still apply, it said.
Google said it aims to support the signal in 2027, and its crawler documentation says early 2027. Google-Extended is Google’s own AI training control. If a site opts out with the token and does not mention Google-Extended, Google will treat it as a block on Google-Extended. Sites that allow Google-Extended can appear in Gemini app answers and get clicks, Google Search Advocate John Mueller wrote.
Microsoft will honour the new preferences from 1 February 2027. They will replace the NoArchive and NoCache tags it has used since 2023. Microsoft is also adding a separate page-level setting for grounding, when an AI answer draws on a live web page. One option allows Microsoft’s own products, such as Copilot. It blocks the grounding services Microsoft sells to other companies.
What the signal does not do
The draft says the token states a preference about how sites want their content used. It is not an order about crawling. A site with no such group has expressed no preference, and existing rules for all crawlers do not count. Private agreements between a site and an AI company can override it.
The draft is an individual submission. The IETF’s datatracker says the IETF has not endorsed it and it has no formal standing in the standards process.
Microsoft said the new preferences “do not establish licensing or payment arrangements”. Blocking AI grounding “will significantly reduce your content’s visibility in AI-generated experiences”, it added. It does not change a page’s place in Bing search results.
Meta communications head Andy Stone voiced support for a common signal on X, The Verge reported. He did not say whether Meta would honour it.
The European angle
Google said the proposal is consistent with the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI under the AI Act. The code recognises robots.txt as a main way for publishers to state machine-readable preferences.
Among the people the draft thanks for shaping the discussion are staff from the Financial Times, the BBC, Bertelsmann and the European Publishers Council.
Publishers have also pushed for payment. In July, Cloudflare told AI crawlers to pay or get blocked. Its chief executive has warned that bots could reach 1,000 times human web traffic. In Australia, the ABC and SBS want AI companies to pay for news.
