articles.title: Google joins OpenAI and Anthropic in promising new scraping controls - Engadget
articles.text:
Google joins OpenAI and Anthropic in promising new scraping controls
The new robots.txt directive will prevent the companies from scraping content for generative AI training.
Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft have committed to honoring a new robots.txt directive, which will allow publishers to specify their preferences when it comes to the scraping of their content for generative AI training. The companies have decided to adopt a proposal under consideration at IETF, the open standards organization for the internet, written by Anthropic technical lead for standards Kevin Kelley.
As OpenAI and Google explained in their announcements, website owners currently have to identify individual crawlers and add separate rules for each provider. Kelley's proposal will change that by getting multiple AI companies to recognize and honor a single common signal. Publishers have to set up a new user agent in the robots.txt file that's specifically for AI training, which will look like this:
User-Agent: __usage_ai-training
Disallow: /
Allow: /press-kit/
That will block crawlers specifically meant to gather data for AI training. The "Allow" section gives website operators the option to allow scraping for AI training for specific parts of the page, such as if there's a press kit on it. But this new user-agent section doesn't prevent crawling altogether or prevent content from showing up on Google search. For instance, Google will specifically interpret it as a stop sign specifically for the "Google-Extended" user agent, which crawls websites for materials used to train Gemini models.
Another thing to note is that this directive cannot undo any past scraping the companies have already done. If they'd crawled a page previously, they already have its content. This will just prevent them from scraping websites or specific pages in the future. Anthropic has already started supporting the new directive, while Microsoft said it will start supporting it on February 1, 2027. Google said it will support it in early 2027, as well, while OpenAI pledged to implement the new signal in the coming months.

articles.title: Phòng tập gym sang chảnh, chỉ 500.000 đồng/tháng: Bẫy mua thẻ dài hạn
articles.text:
Thu phí hội viên trước nhiều năm là mô hình được một số chuỗi phòng tập áp dụng.
Theo ông Nguyễn Đức Duy, một người từng kinh doanh phòng tập gym, khách hàng thường được chào mời các gói tập 1 năm, 3-5 năm, thậm chí thẻ trọn đời. Điểm hấp dẫn của mô hình này nằm ở mức giá bình quân mỗi tháng. Khi chia tổng số tiền phải trả cho nhiều năm sử dụng, chi phí có thể thấp hơn đáng kể so với các gói ngắn hạn. Điều này tạo động lực để khách hàng thanh toán một lần với số tiền lớn.
Theo mức giá được giới thiệu trong các gói tập, chi phí ngắn hạn có thể khoảng 1,2-2,5 triệu đồng/tháng. Nếu thanh toán trước từ 1,5-5 năm, mức phí bình quân có thể giảm còn 500.000-700.000 đồng/tháng, tùy hạng thẻ và chương trình bán hàng.
Đơn cử tại California Fitness & Yoga, nếu chọn hình thức đóng theo tháng, mức phí niêm yết khoảng 1,3 triệu đồng cho loại thẻ Diamond. Nếu thanh toán trọn 24,8 triệu đồng trong 27 tháng, chi phí bình quân giảm còn khoảng 918.500 đồng/tháng. Khách hàng tiết kiệm khoảng 10,3 triệu đồng. Thẻ này còn cho phép hội viên đi kèm một người thân hoặc bạn bè. Nếu hai người cùng sử dụng, chi phí bình quân mỗi người còn khoảng 459.000 đồng/tháng.
Ngoài ra, mô hình thẻ tập trả trước còn đánh trúng tâm lý quan tâm đến sức khỏe của nhóm khách hàng có điều kiện tài chính. Đây là nhóm sẵn sàng chi tiền để duy trì việc tập luyện lâu dài.
Khoản thu trước giúp tạo nguồn tiền để doanh nghiệp đầu tư trang thiết bị, thuê mặt bằng, mở rộng hệ thống và chi trả hoạt động thường xuyên. Tuy nhiên, khi doanh nghiệp gặp khó khăn hoặc phải đóng cửa cơ sở, hội viên mua thẻ dài hạn thường ở thế bất lợi.
Hợp đồng tập luyện do doanh nghiệp soạn sẵn có thể bao gồm các điều khoản về hoàn tiền, chuyển đổi cơ sở hoặc điều kiện duy trì thẻ. Nếu không đọc kỹ, hội viên có thể gặp bất lợi khi phòng tập ngừng hoạt động hoặc không cung cấp dịch vụ như cam kết. Rủi ro tài chính càng phức tạp với người thanh toán bằng thẻ tín dụng hoặc vay trả góp, bởi nghĩa vụ trả nợ có thể vẫn tiếp tục dù dịch vụ tập luyện bị gián đoạn.
Gần đây, thị trường ghi nhận một số chuỗi phòng tập rơi vào tình trạng như trên. Điển hình, California Fitness & Yoga thông báo tạm dừng hoạt động tại hàng loạt địa điểm từ ngày 26/10 với lý do liên quan đến vận hành. Trước đó, Lumi Fitness & Yoga cũng đóng cửa nhiều phòng tập.
Rủi ro khi phòng tập chuyển địa điểm, ngừng hoạt động
Luật sư Nguyễn Hoàng Duy, Giám đốc Công ty Luật TNHH Hoàng Duy và Cộng sự, cho biết tình trạng phòng tập gym thu tiền trước rồi ngừng hoạt động, thay tên hoặc lập cơ sở mới để né tránh trách nhiệm không phải là hiện tượng mới.
Theo luật sư, một kịch bản thường gặp là phòng tập đưa ra các gói ưu đãi lớn, bán thẻ dài hạn hoặc trọn đời với giá thấp để thu hút khách hàng thanh toán trước. Hợp đồng có thể cài điều khoản cho phép chuyển hội viên sang cơ sở khác nếu địa điểm đăng ký đóng cửa.
Sau khi thu được khoản tiền lớn, phòng tập thông báo ngừng hoạt động và chuyển khách hàng sang một cơ sở khác. Địa điểm mới có thể cách xa nơi cũ hàng chục cây số hoặc không bảo đảm chất lượng dịch vụ như cam kết. Khách hàng không chấp nhận phương án này có nguy cơ mất khoản tiền đã đóng.
Luật sư Nguyễn Hoàng Duy nhận định, việc tự ý chuyển giao dịch vụ cho bên thứ ba khi chưa có sự đồng ý tự nguyện của khách hàng có thể vi phạm quy định của Bộ luật Dân sự năm 2015. Những điều khoản đẩy toàn bộ rủi ro sang người tiêu dùng cũng có thể có dấu hiệu vi phạm Luật Bảo vệ quyền lợi người tiêu dùng.
Trường hợp có căn cứ cho thấy doanh nghiệp ngay từ đầu đã sử dụng thủ đoạn gian dối nhằm chiếm đoạt tiền của khách hàng, cơ quan chức năng có thể xem xét dấu hiệu tội phạm theo quy định của Bộ luật Hình sự.
Tuy nhiên, việc doanh nghiệp không thực hiện cam kết hoặc chậm hoàn trả tiền chưa đủ để kết luận có hành vi chiếm đoạt tài sản. Việc xác định trách nhiệm hình sự phải dựa trên chứng cứ và kết quả điều tra cụ thể.
Luật sư khuyến nghị các hội viên bị ảnh hưởng nên phối hợp, tập hợp hợp đồng, chứng từ thanh toán và tài liệu liên quan để gửi đơn đến cơ quan chức năng, đề nghị xác minh, làm rõ dấu hiệu vi phạm. Người tiêu dùng vẫn có quyền khởi kiện dân sự để yêu cầu bảo vệ quyền lợi; việc tập hợp thành nhóm có thể giúp chia sẻ chi phí và củng cố chứng cứ.
Đối với những người có nhu cầu tập luyện, luật sư khuyến nghị cần tìm hiểu kỹ uy tín của phòng tập và nghiên cứu cẩn trọng các điều khoản hợp đồng trước khi thanh toán để hạn chế rủi ro pháp lý.

articles.title: Touchscreens everywhere!
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy Halloween, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Touchscreens everywhere!
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A new place to read books, a huge new game for iOS, an impressive new robovac, and more.
This week, I was in the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee on a family vacation. It was delightful (and the reason this week’s Installer is a little short). I’ve also been reading about job hunting and 30 Rock and crypto detectives, testing the DuckDuckGo browser after a bunch of you told me to add it to the list, watching the adorable new Pixar short over and over, getting caught up on VisionQuest, playing with my new Pebble Index 01 now that it finally arrived, listening to music on my rad-looking new CMF Speaker S, and eating a worrying number of pumpkin chocolate chip muffins.
I also have for you some new gear from Apple and Amazon, a better way to read books on your phone, a resurrected note-taking app, an absurdly expensive robovac, and much more. Let’s do it.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / giving to trick-or-treaters this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The new iPad Mini. With apologies to the touchscreen MacBook, this is the most intriguing new Apple product of the week. I, too, am annoyed that there’s no ProMotion screen, but I’m excited about thinner and lighter, and I’m very excited about the idea of a functionally water- and dustproof tablet.
- The Alexa Photo Frame. The Echo Show 16 is a cool smart home hub, but $500 is just too much for me. But a $200 digital photo frame that is also, sometimes, only when you need it, a smart home hub and timer-setter? That will end up in my living room. And my parents’. And my in-laws’.
- nvAlt. One of the all-time great note-taking apps got its first update in forever, and now it can run on modern Macs. (The developer is also working on nvUltra, which is in beta and even better.) If you’re a plain-text notetaker, you’re gonna want to get back into this app.
- Chromagraph. The director Rian Johnson — yes, that one — worked with his favorite cinematographer to make it possible to process iPhone photos the way they like best. An extremely opinionated camera app from people who have very much earned those opinions. I love it.
- “I love the iPod. It ruined everything.” This Mic The Snare video is both a very good history of the iPod and a surprisingly cogent theory that the iPod is to blame for some of the worst things about modern life. I still miss my gold iPod Mini.
- Readwise Books. A really nice-looking, really powerful app for buying, reading, and tracking your books. Right now it’s a little bit “better Kindle” and a lot “better Goodreads.” So far I’m mostly using the social feed to get recommendations from strangers, which suits me just fine. This went right onto my Boox Palma homescreen.
- Phantom Blade Zero. Currently burning up the Steam charts, this one. People love the martial arts-inspired combat system and the game’s overall aesthetic, and I’m even hearing good things about the music.
- No Man’s Sky. This is definitely one of the biggest and most ambitious games to ever come to iOS (and all it took was a decade!). It works on pretty much all recent iPhones and iPads, too. Just don’t be fooled by the Free sign at the top; the game costs $20. But it’s worth it.
- The Matic Serene. Two things here. One, $1,700 is an absolutely ludicrous price for a robot vacuum, no matter how good it is. Two, “we made it quieter” is maybe the quickest way to get me in particular to want your robot vacuum. Please, friends, do not let me buy this.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Currently watching: VisionQuest. It’s quite good! James Spader has really stolen the show, but I am a little biased as a huge Blacklist fan.” — Spencer
“I’m using CallMe to coordinate when my friends and I call each other. You can tap ‘I’m free for the next 15/30/60 minutes’ and your friends will get a notification. When you’re both free you can call each other (outside of the app). Makes it easy to reconnect.” — Jordan
“I’ve been spending the last few days working on my Top 10 for WXPN’s annual Top 885. This year is ‘Top 885 Songs from Movies and TV,’ and it’s especially challenging.” — Ben
“The one game that I play religiously is Clues By Sam, a daily logic puzzle game where speed and accuracy is the goal. Because everyone starts at the same spot, your time is your score, and it’s very fun competing with friends every day. Puzzles range from easy (~2 minutes) on Mondays to Brutal (up to ~15 minutes) on Sundays. Would 100% recommend adding it to your daily rotation.” — Adam
“Maybe niche, but Steam Frame and trying out older 3D media on it that flopped or became obsolete. Stereoscopic 3DS games and 3D movies work better than they ever did on original hardware, on devices with a dedicated individual display for each eye.” — Mango
“I am sooo into the Vivaldi browser now, with the look and feel, and all the customisations! 😍” — Oscar
“Spending some more time learning about the AT Protocol for a class project. The tech is neat. Fell down the rabbit hole of mental poker cryptography.” — James
“The YouTube channel Digging the Greats by Brandon Shaw is fantastic for music lovers like myself. He deeply analyzes albums and songs in long-form videos, from Prince’s ‘Purple Rain’ to Kendrick Lamar’s To Pimp a Butterfly. I also recently finished two of a four-part video series: one where he only listened to music on an iPod for a month, and another where he explored the history of cassettes and mixtapes. I highly recommend checking out his channel if you love music!” — Josh
“The Dark Matter finale is this week.” — Steve
“I used Firefox for a long time but really don’t like their stance on AI and all the junk they keep adding (VPN, for instance). So I went to Librewolf, which is a Firefox fork that strips out all of the telemetry and AI and also pre-configures a bunch of hardening. I’ve encountered no problems whatsoever with any websites or streaming content.” — Nicholas
Signing off
Back in the day, before I worked in the basement and actually left my house on occasion, I had a real weakness for laptop bags. Even now, I have absolutely no need for a new one, but after watching Byron Seven’s video about designing a laptop sleeve / desk organizer / backpack thing, I desperately want the one he made. Even if you don’t want the product, watch the video — it’s a cool look into product design and just a fabulously made video about a bag.
See you next week!

articles.title: Sam Altman: DRAM in home PCs is ‘quite terrible’, used 5% of the time
articles.text:
Samsung hosted OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman for talks with about 50 of its presidents on Saturday. Two days earlier, a podcast went out in which Sam Altman said it is “quite terrible” for the world’s limited DRAM to sit in people’s own computers. DRAM is the memory chip Samsung makes.
Samsung set out the details in a statement on its Korean newsroom. The presidents came from its electronics, finance and biotech affiliates, and met Altman at Samsung’s training centre in Yongin, south of Seoul.
Inside the Samsung session
The talk ran under the theme of how AI will change the next ten years, and what companies should choose to do. Samsung’s presidents and Altman looked at where AI technology is heading and how it can be used, Samsung said. They also traded views on the new markets and business opportunities it could create.
They discussed how AI will change decision-making and the way organisations run, and what skills managers will need, the statement said. Samsung did not publish anything Altman said, and it did not name the Samsung executives in the room.
Samsung said the session was part of its training for presidents. Its view is that a company’s strength in the AI era comes from its managers’ judgement and execution, so the presidents are meant to lead by learning AI themselves.
Before meeting Altman, the presidents took a hands-on generative AI course, their second after one in June. They used AI to sort scattered management documents into their own “knowledge repository”, and practised using AI in decisions, Samsung said.
Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee reported that Altman is the latest American tech leader to visit South Korea. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and AMD’s Lisa Su have each visited twice since last year to strengthen supply ties, Bloomberg reported.
Samsung’s ties to OpenAI
Samsung Electronics and OpenAI signed a letter of intent on AI infrastructure in October 2025, Samsung said. Since then, Samsung has worked to supply memory chips for OpenAI’s Stargate data centre project.
Under the same agreement, Samsung SDS is to work with OpenAI on AI data centres and AI services for businesses. Samsung C&T and Samsung Heavy Industries are developing floating data centres together. Samsung Electronics chairman Lee Jae-yong visited OpenAI’s San Francisco headquarters in July, the statement added.
In June, OpenAI said Samsung Electronics would roll out ChatGPT Enterprise and Codex to its employees in South Korea and in its global Device eXperience division.
Samsung has been bringing AI into research, production, marketing and support work since June, it said. Each affiliate has its own AI team. About 2,300 executives have been trained so far, and all employees are due to finish AI training by February 2027.
What Altman said about DRAM
Altman made the remark to Stripe co-founder John Collison on Collison’s podcast, Cheeky Pint, released on Thursday. TNW covered the episode when it came out, leading on his plan to point OpenAI’s robots at building data centres.
Collison asked why high prices for memory and chips had not yet brought more supply. Altman said memory makers were now “each going to make like $100 billion of free cash flow in a year”. Their history of near-bankruptcy from building too many factories keeps them careful with spending, he said.
He then turned to people who want to run AI models on their own machines.
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now,” Altman said.
Those people expect open-source models to run on their own computers. They think data centres will then need less, he said.
“From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time,” Altman said.
“You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment,” he said.
Many people’s intuition is the opposite of that, he added.
A market short of memory
SK Hynix said this week that memory shortages will last to 2030. Samsung posted a record quarterly profit on AI memory demand on Thursday. Apple chief executive John Ternus has called the shortage a crisis, TIME reported.
Later in the episode, Altman said the cost of chips and energy should fall. For that to happen, he said, supply has “got to go way up”.

Get the most important tech news in your inbox each week.

articles.title: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
articles.text:
“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”
Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts
You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.
“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”
“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”
“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”
“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”
If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.
There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”
There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.
“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”
The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.
“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”
How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).
“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”
“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.
“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.
“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”
Geoghegan worries that the harm of being bombarded with unwanted political texts isn’t just that people get annoyed, but that they stop engaging civically as a result. “Having this surveillance apparatus that invades people’s privacy and really annoys them actually pushes people away from this,” she says. “I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”
Unfortunately, you might get on some political text lists whether you engage in the civic process or not because of data brokers. Murray says the best long-term solution to minimize these spam messages is to limit how frequently you give out your phone number in general, like in an online shopping portal. If you need to give a number, you might consider using a VoIP number like a free Google Voice number, so at least you can silo those messages into another app you don’t need to frequently check or get notifications from.
Murray says she rarely gives out her personal number and limits where she gives out her Google Voice number, too. But even she has seen an uptick in political texts over the past couple of weeks. That’s likely in part because some groups may try to dial numbers in order in a certain area code, or her number could still be floating around on lists from long ago. “You can’t really do anything about the people or the businesses or the political entities that you have already shared your number with in the past,” Murray says. “But I would encourage people to just draw a line in the sand.”
Murray and Geoghegan encourage consumers to take the actions available to them to help limit the unwanted texts they receive, but they say the real solutions to the broader issue will likely come from Congress or regulators. Geoghegan says greater enforcement of existing laws could limit robocalls and texts, and Murray says concerned voters could contact their representatives about putting more pressure on the FCC to address the problems.
“Don’t get just frustrated with what you can’t change in four days, but you may be able to make a difference for the future,” Murray says. “By all means, reply to a text and say, ‘Stop.’ … But just don’t make it your life’s quest because it’s probably a fool’s errand.”

articles.title: OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round
articles.text:
OpenAI is seeking to raise up to $20 billion in a new funding round, CNBC confirmed on Saturday, paring back its earlier target of up to $30 billion.
The funding round is still in progress and has not closed, so the figures are subject to change, a person directly familiar with the deal told CNBC, asking to remain unnamed as they were not authorized to discuss the details publicly.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Financial Times first reported that OpenAI had reduced its target for the round by $10 billion, and said the company would seek a post-money valuation of $1.25 trillion. According to FT, the ChatGPT developer set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the newest round, with some investors opting to reduce their allocations.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, as CNBC previously reported.
News that the ChatGPT developer slashed its funding round follows a week when investors asked whether big tech firms' spending on AI, especially to build out data centers and snap up GPUs, will deliver adequate returns.
AI-linked stocks sank on Friday, with chip maker Intel down 25% on lackluster revenue guidance, Micron down 5.5%, and Nvidia falling 4%.
Microsoft, Alphabet's Google and Amazon have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts last week that came in below analysts' estimates.
Alphabet saw its worst trading day ever on Thursday after its search revenue fell short of expectations. Philipp Schindler, the company's chief business officer, said the impact on search was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode.

articles.title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
articles.text:
A federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejudice President Donald Trump's amended defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter from the president to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
District Court Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump had again failed to plausibly allege the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025.
"As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which came more than six months after he dismissed Trump's first version of the suit. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."
By dismissing the suit with prejudice, the judge blocked Trump from filing another suit alleging the same claims about Murdoch and the paper in federal court.
Gayles said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation," and he rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.
The judge did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter. Trump has adamantly denied writing it.
When Galyes first dismissed the suit in April, he allowed Trump to file an amended version of the complaint to cure legal defects the judge had identified.
Trump was seeking $10 billion in damages from Murdoch and the Journal, which is owned by Murdoch's News Corp.
A spokesperson for the newspaper's publisher, Dow Jones & Co., in a statement to CNBC on Saturday, said, "We're pleased with the court's decision."
A spokesman for Trump's legal team confirmed to CNBC that the president plans to appeal the ruling.
"President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," the spokesman said in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."
Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending the letter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."
Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to Supreme Court decisions that Gayles cited at the beginning of his ruling.
Trump's amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told the president "I will handle it" during a phone conversation they had about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature, Newsweek previously reported.
Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and that the article was published after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.
Gayles said that accepting that last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.
Saturday's ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media.
Another federal judge in Miami on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The Journal's article on July 17, 2025, said a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday.
The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.
The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker."
"A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article.
"The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.
Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'
"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

articles.title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
articles.text:
SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday.
The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis.
The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.
The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026.
The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby."
(SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)
The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit.
Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.
The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."
The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses are now covered, plans to resume withdrawals Sunday
articles.text:
Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday.
Separately, the FBI said late Saturday that it has determined North Korea was responsible for the theft.
Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.
"All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users."
The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.
Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.
Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement.
It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place.
The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
North Korea responsible for theft
The FBI said malicious North Korean actors laundered Binance's stolen assets by converting them into Ethereum. The agency expects that the thieves will convert the digital assets as they prepare them for "further laundering stages."
TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, had initially pointed to North Korean hackers as the culprits.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.
— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report.

articles.title: Stocks started the week with promise but ended in despair. Our take on the big reversal
articles.text: It was a Jekyll-and-Hyde kind of week in the market. Wall Street's enthusiasm for artificial intelligence stocks proved short-lived. A promising week early on gave way to sharp back-to-back selling after a run of disappointing tech earnings. The Nasdaq had climbed more than 2% through Wednesday before losing 1.4% on Thursday and nearly 3% on Friday. The tech-heavy index lost 2% for the week and sank 5.3% for October. The S & P 500 followed a similar pattern, culminating in a nearly 2% decline Friday and a similar loss for the week. The broader market index fared better for the month, only losing nearly 1%. The rotation out of tech and into defensive stocks showed up the most in the Dow , which fell less than 1% for the week and actually gained 1.7% for the month. Semiconductor stocks staged a sharp rebound before renewed concerns about the AI trade sent shares tumbling. It didn't help that expectations remained high for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December. While central bankers held rates steady Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh talked tough on inflation, signalling it's only a matter of time before another hike. The prospect of higher rates only exacerbated investor worries that tech companies may be borrowing too much in the race to keep building out AI. Here's a closer look at the three developments that drove last week's market. What reversed the chip stocks Monday started the week off strong. Anthropic's IPO filing helped reignite enthusiasm for the AI group, while SK Hynix's record quarterly profit on Wednesday reinforced confidence in strong memory demand. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) surged roughly 9% over the first three trading sessions. But the rally fizzled as disappointing Big Tech earnings revived concerns about AI spending. Intel added to the pressure with a weak outlook Thursday evening that sent shares plunging more than 28% on Friday, making it our worst performer of the week. We cut our price target and placed our rating under review. Jim Cramer said Friday that he can't rationalize selling Intel after such a big decline. Portfolio director Jeff Marks summed it up in the Homestretch: "The data center story at Intel is still mostly intact, but what we got wrong was the sharp drop in personal computer CPU demand due to the high cost of memory and some execution hiccups." Wall Street's AI priorities changed Earnings from Microsoft , Alphabet , and Amazon reinforced a shift in sentiment: Investors are increasingly prioritizing financial discipline and a line of sight to returns on AI investments over aggressive spending. Microsoft delivered strong results Wednesday, with Azure revenue growing 48% and capital spending coming in below expectations. Shares initially rallied before giving back their gains, but Jim praised management's ability to deliver robust cloud growth while keeping spending in check. We raised our price target to $580 from $550 and maintained our hold-equivalent 2 rating . Microsoft shares only fell 0.5% for the week, certainly a win considering how bad tech performed. Alphabet faced a much harsher reaction. Shares plunged roughly 12% on Thursday, the day after the Google parent missed earnings and revenue expectations and reported negative free cash flow. Strong cloud growth wasn't enough to offset disappointing advertising results and concerns about its massive AI investments. Alphabet was our second-worst performer of the week, down 12.6%. While still encouraged by its cloud business, we were not ready to buy the dip . Amazon also disappointed Thursday evening , missing earnings and revenue expectations as weaker retail and advertising results overshadowed accelerating growth at Amazon Web Services. Shares fell 1.4% on Friday, which was pretty considering it was down over 6% at session lows. Investors scrutinized the company's negative free cash flow and next year's big capital spending plans. AWS remains a bright spot, with revenue growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. Just after Friday's opening bell, Jim said, " I think you buy Amazon here ." For the week, Amazon lost 3%. Winners (and one loser) away from pure tech Eli Lilly surged more than 6% to a record high Thursday after another beat-and-raise quarter fueled by strong demand for its obesity and diabetes drugs. The stock extended its gains on Friday, making it our second-best performer of the week, up more than 11%. Healthcare was the best sector for the week as the flight from tech benefited more defensive names. We raised our Lilly price target to $1,500 from $1,300 and maintained our hold-equivalent 2 rating after the stock's impressive run. Despite issuing a softer-than-expected current outlook, FedEx shares rallied Thursday and Friday as investors focused on the company's progress improving efficiency and profitability under CEO Raj Subramaniam. Jim said Friday he still sees FedEx as a buy but might not chase it right now. The stock gained nearly 5% last week. FedEx Freight performed even better, surging nearly 15% on Friday and nearly that for the week. In its first official earnings report as a standalone company, Freight topped expectations. Encouraging commentary on pricing and operational improvements made the less-than-truckload stock our best performer last week. We continue to prefer FedEx over its former subsidiary, but both reports reinforced our confidence in their long-term strategies. Linde and Starbucks also delivered encouraging results. Linde posted record quarterly sales and profits , supported partly by semiconductor demand, while Starbucks reported stronger-than-expected profits and comparable sales growth as CEO Brian Niccol's turnaround gained traction. Jim called Starbucks a buy during Friday's Morning Meeting. For the week, Starbucks rose nearly 3%, and Linde gained 1%. GE Vernova initially struggled despite delivering a beat-and-raise quarter Wednesday and announcing a $9 billion acquisition of grid equipment maker Trench Group. Investors appeared concerned about the pace of gas turbine order growth next year, but we believe the reaction overlooked strong underlying demand. GEV is not a pure-play AI stock but is tied to the data center build-out. But the electrification opportunity is looking promising. The Trench deal supports that. GE Vernova rose more than 5% last week, clawing back nearly half the prior week's decline. Moving from the winners to our third-biggest loser last week. Boeing tumbled more than 10% Tuesday after management pushed back its timeline for reaching $10 billion in annual free cash flow to 2029, overshadowing a record $745 billion backlog. While the recovery is taking longer than expected, we view the guidance reset as a potential clearing event . We maintained our buy-equivalent 1 rating but lowered our price target to $225. For the week, Boeing lost nearly 9%. (See here for a full list of the stocks in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust.) Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: I house sit year-round and live in NYC for $800/month: 'I love the freedom this lifestyle gives me'
articles.text:
Every time I tell someone how I live, I inevitably get the same question: "Wait, you can actually do that?"
I started house-sitting in 2023 as a way to save money while I was traveling. A year and a half ago, I decided to make New York my home base. I spend about 85% of my time here, but I've never paid any rent to live in the city, because I house sit all year round.
In 2026, so far, I've spent about $4,000 on travel expenses — including planes, trains, buses, subways and Ubers — and any fill-in accommodation I need between house sits. I pay $19 per month for my phone and spend about $75 per week on groceries. Without bills like rent, electricity or Wi-Fi, these are essentially my only consistent overhead costs. I'm spending about $800 per month.
House-sitting has completely transformed my life. I may not have a place of my own, and the structure of my calendar is unusual. But my life is rich in travel and all the wonderful people and animals I meet. To me, that's a pretty good trade.
My unexpected path to becoming a house sitter
Four years ago, I was about to turn 30 and my life looked really different. I had a 9-to-5 role working as a project manager in a real estate office in the San Francisco Bay Area. When the pandemic hit, my steady routine was completely upended.
At first it was freeing, but after a while it just felt like I was losing time. Ready for a change, in 2022, I did what many people would probably advise against — I quit my job and bought a one-way ticket to Italy.
My plan was to live off of my savings for as long as I could. I traveled throughout Europe, Southeast Asia and Central America for two years. During that time I spent roughly $50,000. I knew that my savings would eventually run out, so I started searching for ways to travel more economically. House-sitting seemed like a real possibility.
I was back in the Bay Area and living temporarily with my family when I did my first house sit in San Francisco. I found it through TrustedHousesitters, where I still find a lot of my bookings. It lasted for three days over a long weekend and I cared for one dog. I did five local house sits before I started traveling for them.
I quickly realized that I genuinely loved taking care of people's homes and, especially, their pets. Travel has long been a huge passion of mine, so knowing that I was helping someone else enjoy their own trip made me so happy.
If you want to become a house sitter, I also recommend starting local. It helped me get experiences and references in familiar surroundings before I jumped to places where I had to learn to do everything on the fly.
'Sometimes I move as many as eight times in a month'
A typical house sit for me can range anywhere from two to 30 days, although my average is around one week. During periods with shorter sits, sometimes I move as many as eight times in a month. The majority of my sits — about 80% — are unpaid and in exchange for housing.
When I do charge, my fee is generally $50 to $100 per day. My bigger expenses come when my bookings don't line up perfectly in my calendar. In the past year, I'd estimate it has happened around 10 to 12 times. When I have a gap, I have a few options. If it's just one night, I'll usually stay with a friend. If it's a few nights, I might book a hotel or Airbnb. If I have a longer gap, I'll often use it as an opportunity to travel somewhere else.
I'm definitely a budget traveler, and I'll always look for the best deal possible. But I'm generally not willing to sacrifice too much convenience to save money. I'm not taking flights at terrible times or booking two- or three-stop itineraries just to save $50. I still want to enjoy my travels.
The costs that don't show up in my bank account
Even though my overhead expenses are low, there are definitely costs to doing this that don't show up in my bank account. I love the freedom this lifestyle gives me, but it's definitely not for everyone. The biggest trade-off is the uncertainty and the need to be flexible.
I'm constantly planning where I'm going to live next and how I'm going to get there. Moving from one home to another means that I'm always adjusting to a new space, neighborhood, gym routine, pet care routine and trash pickup days.
Sometimes I'm booked months in advance. Other times, I'm figuring things out just a few days before a house sit begins. I've also had to deal with last-minute cancellations and unexpected changes. I devote a lot of time to figuring out my days. I spend hours planning and doing the administrative work required to set up my next house sit and make sure my bookings line up as seamlessly as possible.
Space is also not something I take for granted. I live out of a suitcase, so I have to be incredibly selective about what I buy and what I keep.
I get to live like a local all over the world
From my years of full-time travel, I'm used to figuring out where I'm going next, how I'm going to get there and where I'm going to stay. The difference is that now, instead of paying for accommodation, I usually have a home waiting for me.
Because I'm staying in these houses often for weeks at a time, I get to explore neighborhoods, develop routines and experience places more like a local than a tourist passing through. It can be lonely at times and I have to be proactive about building community. To expand my network, I make a point to meet friends of friends, put myself in social situations and simply say yes.
To date, I have done close to 100 house sits in 22 different cities around the world. This year, I have done house sits in Edinburgh, Los Angeles, Montreal, Philadelphia, San Francisco, and, of course, New York.
I know I won't be able to do this forever, and I would like to have a place of my own one day, but I don't have a time frame at the moment. In the future, I would like to be able to live in two to three cities throughout the year.
In the meantime, last year, I got a remote job working as a patient support specialist for a telehealth company. I can work from anywhere, so I'm not tied to one city. The regular change of scenery keeps remote work from becoming monotonous.
I love giving people peace of mind while they're on vacation or in another part of the world, knowing that their home is being looked after and their animals are cared for, safe and happy. It's wild to me that something I started as a way to save money while traveling has turned into a lifestyle and career. I know it sounds unconventional, and it definitely is. But I truly love it.
Alanna Parrish is a writer and a digital nomad who has turned house- and pet-sitting into a way to travel while experiencing new places like a local. She has completed sits in more than 20 cities and has visited over 40 countries.

articles.title: Binance, crypto and hacks: What to know about keeping coin safe as cyber criminals advance
articles.text:
For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression.
Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.
In a security update on Saturday, the exchange said it had replenished 90% of stolen assets and was committed to covering the remaining 10%. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea, but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack.
Understanding how crypto is protected online and what mechanisms exist to serve a role similar to insurance is increasingly important as more Americans invest in cryptocurrency.
Roughly one in five U.S. adults say they have invested in, traded, or used crypto, according to Pew Research Center, a figure that is even higher among upper income households (27%). The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy.
While Binance was making good on its pledge in the aftermath of the hack to cover all losses with its SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users) and other company's funds — and that there's no evidence of a wallet private-key leak in this incident — Nikolas Behar, a cybersecurity expert and professor at the University of San Diego, said crypto investors need to understand when using crypto platforms that a pledge is just a pledge "until there's an actual payout."
If something happens to your crypto, most consumers are left to navigate a patchwork of options that vary from exchange to exchange and are often very ambiguous. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong.
Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance."
Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said.
Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so."
"Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said.
"Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone.
Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack.
"When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute.
Storing your own digital currency
Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach.
"The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. But he added that the details of this hack point to a larger problem.
"Binance says no keys were leaked. The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one.
"On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death.
"Moving savings off an exchange trades one kind of risk for another. It does not remove risk," Tanguma said.
The chances of getting money back after a crypto hack
Sarah Downey, executive vice president and global blockchain and digital assets advisory leader at Lockton, an insurance brokerage, said other factors also come into play in determining whether you can get your crypto back, including how quickly the theft is discovered, where the funds were moved, whether the exchange or wallet provider has insurance that covers the event, and whether it holds enough reserves to repay customers.
"Some companies have set up FDIC-like insurance or other backstops, but whether these pay out depends heavily on the facts of each case. Even without insurance, many exchanges try to repay customers from their own reserves to protect both their customers and their own reputation," Downey said.
Crypto exchange reimbursements have followed other security compromises, such as after rogue overseas support agents were bribed to help scam Coinbase customers in May 2025. Bitget, another major exchange, had to tap an in-house fund to reimburse customers after a $388 million hack in September. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said its User Protection Fund, which held more than $464 million, covered the loss. "The Protection Fund was created for moments like this and absorbed the financial impact of the incident," Chen said in a post on X at the time.
By comparison, Binance's emergency reserve, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, is estimated at roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, and excluding the funds that were frozen, this represented about one-third of the loss. The company said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds and already held more than $5 billion in corresponding token assets.
Downey said the steps to take if your crypto is hacked depend on whether investors self-custody or use a third party, such as a regulated exchange.
"If they use a third party, they should check that most funds are stored offline or protected with multi-party computation. An investor's own funds should also be stored separately from the exchange's own funds," Downey said, adding that customers should also understand how the custodian authorizes transactions and governs storage.
Ryan Reck, founder and principal of Reck Advisory, an independent cybersecurity advisory firm, points to the lack of oversight of crypto.
"Crypto has no undo button. Once a transfer confirms, there's no chargeback and no one who can reverse it," Reck said. In some cases, stolen funds can be frozen by an exchange that receives them, or by a stablecoin issuer at a specific blockchain address, but tracing the money and getting it back are two different things.
Among the common reasons investors cite for making crypto investments is diversification away from traditional assets, as well as use of crypto as a digital version of gold, investing in the decentralization of finance theme, and betting that as more institutions adopt digital currencies, that will serve as a tailwind. And there's of course also speculation. Today, there are ways to invest in crypto that don't require holding the underlying currency in a wallet, such as exchange-traded funds, including the iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), which has over $62 billion in assets, or the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), which has over $15 billion in assets. There are also diversified crypto index ETFs holding a basket of top digital currencies, including the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index Fund (BITW) and the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF (GLDC).
For investors who want to hold crypto directly, Reck says that before trusting any platform, ask four questions:
- What's covered?
- What's excluded?
- How much coverage exists for all customers combined?
- Do I have an enforceable right to be repaid?
"'Insured' is where the conversation starts, not proof your money is protected," Reck said.
—CNBC's Jenny Lee contributed reporting

articles.title: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
articles.text:
Leaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under $1,000 or move slightly larger balances into an IRA. Taking the money in cash and moving on can feel like the simplest option, but it can have short- and long-term financial consequences.
A system backed by major 401(k) administrators aims to make it easier for those savings to follow workers to their next job. New research from one of those companies, Vanguard, shows it's helping fewer people cash out — although most of the money has yet to reach workers' new retirement plans.
Among workers with less than $1,000 in their 401(k), the share who cashed out within 10 months of leaving their job fell to about 9% from roughly 50% after their employers began participating in a new system called the Portability Services Network, according to the Vanguard research. Among those with balances of between $1,000 and $7,000, the share cashing out fell to 31% from 39%.
Portability Services Network is a coalition of large 401(k) administrators — including Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and Alight Solutions, among others — in conjunction with Retirement Clearinghouse and has been in operation since late 2023.
How it works: When a worker with a small 401(k) balance leaves an employer that participates in the network, the money is generally automatically rolled into a safe harbor IRA, where it remains until the network matches it with the worker's new employer plan. The balance then gets rolled into the new 401(k) from that interim IRA. The catch, however, is that the receiving employer must also participate in the network for the money to move to the next employer's plan.
In Vanguard's research, just 6% of accounts that have been transferred into IRAs as part of this automatic portability network successfully made it to a new employer's plan as of early 2026, largely because few employers have opted in. The rest generally remained in those interim IRAs, waiting to be matched with another employer plan that participates in the network. While workers can always roll over the money into their new 401(k) themselves, the point of the network is for it to happen automatically.
Of the roughly 220,000 outbound rollovers involving Vanguard participants analyzed, the median balance was just $200, and nearly three-quarters involved less than $1,000. The typical saver affected was 31 years old, earned about $20,000 annually and had worked for their employer for roughly six months, according to the research.
The cash-out analysis is based on workers at 83 employer-sponsored retirement plans administered by Vanguard that have adopted the automatic portability.
Financial consequences of cashing out
Typically, when you part ways with an employer, you can leave your money in its 401(k) plan if the account value is above $7,000. Balances under $1,000 usually result in the plan cashing you out and mailing you a check. For amounts between $1,000 and $7,000, most plans roll the balance over to an IRA if the former employee takes no action to move it themselves.
Cashing out a 401(k) when leaving a job, whether done by an employer or the employee, can have lasting financial consequences. Workers who withdraw their savings can owe income taxes on the money and may face a 10% early withdrawal penalty if they're younger than 59½. They also lose the opportunity for that money to grow over time.
Most workers — 84% — have changed employers at least once during their careers, while 53% have switched three or more times and 27% have made at least five moves, according to a new study from Empower, a 401(k) recordkeeper and a founding partner of the portability network. The report is based on an online survey of 2,005 adults.
Additionally, 50% of Generation Z respondents and 45% of millennials said they may have retirement savings from a previous employer that they've lost track of, the survey found. That compares with 30% of Gen X and 14% of baby boomers.
$71.3 million in assets have made it to new plans
Since the Portability Services Network's launch in November 2023, there have been 53,118 completed transactions, totaling $71.3 million in assets transferred from a previous employer plan to a new employer plan via automatic portability, according to Steve Holman, senior vice president of Portability Services Network strategy and development at Retirement Clearinghouse.
There are 23,787 plans that have adopted automatic portability, representing 7.73 million participants, Holman said. The overall estimate of participants in 401(k)s and similar workplace plans is about 96 million, he said.
There are 1.22 million eligible participants waiting to be matched with a new employer, up more than 25% since the beginning of 2026, Holman said.
Snags remain with the automatic portability process
Keeping the money in a safe harbor IRA can be better for investors financially than cashing out — but management fees may take a toll on small balances, especially when the money is in an interest-bearing cash account or other conservative investment.
"For many of these small accounts, earnings on the conservative default investment may not be sufficient to offset recurring account-level fees while the account remains unmatched, leaving the balance vulnerable to gradual erosion," the Vanguard study said.
Workers with Roth savings face another complication. If retirement savings are in a traditional 401(k) — funded with pretax contributions and taxed when withdrawn in retirement — it goes into a traditional IRA. Likewise, Roth 401(k)s, funded with after-tax contributions and withdrawn tax-free down the road, go into Roth IRAs.
However, IRS rules don't allow for a Roth IRA to be rolled into a new employer's 401(k), even a Roth 401(k).
"We are advocating for future legislation to allow for Roth dollars to be eligible for auto-portability — our technology can support it today," Holman said.

articles.title: In the wake of Weil, a legal recruiter's advice for surviving a company wind-down
articles.text:
It's hard to believe a corporate giant like Weil, Gotshal & Manges — a top 20 U.S. law firm that reportedly had over $2 billion in revenue in 2025 — could move toward ceasing operations just like that. But occasionally a Weil-like wind-down — or even a collapse like Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank or FTX — is bound to occur.
And here we are, seeing a major law firm move toward shutting down in real time.
The firm's management committee recommended that its partners prepare to close its doors after more than 90 years in business, Weil, Gotshal & Manges said on Wednesday. "Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm's Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down," the firm said in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday. "The partners are expected to vote in the coming days."
As a legal recruiter and former big law associate, I'm here to provide practical insights to the employees, lawyers and non-lawyers alike, who've just learned they're about to be out of a job — and those who are scared their company might be next.
First, let's be clear: From where I stand, Weil is an anomaly. But when a company does make headlines for winding down, or failing and shutting down, it's rarely the employees whose plight is highlighted: the people whose careers have been destabilized, whose anxiety shoots through the roof and who become the collateral damage of business decisions they had no idea were being made until far too late.
Here are my top tips, for both lawyers and non-lawyers, for when your company announces or is headed toward dissolution. In the case of Weil, it's advice I hope the firm's roughly 1,200 lawyers plus staff take to heart in the next 90 days.
1. Don't wait for the dust to settle
Yes, you can worry. Yes, you can grieve. But you should also mobilize quickly.
A lot of Weil associates are in a holding pattern right now: either waiting to see where their favorite partners are going and hoping they offer to bring them along, or thinking 90 days of pay, as reported by Reuters, means they have 90 days in which to start looking.
While many associates will eventually follow their partners, I suggest looking for a new job on your own while you wait. The market is absolutely inundated with Weil associates right now, on top of everyone else whose firm isn't dissolving but was already looking to make a lateral move. You don't want to be late to the party and find all your peers are ahead of you in line.
Partners are also under no obligation to bring you with them, and you have no say in where they choose to go. There's no guarantee it would be a good fit for you. It's best to have options and it's comforting to feel like you have some control over those options, especially in such uncertain times.
I'd give similar advice to non-lawyers. Don't wait too long. Options are always good. Be proactive. The people who tend to come out of these situations the least scathed are the ones who start looking before any announcement is made, in cases where the writing's on the wall and everyone else is still hoping for a last-minute save.
2. Don't act from a place of fear
Even as you move fast, try to be cautious. You don't want to be taken advantage of.
Just this week, I've counseled about a dozen Weil associates to do their homework, however quickly, before blasting their resume to every firm and recruiter on the block. Some recruiters — especially in the legal industry — will take you sending your resume as blanket consent to submit you anywhere they like.
But from what I've seen working in legal recruiting, if more than one recruiter sends your materials to the same firm, you're very unlikely to ever hear from that firm again. They see it as sloppy, bad form and too much of a headache to manage the inevitable fight over who's entitled to the hypothetical fee for your placement.
So keep a firm grasp on where your resume is at all times. You should know exactly which companies have it and who they got it from. If you plan to use a recruiter, pick a reputable and trusted one. Don't race to the first recruiter who cold calls you or the last recruiter in your inbox. Instead, get referrals from friends, set up intro calls with multiple recruiters to get a vibe check, pick one and only send that one your resume.
For non-legal folks, recruiting may not be so cutthroat. But I still recommend caution regarding how and where you share your information. Focus on trusted connections, including verifiable HR professionals at your target companies, friend and colleague referrals, your college career services office and known job boards. Be wary of answering outreach from questionable sources.
3. Don't worry so much about resume gaps or job hops right now
A short unemployment stint won't kill your career, and neither will multiple moves in quick succession.
When the unexpected occurs and the resulting job market frenzy ensues, sometimes, even when you mobilize early and wisely, you won't land a new job right away. Perhaps the only upside to the mass publicity of these surprise dissolutions is that every prospective employer is going to take one look at your resume and understand why you're out of work. They won't wonder what you did wrong, whether you got fired or if you're qualified.
But those favorable assumptions don't last forever. I'd give it one to six months. That's another plug for not waiting until a dissolution date to start your search, especially in the current job market, where as of September 27.1% of those who are unemployed have been searching for over six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Keep in mind too that job decisions made in haste or with your back against a wall are much more likely to end in a mismatch. Most people will take the first offer they get. Some will accept an unsustainable commute or a tyrant of a boss for short-term job security. And if it's your only option, that might be the right decision for you — we all have bills to pay and mouths to feed.
If that's the case, know it's also okay to move on quickly. I don't begrudge anyone who makes a job decision out of necessity and then course corrects when they're out of survival mode. And from my experience as a recruiter, neither will most future employers.
4. Be kind to yourself and others
None of this is your fault and all of it is horribly unfair. It's okay if you're feeling angry, terrified, overwhelmed, frozen, devastated or even a little relieved. Whatever you're feeling, both in the immediate aftermath and in the weeks and months after, is completely valid. Give yourself ample space and grace for whatever comes up and seek help and support.
On the flip side, lend a helping hand wherever you can, especially once you find a job, which I believe you will. Pay it forward by helping others who are still looking or looking again. Share a good resource, refer them to a trusted recruiter and connect them to any job opportunities you've passed up or heard about.
Corporations don't have feelings or loyalty to any given employee. But people do. We are nothing without our empathy and our communities. Hard times are when we need both the most.
Danielle Thompson is a legal recruiter and former big law employment lawyer based in the Bay Area. A managing director at Damato Search Group, she holds a J.D. from Columbia Law School and a B.A., magna cum laude, from UC Santa Barbara.
