articles.title: 35-year-old took on $20K in debt to launch a business from her dining room—now it brings in 8 figures a year
articles.text:
Set Active CEO Lindsey Carter used to lose sleep, cry to her friends and struggle to be present in her personal life after a rough day at work.
It's not that she expected entrepreneurship to be easy. Carter took on $20,000 in personal credit card debt and filled her Los Angeles home with inventory when she started the athleisure company in May 2018, she says. Yet years of obstacles — familiar to many an entrepreneur — followed as she tried to break Set Active into a crowded activewear industry. It took her time to figure out how to separate her professional stress from her personal life.
"I started understanding that struggle wasn't necessarily a sign that something was going wrong. Sometimes it's just the reality of building something ambitious," says Carter, 35. "And if I was going to let every setback rob me of my happiness, I'm going to be spending a very long time being unhappy."
Set Active is no industry giant, but it brought in eight figures in 2025 net sales and is profitable, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. That comes as growth in the broader activewear market has slowed: Women's activewear spending in the U.S. increased 2% between October 2025 and September 2026, down from 7% over the preceding 12 months, according to data from market research firm Circana.
Activewear still makes up 30% of U.S. apparel spending, says Circana apparel industry analyst Kristen Classi-Zummo. Shoppers these days particularly gravitate toward casual outfits and loungewear, like sweatpants and sweatshirts, over more active items like leggings and sports bras, Classi-Zummo says. That's good news for Carter, who sells color- and pattern-filled clothing sets that aren't solely intended for workouts. Set Active's Instagram posts feature women sitting on pickleball courts or the banks of the Seine in Paris.
Before launching Set Active, Carter ran her own social media company. While shopping around Los Angeles, she struggled to find matching sets of workout clothes she could wear while running errands, meeting a friend for coffee or working from home. "Everything was like yoga poses and upside-down headstands, and I was just like, 'That's not me,'" she says.
Her business idea became more real when an associate connected her with a production professional, she says. She decided to order some samples, collected feedback from friends and drew directly on the products with a permanent marker at her dining room table before sending them back to the manufacturer's designers, she says.
Going into debt to officially launch the business was just the first among many obstacles while growing Set Active. Some were personal: Carter had two children after starting the company and has never taken maternity leave. She now calls that decision "probably one of the biggest mistakes I've ever made."
She experienced what she describes as symptoms of postpartum depression in 2023, and felt like "a horrible version of myself" while simultaneously running the startup. "I let people down. I let friends down. I let employees down and I just wasn't my best self."
Other challenges have been professional. In 2026, Set Active has struggled to consistently deliver orders to customers on time, says Carter. The reasons are varied, she says, declining to go into detail, and the stakes are high approaching the holiday shopping season.
On Oct. 19, Carter wrote on Instagram that Set Active would cancel its Black Friday and Cyber Monday product launches until further notice. The company won't "drop" any clothes until the products arrive in the company's Los Angeles warehouse, putting a projected $10-plus million in sales during the most popular shopping days of the year at risk, she wrote.
"I'm walking away from a hefty revenue number," Carter now says, adding: "But at the end of the day, I built this brand on transparency and community, and the customer comes first to me always. And I'd rather make it right with the customer than hit a revenue goal."
A hard workday can still make her toss and turn at night, but she's learned how to return home to her family feeling grateful, she says. She gets satisfaction from solving problems and doing a job she believes in, she adds.
"I just take things day by day with the mindset that challenges are opportunities, and I don't really see them as the enemy," says Carter. "I think that when you sign up to be an entrepreneur, you're signing up for what that journey is going to bring."

articles.title: Crypto industry pours more than $200 million into 2026 midterms to pressure Congress on favorable rules
articles.text:
The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country.
Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen. Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle.
The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress.
Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities.
The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada.
Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global.
Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets. That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023.
Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC.
"The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC.
"In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said.
The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures.
Shifting voter priorities
The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread.
Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July.
"Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million.
Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty.
"It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods."
A test of influence
November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington.
The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown, a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat.
Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown.
A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%.
"A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023.
This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate.
Lynaugh told CNBC one of the reasons the group endorses candidates is because of their legislative record.
"We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added.
Money well-spent?
Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets, and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake.
Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return."
Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States.
Alderoty noted that the industry has gotten clearer rules from both the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures and Trading Commission. He also pointed to advancements for the industry from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, noting that Ripple received final OCC approval this week to charter Ripple National Trust Bank, a federally supervised national trust bank.
But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing.
Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January.
"You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said.
Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence.
"Every stakeholder needs to stay at the table and to continue to make the case why legislation is needed," he said.
If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation.
"Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC.
"It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added.
— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

articles.title: Intel stock plunges 29%. Analysts urge caution on buying the dip
articles.text: Should investors take advantage of the plunge in Intel to pick up shares? Many Wall Street analysts advise staying on the sidelines, with no clear consensus on when Intel may regain momentum. The stock took a massive hit on Friday, declining 29% to about $65 a share, its worst one-day performance since 1974. It was a painful slide for a stock that had been up about 150% this year prior to a third-quarter earnings report that raised doubts about the pace of Intel's turnaround and operating results. Intel beat third-quarter earnings estimates but reported revenue slightly below consensus. Investors were particularly disappointed with weakness on the personal computer side, given high memory chip pricing. Intel also revealed supply and production problems on the server side, holding back its growth in a hot area. Intel's fourth quarter revenue guidance also came in below consensus. The results prompted multiple downgrades on Wall Street with Bank of America, Roth Capital Partners and Seaport Research Partners all downgrading the stock to neutral from buy on Friday. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs maintained their neutral ratings but lowered their price targets on the stock while New Street upgraded Intel to buy from neutral. Intel now faces a double whammy: weak demand for personal computer chips and lack of capacity to produce enough server processors to capitalize on the artificial intelligence buildout. INTC YTD mountain Intel, YTD Analysts see a path to improvement but disagree on whether investors should buy before a recovery takes hold. Intel's sell-off was "quite overdone," said analyst John Vinh told CNBC. He thinks "there's a buying opportunity here" because he believes Intel's problems are temporary. Yet others like Seaport's Jay Goldberg recommend staying on the sidelines. In the near-term, the company "clearly has planning and capacity issues, which they need to grapple with," he said. "Until they do, it's kind of dead money. I think it trades flat for a while." Part of the problem, Goldberg said, is that the company made too many PC chips during a sharp downturn and too few server chips to meet booming demand. He attributed the mismatch to "bad planning assumptions" and difficulty getting "all the components they needed." Goldberg believes once Intel fixes capacity issues, "they'll be in good shape." The strength in server demand was evident in Intel's results. Data center and AI revenue rose nearly 80% year-over-year to $7.3 billion, exceeding expectations as demand was strong across hyperscalers, enterprise and neocloud customers. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company expects industry server CPU units to grow 30% in 2026 and 2027, a figure that "would be higher in both years if additional industry supply were available," he said, suggesting that growth is capped by supply rather than demand. Some analysts say it may be best to wait for the chipmaker to resolve production problems holding back growth. Management blamed the stalled momentum in its data center segment, which was impacted by an explosion at a fab plant in Israel earlier this month. Intel also warned the PC slump would last into next year. If Intel can bring on "incremental capacity in the second half of next year, things could start moving in the right direction," KeyBanc's Vinh said. Looking ahead to the second half of 2027, "server CPU capacity should come online for them," Vinh said. On PCs, he explained, corrections typically last a couple quarters. He sees the business stabilizing in the second quarter with "some level of recovery in the second half from natural restocking." KeyBanc's Vinh tempered his bullish take by noting the market "needs to think about evaluating Intel on 2030 numbers." That's when he expects the domestic foundry business to become a meaningful contributor. If investors look at the company through the lens of 2027 figures it's "clearly expensive." Even firms that downgraded Intel see longer-term promise. Bank of America acknowledged the company's ability to develop a foundry, noting "any signs of traction potentially driving a recovery in a relatively under-owned stock." Roth Capital Partners also praised Intel's "continued data center growth and increasing custom data center business." Following Intel's drop, the U.S. government's 433 million share stake shed about $11 billion in value, according to CNBC analysis. However, thanks to the low average purchase price of $20.47 per share, the stake remains up about $20 billion overall. The government's ownership offers little reason on its own to buy the dip, according to both Vinh and Goldberg. For Goldberg, Intel's next few quarters need to bring tangible improvement in capacity before the stock becomes a buy. While it may take a while, Intel can "get supply up to where it needs to be," he said in a note. "We think the company will sort itself out but see no reason to own the stock while management sorts itself out."

articles.title: How to start an art collection on any budget
articles.text:
The decision to invest in any collectibles market should start with curiosity and love, and buying art is no exception. While the rarest works of art in the world have sold for hundreds of millions of dollars, for most collectors, art is unlikely to match the returns offered by traditional investment markets.
A recent analysis of 10-year annualized returns including data through 2024 showed that the stock market vastly outperformed art. True, it has been an incredibly strong bull market on a historical basis, but the performance from the art market over the same time period produced some of the worst 10-year returns in seven decades.
As with any asset class experiencing a downturn, some experts see the recent weakness as a buying opportunity. The 2025 market did see some improvement, and 2026 has been an ever better year to date, with younger buyers showing up in a big way. But experts also stress that the art world is the least transparent market imaginable, with significant "insider information" involved in anticipating big jumps and the next major wave of hype.
"What I tell people is that there is so much inside information in the art world — for instance, who has bought a particular artist or who is getting a museum show in two years — that if you are an outsider, you have little hope" of catching the next big wave early, said Canice Prendergast, economics professor at the University of Chicago, who also oversees that Chicago Booth School of Business Harper Center's contemporary art collection, which houses more than 650 artworks.
It is important to understand that generating a repeatable investment strategy can be difficult — if not impossible.
"Most art is not a good investment," said Magnus Resch, who teaches art economics at Yale University and is widely recognized as a leading art market expert. "If you're buying on a limited budget, you're unlikely to see a financial return," he said.
Still, despite the complexities and opacities associated with art, experts advise that for anyone wishing to enter the market there are some basics to understand — from how to research art, to the various mediums, to what to buy at various budgets, and where to buy — before getting started.
Learn about galleries, auctions, and how artist values rise
Prendergast said a fundamental understanding of the market begins with knowing it is divided in two. The primary art market consists of galleries and the secondary market is typically auctions. And significant increases in value typically occur as art moves from one level of gallery to another and finally to auction.
"It's in anticipating moves between levels that most of the action is," Prendergast said. "There are many collectors trying to work out who is going to turn into a star [and] the key intermediaries here are galleries," he added.
Buying in the primary market first requires the squishy "knowing something about art," he said, but also understanding the hierarchy of galleries. The big moves happen as relatively undiscovered talents appear in galleries that have a history of discovering and elevating artists. Inside such jumps — from a lower tier gallery to a mid-tier one — there can be big, embedded returns.
Prendergast gave as one recent example mid-tier gallery David Fierman in New York City that showed artist Louis Fratino several years ago. Fratino's work jumped to New York-based mega-gallery David Zwirner, and is currently featured in a London show. Along with that jump came a 20x increase in the price of Fratino's paintings. Such moves, Prendergast said, are precisely the type of play investors dream about, but the reality is that they take a long time to unfold and are exceedingly hard to predict.
"The thing that people overlook is actually mid-career artists," Prendergast said. "My advice would be to go to a major art fair – at every art fair, the galleries they put in the corners are the up-and-comers," he said.
Keep it local as a beginning collector
Resch says that the difficulties in the art market should not necessarily discourage new collectors. Rather, they need to enter the market with clarity of purpose, as well as realistic expectations and aims. "Buy art you love from local galleries, artists you discover on Instagram, or art fairs where artists exhibit directly," he said. The limited possibilities for investment success can actually emphasize other, more essential advantages to the endeavor: "Assume you'll never see your money again. You're not investing for financial returns. You're investing in yourself, the artist, and the gallery," he added.
Roman Kräussl, professor of finance at the Bayes Business School in London who specializes in art as an alternative asset class, says that when it comes to art, the greater opportunity is to engage with culture than to beat the market.
Kräussl's research-based conclusion is that for the most actively engaged investors, art will provide a lower risk-adjusted return than financial market investments, but it can still be a positive return, and it can serve as a hedge against financial market risk. But when considering all the costs and fees associated with buying art, he says picking "winners" is critical.
Buyer's premiums, shipping, insurance, framing, storage if necessary, and resale fees, all factor in the overall return on investment.
This offers another reason to stick to the galleries and fairs over auction houses, since the atmosphere involves more opportunities for social interaction with other collectors and even the artists themselves. "Art is the most illiquid, nontransparent, opaque investment you can engage with. But it is also tons of fun," Kräussl said.
The enrichment is more likely to be to yourself as a person, not to your bank account, with the big payoffs coming from "intellectual, cultural, and human-relevant perspectives."
"You will meet the most interesting people of your life," Kräussl said. "Do not 'Spotify' art," he said. "Go to small events. See the artists. Experience. And if you like, go for it. If not, search further. But do not wait for someone to tell you what to buy. Develop your own taste," he said, "and then trust it."
How to invest on a $5,000, $10,000 and $100,000 budget
Traditional mediums still dominate in the art market.
Painting remains the most popular medium for collectors, according to the 2026 Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting, which focuses on the high-net-worth end of the market, surveying 3,100 collectors across 10 markets. That is measured by both participation (76% of buyers) and value (31% of total fine art expenditure). Sculpture was the second-largest area of spending (15%), followed by works on paper (10%) and digital art (9%).
But that may not necessarily be the best place to start for everyone, and one point emphasized by multiple experts is that the smarter plays happen in the less-hyped areas. Hype can drive extreme pricing disparity and inflation, and it is often evidence that there has already been movement behind the scenes that preceded all of the hype. In other words, hype may indicate already being too late to the table.
Another way to approach the art market, according to Resch, is through a focus on prints and editions — multiple, authorized copies of an artwork from an original source — which he says are often overlooked. "They offer access to blue-chip artists at a fraction of the price," he said.
That contrasts with investments in emerging artists, which can be riskier. "An artist can sell out every gallery exhibition and still have virtually no resale market," he said, "so don't believe in popularity. Instead, check if an artist has an auction market."
Resch says for any individual "willing to gamble at $5,000," he would look for prints or works on paper by blue-chip artists, ideally at auction.
At $10,000, he says original works in contemporary art day sales at major auction houses are an option, though works of art on auction at these events can start at much higher prices.
At $100,000, Resch says the focus can turn to artists represented by leading galleries who have exhibited at major museums. "I'd rather buy one exceptional work for $100,000 than five mediocre ones for $20,000 each," he said. But no purchase should be made without doing considerable homework: "Visit galleries, research artists, and compare gallery and auction prices. People compare prices when buying a $500 television. Why wouldn't they do the same when buying a $50,000 painting?"
Georgina Adam, editor at large for The Art Newspaper and a lecturer at Sotheby's and Christie's in London, said liking a piece remains an essential criterion, especially at lower price points and in areas of the art market that aren't particularly strong. That can lead to buying prices that are lower, but the ability to resell will also be very difficult, she said, adding that many pieces in 19th-century painting, as well as antiques, silver, and porcelain, feature these dynamics. "While it is a sum, $10,000 is not life changing if you lose it, but from the higher price points up, then readers will at least want the art to hold its value."
Higher price points are also more typically associated with the benefit of auction records and clearer research to track pricing, provenance, and resales, according to Adam.
How to research the art market and choose advice sources
Whatever you buy, "Don't buy on a whim," Adam said. "Study the artist first."
Such study can occur with the assistance of a trusted advisor, but even taking on an advisor takes research, Adam said, who is herself a member of the Association of Professional Art Advisors.
She also cautioned that while specialists at auction houses and dealers will be knowledgeable, they all have "skin in the game."
"Look for dealers who have a proven track record, and belong to a professional association with a code of ethics. Inclusion in a well-known fair (Frieze, Armory, et cetera) is a sign of seriousness," she said. "Fairs enable the buyer to look around in a less pressured environment and get prices. Galleries will generally be happy to talk about their artists," she said.
One platform she strictly advises serious collectors to avoid is eBay. "Don't buy art from eBay, unless you just want a poster that goes with your décor. There are plenty of bad actors out there. Remember that fakes can be accompanied by fake certificates of authenticity," Adam said.
Christoph Noe, the co-founder of Larry's List, which covers the current art collectors market, said direct relationships with artists, studio visits, making collections public, and openly rejecting hype and FOMO (fear of missing out) buying are all important practices for collectors. "Notably, not one collector in our listing mentioned TikTok, YouTube or LinkedIn as relevant to their collecting practice/research," he said.
According to the Art Basel/UBS report, most collectors did their own research before buying, with 72% undertaking moderate or significant research, and that figure rising to 80% among Gen Z collectors. The most commonly used external sources of advice were auction house experts (31%), art advisors (30%), artists (29%), and dealers (27%).
Digital research is being used more often, according to the Art Basel/UBS data, with 58% of respondents using digital resources for advice, led by online publications and press (27%) and apps or AI tools (22%, up from just 4% in 2024). And despite Noe's comments, social media is becoming more influential: 32% of collectors cited either Instagram or X/Twitter as sources of advice, according to the Art Basel/UBS report.
While most experts emphasize in-person research and interaction as critical to the collecting process, collectors surveyed in the Art Basel/UBS report were broadly positive about AI's role in finding and buying art, with 67% saying AI made a positive impact on artist and artwork discoverability; 66% citing it for personalized advice and recommendations; 65% on provenance and authenticity verification; and 64% on pricing and valuation analysis.
"The biggest mistake investor collectors make," according to Prendergast, "is their belief that 'I just know this is great art.' You don't. You cannot evaluate a piece of art without knowing what came before. The art market is also very professionalized in that a good MFA can often copy pretty much anything. So just because something looks nice does not mean it's of much monetary value," he said.
When it comes to properly researching art, there is no replacement for getting out into the world.
"Get a double espresso in a nice gallery, stay for a glass of red wine, meet the artists, participate," Kräussl said. "Buy your first piece, risk it, and you will have something interesting to say at the next dinner."
Kräussl says he concludes all of his art-finance presentations and seminars with the same piece of advice that he would give to a dinner party guest: "'Buy what you like!' After all, they may have to live with it for the rest of their life," he said.

articles.title: Trump promised to slash energy costs — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
articles.text:
President Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office.
"My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign.
"Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon."
But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
"Prices have never been this high this late in the year," De Haan said.
Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year. The price of diesel, critical to transportation and agriculture, has surged about 70% over the past year, to $6.32 a gallon.
During the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, the year that Russia invaded Ukraine and triggered an energy crisis, retail gas prices stood at $3.80, according to AAA data.
Own goal
"Trump got in his own way," De Haan said. "Back in December, we predicted that 2026 was going to be the cheapest year for gas since 2020. That required no effort. And obviously, it hasn't gone that way."
Fuel prices have spiked since Trump decided to attack Iran in a joint attack with Israel on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with a wave of strikes on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, severely depressing oil flows through the vital shipping route.
Trump told voters at a rally in Michigan last Sunday that rising fuel prices are a "small price to pay" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The White House said gas prices when adjusted for inflation have been higher around previous election days.
Exports through Hormuz have rebounded since the summer as the U.S. military helped ships through the strait. But the Middle East disruption has been compounded by Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi Arabian refineries, and Ukraine's strikes on refineries in Russia. Trump had promised to end that war in the first week of his second term, but the conflict is stuck in an intractable stalemate.
"Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth," ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday after the nation's largest oil company posted huge profits thanks to the disruptions.
Airlines have hiked their fares to cover high costs from jet fuel, their biggest expense other than labor, hurting the fight to contain inflation.
Political pressure
Trump came under political pressure from Republicans to take action on fuel prices ahead of Tuesday's election. The cost of diesel is hurting big farm states like Iowa that have overwhelmingly backed Trump in his presidential campaigns. The senate race in the Hawkeye State has become competitive.
Trump briefly contemplated a diesel export ban as Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) lobbied to help the state's farmers. The president decided against it because it might also have raised gasoline prices.
Instead, Trump issued an executive order to allow truckers to use tax-exempt, offroad diesel on U.S. highways, and announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Trump later struck a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to export about 6 million barrels of diesel into the global market through November.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and even some Republican senators slammed the agreement as rewarding Russian aggression. Energy analysts said the diesel volumes in the Russia deal are small compared to global demand and won't have a meaningful impact on prices.
More recently, crude oil prices have rallied ahead of the election. Trump has said he will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterms. But the market is pricing in the risk of another round of fighting after voting ends on Tuesday. International Brent crude oil prices are up more than 13% in October and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 15%.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," De Haan said, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."

articles.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety
articles.text:
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange.
A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents.
Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens.
Questions over the safety of users' funds
"I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place."
For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure.
There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore.
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan, CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this."
Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
Vulnerabilities on offshore platforms
A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note.
"They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today."
Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X.
"Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach, though the company didn't specify what they were.
A unique target in a changing landscape
Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack.
Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach.
It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure.
"I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said.
"Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added.

articles.title: Berkshire ekes out some new highs, but October rally stalls
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire ekes out some new highs, but October rally stalls
Berkshire Hathaway shares managed to set a few more all-time highs in an otherwise lackluster week of trading.
The Class A stock closed Monday at a record high $821,931 but ended the week up just 0.3% at $815,600.
It spiked at Friday's open to almost $822,929, but that wasn't enough to top its record intraday high of $824,765 set on Thursday of last week as Berkshire entirely erased what turned into a 15% pullback after Warren Buffett announced last year that he would step down as the company's CEO.
The more widely held Class B shares also set a new record high close on Monday, finishing that day at $548.56.
But their high during Friday's session of $550.47 is enough for a new all-time intraday record, edging out last Thursday's $549.96.
For the week, however, they inched less than 0.1% higher.
Despite losing some steam this week, Berkshire shares are ending October with strong gains, especially when compared to the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite.
The latter index lost 2.9% Friday, its worst one-day drop since June, as money moves away from high-flying AI and tech stocks over spending concerns.
Berkshire appears to be benefiting from the back-to-basics rotation.
It's closing out the month with an 8.9% gain, as the S&P fell 0.9% and the Nasdaq dropped 5.3%.
BRK.B trimmed its year-to-date deficit against the benchmark S&P from 3.5 percentage points last week to 2.8 percentage points this week.
As shown in the "Berkshire Stock Watch" chart below, it's ahead of the S&P over the past 12 calendar months by more than two percentage points.
AI jitters cut Berkshire's bet on Alphabet by billions
While Berkshire's stock is benefiting from Wall Street's move away from AI stocks, one big holding in its equity portfolio is taking a substantial hit.
Google parent Alphabet's market value fell by around $500 billion Thursday as the stock plunged almost 13%, its worst day since going public in 2004.
The company's third quarter earnings report late Wednesday included negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, more than triple the $2.7 billion analysts had expected, raising concerns among investors about the enormous cost of building out AI infrastructure.
At the same time, revenue from web searches missed estimates for the second straight quarter, in what CNBC.com is calling the "first real sign AI is taking a bite" out of Alphabet's core business.
Berkshire's enormous Alphabet stake, initiated by Buffett last year and boosted by a $10 billion private placement during this year's second quarter, hit a Q3 high of $40 billion in early August.
Since then, it's lost a quarter of its value, falling to $29.6 billion Friday, making it Berkshire's fourth largest equity holding.
(That's based on the number of shares held as of June 30. The values in October may change based on Berkshire's September 30 portfolio snapshot that will be released in two weeks.)
Coca-Cola has moved decisively into third place, with the position increasing by almost 16% from a low of $32.5 billion in late July to $37.6 billion now.
Barron's estimates Berkshire likely paid more than $300 a share for Alphabet, and "perhaps close to $320," putting it in the red for the investment, at least so far.
DaVita holding trimmed again under deal to keep percentage stake steady
In an SEC disclosure this week, Berkshire said it sold $69 million of DaVita shares on Tuesday.
The remaining 28.3 million shares of the dialysis provider in its portfolio are worth $5.3 billion.
Don't interpret the reduction as sign Berkshire has changed its view of the company.
This is the latest in a series of quarterly share reductions under a 2024 agreement with DaVita in which Berkshire agreed to keep its stake in the company at 45% or lower.
As DaVita reduces its outstanding shares through buybacks, Berkshire needs to also cut its holdings to keep the ratio intact.
DaVita shares are up 65% year-to-date despite a one-week drop of more than 23% in August when the company released disappointing earnings just days before Berkshire's previous trim under the pact.

HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Robinhood takes advantage of 'gambling instincts' (2021)
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the popular Robinhood trading app, accusing it of encouraging its customers to make short-term bets on stocks and options. Munger calls it "deeply wrong."
BECKY QUICK: This question comes from Robert Miles in Nebraska.
"The trading apps. What do you think about Robinhood and other trading apps, or fintech companies, enabling all ages and experience to participate in the stock market?"
WARREN BUFFETT: (Laughs) Well, I'm looking forward to reading the S-1 on Robin — that's the big thing you file with the SEC when you're going to be offering securities, and —
It's — you know, it's become a very significant part of the casino aspect — of the casino group — that has joined into the stock market in the last year or year and a half.
And I do want to say I'm concerned of how they handle the source of income when they say they don't charge the customer anything. I mean, you know, I'm — it'll just be interesting to watch how they describe it. I mean, but —
But they — they have attracted — maybe set out to attract — but they have attracted, I think I read where 12 or 13% of their casino participants were dealing in (option) puts and calls.
I looked up on Apple, you know, the number of seven-day calls and 14-day calls outstanding. And I'm sure a lot of that is coming through Robinhood. And that's a bunch of people writing — they're gambling on the price of Apple over the next seven days or 14.
There's nothing, you know — there's nothing illegal about it. There's nothing immoral.
But — I don't think you'd build a society around people doing it. I mean, if a group of — a group of us landed on a desert island, and we knew we would never be rescued, and I was one of the group, and I said, well, I'll set up the exchange over here. (Laughs) And I'll trade our corn futures and everything around —
I think — I think the degree to which a very rich society can reward people who know how to take advantage, essentially, of the gambling instincts of the — not only the American public — worldwide public — it's, you know, it's not the most admirable part of the accomplishment.
But I think what America's accomplished is pretty admirable overall. (Laughs)
And I think actually, you know, American corporations have turned out to be a wonderful place for people to put their money and save. But they also make terrific gambling chips.
And if you cater to those gambling chips when people have money in their pocket for the first time, and you tell them they can make 30 or 40 or 50 trades a day, and you're not charging them any commission, but you're selling your order flow or whatever, it —
I hope we don't have more of it, I'll put it that way. And I will be interested in reading the prospectus.
Charlie?
CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, that is really waving the red flag at the bull. (Laughter)
I think it's just God-awful that something like that would draw investment from civilized men and decent citizens. It's deeply wrong.
We don't want to make our money selling things that are bad for people.
WARREN BUFFETT: But we've got the states doing it with the lottery, you know.
CHARLIE MUNGER: No, but that's bad, too.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, I know. I understand, but I'm saying —
CHARLIE MUNGER: That's very bad. That's very bad —
WARREN BUFFETT: Once you —
CHARLIE MUNGER: That's one of the things that's wrong with it. It's getting respectable to do these things.
The states are just as bad as Robinhood.
WARREN BUFFETT: Well, in a sense they're worse. I mean, they're really taxing the —
CHARLIE MUNGER: I know it's — I know, I know.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. They're taxing hope.
CHARLIE MUNGER: Not only that —
WARREN BUFFETT: And they don't get much in the way of taxes from me and Charlie than they do —
CHARLIE MUNGER: The states in America replaced the Mafia as the proprietor of the numbers game. That's what happened.
WARREN BUFFETT: Yep.
CHARLIE MUNGER: They pushed the Mafia aside and said that's our business, not yours. Doesn't make me proud of my government.
WARREN BUFFETT: When I was a kid, my dad (Howard Buffett) was in Congress. They had a numbers runner in the House office building (laughs), actually.

articles.title: Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at restarting direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, source says
articles.text:
Qatari mediators have held talks with Iranian officials in an attempt to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran, an official source familiar with the discussions told CNBC on Saturday.
Iran promised a "geographically unrestricted response" to any new attacks by the U.S.
Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday to reach a deal to avoid a possible resumption of American-led attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Axios first reported the talks, which it said are set to continue in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Saturday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there are no plans to meet U.S. officials, adding that an Iranian delegation has headed to Qatar for talks with mediators, Qatari media outlet Al Jazeera reported.
"What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation," Al Jazeera quoted Araghchi as saying.
A preliminary agreement signed on June 17 between the U.S. and Iran to halt the fighting — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian targets — broke down weeks later.
On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to." Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.
The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran occurred on Sept. 1. Trump previously left open the possibility that attacks on Iran would resume after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which are set for Tuesday. Tehran has said it is preparing a military response to any U.S. strikes.
A statement posted on Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's Telegram account Saturday said that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Shipping attacks continue
The Iranian Broadcasting Agency quoted a Hormozgan province official as saying Saturday that U.S. forces attacked two fishing boats off Masan near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The report has not been independently confirmed.
U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
It's the latest report of attacks on shipping in the economically crucial stretch of water.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported Friday that a crude oil tanker was hit by an unknown projectile as it was heading out of the strait.
Separately, Iran said Friday four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.
Oil prices jumped more than 2% on Friday and settled at their highest levels since the end of April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the war.
Brent crude futures for December, which expired on Friday, settled up $2.76, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43.

articles.title: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
articles.text:
The next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software.
That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI, still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade.
"We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors.
Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes.
Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill.
For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers.
"We work on a model that is not dissimilar from Uber, where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked.
Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably.
"And then we track what happens," Joyce said.
Confused agents
Mayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop.
But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window."
The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete.
"Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution."
Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and even CAPTCHA tests intended to fend off bots from sites.
"I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks.
Chatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works.
Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test using human contractors to handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process."
Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests.
Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies.
Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant.
"We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them."
Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people.
"We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.

Bộ Công Thương vừa thông báo điều chỉnh giá bán các mặt hàng xăng, triển khai Nghị quyết số 45/2026/NQ-CP ngày 31/10 của Chính phủ quy định về thuế tiêu thụ đặc biệt đối với xăng.
Theo đó, xăng E5RON92 có giá bán không cao hơn 24.223 đồng/lít, giảm 1.804 đồng/lít so với giá bán tối đa hiện hành; Xăng E10RON95-III không cao hơn 24.159 đồng/lít, giảm 1.575 đồng/lít so với giá bán tối đa hiện hành
Sau điều chỉnh, giá bán tối đa của xăng E10 RON95-III thấp hơn xăng E5 RON92 là 64 đồng/lít.
Thương nhân đầu mối kinh doanh xăng dầu, thương nhân phân phối xăng dầu thực hiện điều chỉnh giá bán nhưng không muộn hơn 0h ngày 1/11/2026.
Đợt điều chỉnh diễn ra khi thuế suất thuế tiêu thụ đặc biệt đối với các loại xăng được đưa về 0% theo Nghị quyết số 45/2026/NQ-CP. Chính sách có hiệu lực từ ngày 1/11/2026 đến hết ngày 31/3/2027.
Về Quỹ bình ổn giá xăng dầu, Bộ Công Thương tiếp tục áp dụng mức trích lập và chi sử dụng đối với xăng sinh học đều bằng 0 đồng/lít, thực hiện từ 0h ngày 1/11.
Theo số liệu so sánh của Bộ Công Thương ngày 31/10, giá xăng tại Thái Lan tương đương 32.550 đồng/lít, Campuchia 32.010 đồng/lít, Lào 48.276 đồng/lít và Trung Quốc 36.125 đồng/lít. Bộ Công Thương cho biết Thái Lan, Campuchia có chính sách trợ giá, còn Trung Quốc khống chế giá. Với mức giá mới không cao hơn 24.159 đồng/lít đối với E10 RON95-III, giá xăng Việt Nam ở mức thấp so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Bộ Công Thương cho biết sẽ phối hợp với các cơ quan chức năng kiểm tra, giám sát trách nhiệm bảo đảm nguồn cung xăng dầu của các thương nhân kinh doanh, xử lý nghiêm các hành vi vi phạm.

articles.title: ‘Pop-up’ super PACs pour $637 million into 2026 midterm races
articles.text:
A super PAC called Our Heritage Matters registered with the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 15.
Five days later, it began spending to boost third-party candidates and attack Republicans. By Oct. 29, the group had spent about $1.2 million across 10 House and Senate races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
What voters still cannot see is who supplied the money.
Because Our Heritage Matters formed after a key campaign finance reporting deadline on Oct. 15, its first regular report identifying its donors is not due until Dec. 3, a month after Election Day.
The group is an extreme example of a broader surge reshaping the midterm election: late-forming super PACs, including the latest-forming "pop-up PACs," pouring money into races before voters know where it came from.
Federal law requires super PACs and political committees to report large independent expenditures within 24 or 48 hours depending on how close to Election Day the spending occurs, showing how much they spent and which candidates they supported or opposed. Their donors, however, are disclosed less frequently through periodic campaign finance reports.
And in 2026, the practice of creating new, last-minute PACs has exploded. Both parties are using the tactic, with Republican-linked PACs spending about twice what those connected with Democrats have disbursed.
Twenty-two super PACs that registered with the FEC during the final 10 weeks before Election Day have each spent at least $1 million on congressional races, according to CNBC's analysis. Together, they had reported roughly $637 million in independent expenditures by Oct. 29 — about one-sixth of all independent spending reported in House and Senate races this election cycle.
The number of million-dollar late-forming super PACs has more than quadrupled since 2022, while their spending has grown nearly 35-fold.
At the same point in the 2022 midterms, just five comparable groups had spent about $18 million combined, according to CNBC's analysis. In 2018, three had spent about $12 million. The total has even eclipsed the past two presidential elections, when comparable late-forming super PACs spent less than $50 million combined on congressional races in both 2020 and 2024, according to CNBC's analysis.
"The reason for this is almost entirely to avoid disclosure, even if just temporarily," said Michael Kang, a Northwestern Pritzker School of Law professor who studies campaign finance. "Many times, if the donors were known, then it would undercut their cause."
CNBC's analysis includes super PACs formed in the final 10 weeks before Election Day that spent at least $1 million on House or Senate races by Oct. 29. Spending includes regular FEC filings and 24- and 48-hour reports, with duplicates removed.
From zero to millions in late-forming PAC spending
One of the defining features of late-forming super PACs is speed.
Among the 22 groups in CNBC's analysis, 18 began spending within 30 days of launching, and almost all started spending before filing their first regular campaign finance report showing where their money came from.
“It’s happening more often, and they’re spending more money doing it because it works, and they’re getting away with it,” said Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the Campaign Legal Center. The group is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by a former Republican FEC chairman.
Despite their late start, the groups accounted for more than 22% of independent expenditures in congressional races during CNBC's 2026 window, up from less than 2% at the same point in each of the previous two midterms.
Many are new only on paper. CNBC found financial or organizational ties between nine of the 22 groups and established political networks.
Lower Costs Now, for example, formed on Sept. 10 and disclosed an affiliation with the Future Forward PAC, the main outside group that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign. Nineteen days later, Lower Costs Now began spending in Senate races.
But voters did not get a fuller picture of its financing until Oct. 15, when its first regular financial report showed that Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect Senate Democrats, had given the group $23 million, according to FEC filings.
By Thursday, Lower Costs Now had reported about $75.5 million in independent expenditures across eight Senate contests, including Iowa, Texas, Kansas and Ohio, according to CNBC's analysis.
Republicans have used the same playbook.
No Going Back PAC formed Sept. 1 and began spending three days later. Public reporting soon linked it to MAGA Inc., President Donald Trump's marquee super PAC. But its formal financial report did not arrive until Oct. 20 — more than six weeks after the spending began.
By then, No Going Back had already spent roughly $187.8 million, according to FEC filings, which revealed that MAGA Inc. had supplied the group with $200 million. By Thursday, the super PAC had spent roughly $242.2 million, according to FEC filings.
“They are a vehicle designed to emerge from nowhere and spend a bunch of money on an election” before voters can learn “who’s supplying that money and what their motivations might be,” Ghosh said.
PACs built for one race
Many of the new groups are also narrowly targeted.
Fourteen of the 22 million-dollar super PACs identified by CNBC spent all of their money in a single congressional contest.
Take The Maine Standard. It formed Sept. 11 and began spending five days later. Since then, it has spent $8.2 million, all of it opposing Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, according to FEC filings.
The Cornhusker Majority followed almost the same pattern. It formed Sept. 10, began spending Sept. 16 and has spent about $7.1 million in Nebraska's Senate race, almost all of it opposing independent Dan Osborn, according to FEC filings. Osborn is running against Republican incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts in a tight race.
The connection between the two groups did not appear in their regular financial reports until Oct. 15: Both were financed by Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC.
On the Democratic side, Texas Forever launched Sept. 24 and began spending five days later, according to FEC filings. By Thursday, it had spent about $27.5 million to help Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, according to the FEC. Unlike some other pop-up groups, however, its initial FEC filing identified the Senate Majority PAC as an affiliate.
"A locally branded PAC doesn't necessarily hide where the money comes from, but it fragments the picture. Instead of seeing one national organization spending tens of millions of dollars across the country, voters see a series of different groups operating race by race," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks such spending.
But even identifying the national group behind a pop-up PAC can still leave another layer of the money trail hidden.
Texas PAC formed Aug. 28 and soon began spending to help Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race. The money flowed through the SLF, but Elon Musk's role was not public until Oct. 12, more than a month after the spending began.
On Oct. 15, FEC filings showed Musk had given the SLF $158 million in two contributions, with the group transferring matching amounts to Texas PAC the day after each donation.
By Oct. 29, Texas PAC had spent about $181.6 million in the race, according to FEC filings, making it one of the largest late-forming super PACs CNBC identified.
Together, Texas PAC and No Going Back accounted for roughly two-thirds of all spending by the 22 million-dollar groups. But the surge was much broader than those two giants: Even excluding them, the remaining groups spent nearly 12 times as much as comparable late-forming super PACs did at the same point in 2022.
"The growth is huge this year," Kang said. "Maybe you don’t want to be known this election, or want to hide away for a period while you might be unpopular, like AI is right now, but you kind of want to build a reputation for the players inside the system."

articles.title: Viết một dòng trạng thái trên Facebook, chàng thủ khoa được Olympia mời làm vòng nguyệt quế suốt 12 năm
articles.text:
Viết một dòng trạng thái trên Facebook, chàng thủ khoa được Olympia mời làm vòng nguyệt quế suốt 12 năm
Để hoàn thiện chiếc vòng nguyệt quế dành cho Quán quân Olympia 2026, nhà thiết kế Đỗ Vân Trí mất khoảng 4-6 tuần, trải qua nhiều công đoạn từ dựng mẫu 3D, đúc kim loại đến xử lý bề mặt.
Mỗi mùa Chung kết Đường Lên Đỉnh Olympia, bên cạnh cuộc tranh tài của 4 nhà leo núi, chiếc vòng nguyệt quế dành cho người chiến thắng cũng là một trong những chi tiết được khán giả mong chờ nhất.
Đứng sau chiếc vòng nguyệt quế đã trở thành biểu tượng này là nhà thiết kế Đỗ Vân Trí, người đã đồng hành cùng Olympia từ năm 2014. Với anh, mỗi chiếc vòng không đơn thuần là một món trang sức hay phần thưởng dành cho nhà vô địch, mà còn là câu chuyện về tri thức, nghị lực và hành trình trưởng thành của người trẻ.
Trận Chung kết Đường Lên Đỉnh Olympia năm thứ 26 sẽ diễn ra vào 8h30 sáng Chủ nhật, ngày 1/11/2026. Bốn thí sinh góp mặt trong cuộc tranh tài cuối cùng là Trần Võ Gia Bảo (Trường THPT chuyên Lê Quý Đôn - Đông Hải, Khánh Hòa), Lý Thái Dương (Trường THPT chuyên Hùng Vương, Phú Thọ), Nguyễn Huy Quang Minh (Trường THPT chuyên Thái Bình, Hưng Yên) và Đoàn Lê Anh Đức (Trường THPT chuyên Hà Nội - Amsterdam, Hà Nội). Một trong bốn nhà leo núi sẽ là chủ nhân của chiếc vòng nguyệt quế được nhà thiết kế Đỗ Vân Trí dành nhiều tâm huyết thực hiện.
Sáng tạo không phải là làm cho tác phẩm cầu kỳ hơn
Đỗ Vân Trí là nhà thiết kế trang sức và phụ kiện thời trang bằng kim loại. Anh tốt nghiệp thủ khoa ngành Thiết kế thời trang tại Đại học Quốc tế Hồng Bàng (TP.HCM). Trước khi tập trung vào công việc thiết kế, anh từng có thời gian làm trợ giảng tại các trường đại học, hướng dẫn đồ án tốt nghiệp cho sinh viên chuyên ngành Mỹ thuật công nghiệp.
Trong lĩnh vực thời trang, Đỗ Vân Trí từng thực hiện nhiều sản phẩm cho các đại diện Việt Nam tham gia đấu trường nhan sắc quốc tế, trong đó có mấn kim loại dành cho Hoa hậu Trương Thị May (2013) và Hoa hậu Phạm Hương (2015). Anh cũng là người đứng sau bộ sưu tập 6 đôi giày cao gót từng lọt vào "mắt xanh" nữ ca sĩ Lady Gaga.
Mối duyên đưa nhà thiết kế Đỗ Vân Trí đến với Olympia bắt đầu từ sở thích xem chương trình từ khi còn nhỏ. Anh kể mình từng đều đặn chờ đến cuối tuần để theo dõi các trận thi đấu, thậm chí có thời điểm ao ước được trở thành một nhà leo núi, đứng trên bục danh dự và đội chiếc vòng nguyệt quế.
Sau đó, trong một lần xem trực tiếp Chung kết năm, khi chứng kiến khoảnh khắc trao giải, anh bắt đầu chú ý đến chiếc vòng dành cho nhà vô địch và nảy ra ý tưởng muốn tự tay thiết kế một phiên bản mang dấu ấn riêng. Anh đăng tải mong muốn này lên trang cá nhân, không ngờ sau đó nhận được lời liên hệ từ ê-kíp Olympia.
Từ năm 2014, anh Đỗ Vân Trí bắt đầu thực hiện vòng nguyệt quế cho Chung kết năm và hầu như mùa nào cũng được chương trình tin tưởng giao nhiệm vụ. Nhìn lại lần đầu tiên nhận lời, anh vẫn nhớ cảm giác vừa vui mừng vừa lo lắng.
“Lần đầu tiên được chương trình mời thiết kế vòng nguyệt quế, tôi vừa mừng vừa lo vì không biết mình đủ sức gánh vác trách nhiệm này không, thiết kế ra sản phẩm có đẹp hay có được khán giả hưởng ứng tích cực hay không.
Tôi đã đồng hành cùng Đường Lên Đỉnh Olympia nhiều năm và luôn xem đây là một công việc rất đặc biệt. Điều khiến tôi tiếp tục nhận lời là mong muốn mỗi mùa mang đến một thiết kế mới với câu chuyện riêng”, anh kể.
Với NTK Đỗ Vân Trí, việc sáng tạo liên tục cho một biểu tượng đã quen thuộc với khán giả không đồng nghĩa với việc phải khiến chiếc vòng ngày càng cầu kỳ.
“Tôi không cố gắng tạo ra sự khác biệt chỉ để khác biệt, mà muốn mỗi thay đổi đều có lý do và phục vụ cho ý tưởng tổng thể. Sáng tạo không nhất thiết là làm cho tác phẩm cầu kỳ hơn qua từng năm.
Điều tôi hướng đến không phải là một chiếc vòng có quá nhiều chi tiết rườm rà, mà là tác phẩm đạt độ tinh xảo cao hơn, có sự ứng dụng, thay đổi và kết hợp nhiều kỹ thuật chế tác mới mẻ hơn”, anh nói.
4 lớp hoàn thiện, phủ lớp vàng thật 24K cùng câu chuyện về hành trình trưởng thành
Nếu vòng nguyệt quế năm 2025 có cấu trúc lá xếp tầng, kết hợp ngôi sao vàng năm cánh phía sau để nhấn mạnh tinh thần dân tộc và niềm tự hào Việt Nam, thiết kế năm thứ 26 lại lựa chọn một hướng tạo hình khác là những nhánh cây khô đan xen tự nhiên, không đối xứng hoàn toàn, trở thành nền để các lá olive non mềm mại vươn lên.
Ý tưởng chủ đạo của tác phẩm năm nay là “Sự sống được sinh ra từ những thử thách”. Nhà thiết kế muốn sử dụng hình ảnh đối lập trong tự nhiên để kể câu chuyện về quá trình trưởng thành của người trẻ.
“Những cành cây khô đại diện cho thử thách, những lá olive non mọc lên từ những cành khô tượng trưng cho thành quả của hành trình chinh phục tri thức. Sắc vàng của chiếc vòng là hình ảnh của niềm tự hào và sự tỏa sáng sau những nỗ lực bền bỉ, hào quang cho người chiến thắng”, anh Trí lý giải.
Lấy cảm hứng từ biểu tượng vòng nguyệt quế trong văn hóa Hy Lạp và La Mã cổ đại, nhà thiết kế vẫn giữ hình ảnh lá olive quen thuộc với Olympia, nhưng phát triển bằng ngôn ngữ tạo hình hiện đại và kỹ thuật chế tác của người Việt. Điểm anh tâm đắc nhất chính là sự tương phản giữa những cành cây khô và các lá olive mềm mại ánh vàng.
“Cành cây khô gợi nhắc đến những thử thách, những giai đoạn tưởng như không còn sức sống, còn những chiếc lá olive non tượng trưng cho thành quả được hình thành sau hành trình bền bỉ.
Trong học tập cũng như cuộc sống, chúng ta thường nhìn thấy thành công ở thời điểm cuối cùng, nhưng ít khi nhìn thấy hết những khó khăn và nỗ lực đã tạo nên thành công ấy. Tôi muốn vòng nguyệt quế năm nay gợi cho người xem suy nghĩ đó”, anh chia sẻ.
Sự thay đổi trong thiết kế cũng thể hiện quan niệm của anh Đỗ Vân Trí về chủ nghĩa tối giản. Theo anh, tối giản không phải là lược bỏ giá trị, mà là giữ lại những chi tiết thực sự cần thiết để câu chuyện được thể hiện rõ nét hơn, tinh tế hơn.
Để đưa ý tưởng ấy từ bản vẽ thành một tác phẩm kim hoàn, anh kết hợp công nghệ tạo mẫu 3D với kỹ thuật chế tác thủ công. Quy trình bắt đầu bằng việc phác thảo nhiều kích thước lá olive, dựng hình trên máy tính để kiểm soát tỷ lệ, đường cong và góc lá. Sau đó, các mẫu được in bằng sáp resin độ phân giải cao nhằm tái hiện những chi tiết nhỏ, đặc biệt là hệ gân lá.
Từ mẫu sáp, các bộ phận tiếp tục trải qua công đoạn làm khuôn, đúc kim loại rồi được hàn ráp thủ công thành từng cụm cành, cụm lá. Đây là bước quan trọng để tạo nên cấu trúc tổng thể vững chắc. Riêng phần cành cây được xử lý bề mặt bằng tay, tạo những đường vân ngẫu nhiên mô phỏng vỏ cây trong tự nhiên, tránh cảm giác quá cơ khí khi chuyển từ mô hình thiết kế sang kim loại.
“Khó khăn lớn nhất là làm sao để kim loại thể hiện được vẻ tự nhiên của những cành cây khô về đường vân, độ cong, điểm giao nhau và tỷ lệ. Nếu xử lý không khéo, sản phẩm rất dễ trở nên thô ráp hoặc mang cảm giác cơ khí”, anh nói.
Về chất liệu, vòng nguyệt quế năm nay vẫn sử dụng nền đồng thau, kết hợp công nghệ tạo mẫu 3D, đúc khuôn và kỹ thuật kim hoàn thủ công. Sau các công đoạn tạo hình, hàn ráp, chỉnh sửa và đánh bóng, sản phẩm được hoàn thiện qua 4 lớp xử lý bề mặt: đồng đỏ làm lớp nền, niken hỗ trợ tăng độ cứng và chống oxy hóa, vàng thật 24K tông vàng Ý tạo sắc vàng sâu, cuối cùng là lớp keo nano bảo vệ.
Sự kết hợp giữa công nghệ và thủ công giúp kiểm soát độ chính xác, tính đồng bộ và chiều sâu của từng chi tiết, nhưng vẫn giữ được dấu ấn nghệ thuật bởi chỉ một sai lệch nhỏ trong quá trình chỉnh sửa hoặc đánh bóng cũng có thể làm mất đi những chi tiết quan trọng của thiết kế ban đầu.
Toàn bộ quá trình từ lên ý tưởng đến hoàn thiện thường kéo dài khoảng 4-6 tuần. Tuy nhiên, phần tốn nhiều thời gian và tâm sức nhất với anh không hẳn là đúc hay mạ.
“Thực ra phần mất thời gian nhất không phải chế tác mà là suy nghĩ. Tôi thường dành khá nhiều thời gian để tìm một ý tưởng mới, phù hợp với tinh thần của năm đó và không lặp lại những gì mình đã làm ở các mùa trước.
Khi đã tìm được hướng thiết kế phù hợp thì các công đoạn kỹ thuật phía sau sẽ rõ ràng hơn. Với tôi, việc tìm ra câu chuyện của chiếc vòng quan trọng không kém việc hoàn thiện nó bằng kim loại”, anh nói.
Dù được tạo ra để trao cho nhà vô địch, anh Đỗ Vân Trí không muốn chiếc vòng chỉ gắn với khoảnh khắc đăng quang. Anh hy vọng vật phẩm này còn ghi nhận những nỗ lực của cả 4 thí sinh, bởi mỗi người đều đã trải qua một hành trình học hỏi và rèn luyện đáng trân trọng.
“Tôi muốn gửi lời chúc tới cả bốn em luôn giữ được sự bình tĩnh, tự tin và phát huy tốt nhất những gì mình đã tích lũy. Hãy bước vào cuộc thi với tinh thần tích cực và tận hưởng trọn vẹn khoảnh khắc đặc biệt này”, anh nói.
Với anh, người giành chiến thắng sẽ có một dấu mốc đáng nhớ, nhưng những kiến thức, bản lĩnh và trải nghiệm mới là điều các thí sinh có thể mang theo trên chặng đường phía trước bởi “Vòng nguyệt quế là đích đến của cuộc thi, nhưng không phải đích đến của tri thức”.
Nhà thiết kế Đỗ Vân Trí cũng mong những người trẻ không xem thất bại là dấu chấm hết, bởi khó khăn có thể trở thành bài học và nền tảng cho sự trưởng thành
“Dù các bạn có trở thành nhà vô địch Olympia hay không, tôi mong các bạn luôn giữ được tinh thần học hỏi, lòng tử tế và sự nỗ lực không ngừng.
Tri thức không chỉ có giá trị khi giúp một người đi đến đỉnh cao, mà còn vận dụng để tạo ra những điều tốt đẹp cho cộng đồng và xã hội. Và tôi tin rằng, mỗi người trẻ Việt Nam đều có thể trở thành một nhà vô địch trên hành trình của riêng mình”, anh đúc kết.
